It can be helpful to visualize the attention weight matrix to understand how relations are being made between words. This matrix contains weights that indicate how much focus or “attention” each element in the input sequence should give to every other element.
Visualizations of A typically take the form of heatmaps, where the intensity of the colors indicates the strength of the attention weights. This allows us to:

Trace how the model distributes its attention across the input.
Identify potential biases or shortcomings in the model’s focus.
Understand which parts of an input sequence are important to a specific word or token, revealing the model’s internal “reasoning” and how it processes linguistic structures or dependencies.

We’ll come back to this visualization once we have trained a model below (in Section 10), and have an A matrix that has some real meaning!




Imagine trying to understand a complex novel. You might focus on understanding the plot. But you may separately want to better understand a character’s development arc. Or maybe the book’s thematic elements. Real, complex text has many different, simultaneously occurring aspects. In machine learning models, especially in tasks as nuanced as language processing, there’s a wealth of information to be extracted from the data. Multi-head attention allows the model to look at its input from different perspectives (or “heads”), each focusing on different subsets of information, thereby enriching the model’s understanding and capabilities.
The essence of multi-head attention is to run several self-attention mechanisms (heads) in parallel, each with its own set of learnable weights, thereby allowing the model to simultaneously attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.


Multi-head attention simply applies the attention mechanism that we just talked about multiple times, using multiple different “heads”, then takes an extra step to combine them. Each head \(i\) follows the steps of self attention that we just outlined. Namely, for each head, we:

Apply separate linear transformations to the Query, Key, and Value matrices.
Perform the scaled dot-product attention.

Then, we:

Concatenate the attention outputs from each head.
Apply a final linear transformation to the concatenated output.

We can write this as:
\[
\text{MultiHead}(Q's, K's, V's) = \text{Concat}(O_1, ..., O_h)W^O
\]
Where each O here is as it was calculated above:
\[
\begin{align}
O_i &= \text{Attention}(XW^Q_i, XW^K_i, XW^V_i) \\
    &= \text{Attention}(Q_i, K_i, V_i) \\
    &= A_i \cdot V_i \\
    &= \text{softmax} (\frac{S_i}{\sqrt{d_k}}) \cdot V_i  \\
    &= \text{softmax}(\frac{Q_i K_i^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}) \cdot V_i
\end{align}
\]
as we saw above. Here,

\(W^Q_i, W^K_i, W^V_i\) are the learned weight matrices for the \(Q_i, K_i, V_i\) of the \(i\)-th head.
\(W^O\) is the learned weight matrix applied after concatenation.

So, multi-head adds this new matrix, \(W^O\), into the mix, whose job is to learn how to relate all of our different attention heads. This final transformation with \(W^O\) also ensures that the output from the multi-head attention mechanism has the same dimensionality as the input embeddings, so it can be passed on to subsequent layers in the transformer model.
This mechanism allows the model to look at the input from different perspectives simultaneously, improving the model’s ability to capture complex relationships in the data.



Ok so you might be thinking “multiple heads, and the attention calculation already relies on multiple matrices (Q,K,V) - surely this is getting to be an insurmountable amount of compute!”
And it would be, if we just ran \(\text{h}\) full-size attention operations (each on \(d_\text{model}\)-dimensional vectors). Instead though, each head operates on a slice of the embedding: \(d_k = d_\text{model} / \text{h}\) dimensions. So if \(d_\text{model} = 512\) and we use \(\text{h} = 8\) heads, each head works with 64-dimensional Q, K, and V vectors. The total work across all heads is roughly equivalent to a single attention operation on the full 512-dimensional space. The key is that we partition the representation instead of duplicating it.
This is why implementations enforce that \(d_\text{model}\) is evenly divisible by \(\text{h}\). It must be so that the embedding dimension can split cleanly into \(\text{h}\) equal pieces.

📌 Note: It’s important to keep the dimensions of everything straight here, and you might need a refresher for some things. Check Appendix 0 for a quick reference guide!

How it actually works in practice
The formulas above suggest that each head has its own separate weight matrices \(W^Q_i, W^K_i, W^V_i\), each of size \(d_\text{model} \times d_k\). And conceptually, that’s exactly right. But in practice, implementations do something mathematically equivalent that’s more efficient:
Step 1: Project with one big matrix, just the same as single-head. We apply a single \(W^Q\) of size \(d_\text{model} \times d_\text{model}\) to get a full-size Q matrix, and the same for K and V. This is identical to what we did in the Self Attention implementation above:
\[Q = XW^Q \quad \text{shape: } (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model})\] \[K = XW^K \quad \text{shape: } (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model})\] \[V = XW^V \quad \text{shape: } (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model})\]
Step 2: Reshape to split into heads. We then reshape each of these matrices to separate the \(d_\text{model}\) dimension into \(\text{h}\) heads of \(d_k = d_{\text{model}}/\text{h}\) dimensions each:
\[Q: \quad (n_\text{seq},\ d_\text{model}) \longrightarrow (n_\text{seq},\ \text{h},\ d_k)\]
No new computation needs to happen here, it’s just a reinterpretation of the same numbers. The first \({d_k}\) values of each row become head 0’s query, the next \({d_k}\) become head 1’s query, and so on.
This works because the single big \(W^Q\) of size \(d_{model} \times d_{model}\) is mathematically equivalent to \(\text{h}\) separate \(W^Q_i\) matrices of size \(d_{model}  \times d_{k}\) stacked side by side. The reshape just makes this partitioning explicit.

Let’s make this concrete. Say we have \(d_\text{model} = 6\) and \(\text{h} = 3\) heads, so \(d_k = 2\). After projecting, one word’s Query vector might look like:
\[q = [0.5, \quad 0.8, \quad | \quad 0.1, \quad 0.3, \quad | \quad 0.9, \quad 0.2]\]
When we reshape from \((d_\text{model})\) to \((h, d_k)\), it simply slices this into contiguous chunks:
\[\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.8 & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.9 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.8 \\ 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.9 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Head 0 looks at \([0.5, 0.8]\). Head 1 looks at \([0.1, 0.3]\). Head 2 looks at \([0.9, 0.2]\).

Does the order matter? At initialization, no. The weights are random, so which dimensions end up in which head is arbitrary. But during training, yes, the model learns to organize information so that dimensions within the same head are useful together. Head 0’s slice of \(W^Q\) might learn to produce queries about syntactic relationships, while head 2’s slice learns to produce queries about semantic similarity. The model figures this out on its own.
Step 3: Attention per head. Each head now independently computes scaled dot-product attention using its own \(d_k\)-dimensional slice of Q, K, and V - exactly the same self-attention we already learned, just on smaller vectors.
Step 4: Concatenate and project. We reshape back from \((n_\text{seq},\ h,\ d_k)\) to \((n_\text{seq},\ d_\text{model})\), which is just concatenating each head’s output side by side. Then we apply \(W^O\) (size \(d_\text{model} \times d_\text{model}\)) to blend the heads’ outputs together.
To summarize the full dimension flow (ignoring batch size for clarity):
\[X \xrightarrow{W^Q, W^K, W^V} Q, K, V \xrightarrow{\text{reshape}} \underbrace{Q_1, K_1, V_1}_{\text{head 1}}, \ldots, \underbrace{Q_h, K_h, V_h}_{\text{head } h} \xrightarrow{\text{attention}} O_1, \ldots, O_h \xrightarrow{\text{concat}} O_\text{cat} \xrightarrow{W^O} \text{Output}\]
\[(n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model}) \rightarrow (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model}) \rightarrow h \times (n_\text{seq}, d_k) \rightarrow h \times (n_\text{seq}, d_k) \rightarrow (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model}) \rightarrow (n_\text{seq}, d_\text{model})\]
The input and output are the same shape. The “multi-head” part lives entirely in the middle - the embedding is split, attended to from \(\text{h}\) different perspectives, and recombined.




At this point you might be wondering - if we don’t add any new parameters (aside from \(W^O\)), and the total amount of computation is roughly the same as single-head attention, what’s the point? We’re doing the same work, just split into smaller pieces. How does multi-head learn anything that a single large attention matrix can’t?
The answer lies in a fundamental limitation of single-head attention: the softmax bottleneck.
Single-Head Attention: One Softmax for Everything
Say we have a 3-word sequence with \(d_\text{model} = 4\). In single-head attention, we compute one attention weight matrix \(A\) of shape \((3 \times 3)\) - one weight per word pair:
\[A = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.3 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}\]
Each row is a probability distribution. Now, the output for word 1 is:
\[o_1 = 0.1 \cdot v_1 + 0.7 \cdot v_2 + 0.2 \cdot v_3\]
Here’s the thing to notice: \(v_1\), \(v_2\), and \(v_3\) are 4-dimensional vectors. Every single dimension of the output gets the same weights - 10% of word 1, 70% of word 2, 20% of word 3. Writing it out explicitly for each output dimension:
\[o_1[0] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[0] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[0] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[0]\] \[o_1[1] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[1] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[1] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[1]\] \[o_1[2] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[2] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[2] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[2]\] \[o_1[3] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[3] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[3] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[3]\]
The same 0.1, 0.7, 0.2 everywhere. All four output dimensions are forced to use the same blend of input words.
Multi-Head Attention: Multiple Softmaxes
Now take the same \(d_\text{model} = 4\) but split into \(\text{h} = 2\) heads, so \(d_k = 2\). Each head computes its own attention weight matrix from its own \(d_k\)-dimensional slice of Q and K. Critically, each head runs its own softmax:
\[A^{\text{head}_0} = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_0 K_0^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ \ldots \end{bmatrix}\]
\[A^{\text{head}_1} = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_1 K_1^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ \ldots \end{bmatrix}\]
These will generally be different distributions, because they’re computed from different slices of the projected Q and K. Now the output for word 1 is:
From head 0 (dimensions 0-1): \[o_1[0] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[0] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[0] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[0]\] \[o_1[1] = 0.1 \cdot v_1[1] + 0.7 \cdot v_2[1] + 0.2 \cdot v_3[1]\]
From head 1 (dimensions 2-3): \[o_1[2] = 0.6 \cdot v_1[2] + 0.1 \cdot v_2[2] + 0.3 \cdot v_3[2]\] \[o_1[3] = 0.6 \cdot v_1[3] + 0.1 \cdot v_2[3] + 0.3 \cdot v_3[3]\]
Dimensions 0-1 are mostly attending to word 2 (weight 0.7). Dimensions 2-3 are mostly attending to word 1 (weight 0.6). Different parts of the output vector are blending information from different words.
What’s Gained by Dividing Attention
In single-head attention, softmax acts as a bottleneck. No matter how rich the Q, K, and V projections are, everything gets squeezed through one probability distribution, and some of that richness is lost in that action.
You might think that having more dimensions contribute to that single softmax (the full \(d_\text{model}\) is much bigger than our \(d_k\)’s) would be an advantage. And it does give each score more information to work with. But one distribution can still only express one attention pattern. If word 1 needs to strongly attend to word 2 for some semantic purpose and simultaneously strongly attend to word 3 for some syntactic purpose, a single distribution can’t express that, and that’s a much bigger problem than having a full \(d_\text{model}\) of dimensionality is a potential advantage.
In multi-head attention, where each head’s softmax can specialize in a different type of relationship and each head controls its own slice of the output, different aspects of the representation can be built from different attention patterns. What you lose in “focus” on one aspect by having only \(d_k\) dimensions instead of \(d_\text{model}\) is more than made up for by getting to put that focus in more places.
What This Looks Like in Practice
In trained transformers, different heads demonstrably learn different roles. Some attend to the immediately previous word. Some attend to syntactically related words (like a verb attending to its subject). Some attend to semantically similar words. Some learn specific positional offsets. This specialization emerges naturally from training - the model discovers it’s useful to partition its attention into different purposes.
A single head couldn’t express all of these patterns simultaneously. Multi-head allows the same number of parameters to act much more usefully.



Below is an implementation of the multi-head attention mechanism in PyTorch. It reuses some of what we already wrote in the SimpleSelfAttention class that we built above to apply multi-head attention instead, so many lines here will be repeated from there.

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, embed_size, heads):
        super(MultiHeadAttention, self).__init__()
        self.embed_size = embed_size
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_dim = embed_size // heads

        assert (self.head_dim * heads == embed_size), "Embedding size must be divisible by heads"

        # Linear layers for to get query, key, value, and out
        self.values = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.keys = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.queries = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)

    def forward(self, values, keys, query):
        N = query.shape[0]
        value_len, key_len, query_len = values.shape[1], keys.shape[1], query.shape[1]

        # learned projections
        values  = self.values(values)
        keys    = self.keys(keys)
        queries = self.queries(query)

        # split into heads
        values  = values.reshape(N, value_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        keys    = keys.reshape(N, key_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        queries = queries.reshape(N, query_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)

        # move the head axis up so each head holds a (seq_len, head_dim) matrix
        values  = values.transpose(1, 2)    # (N, heads, value_len, head_dim)
        keys    = keys.transpose(1, 2)      # (N, heads, key_len,   head_dim)
        queries = queries.transpose(1, 2)   # (N, heads, query_len, head_dim)

        # scores: Q @ K^T, per head -> (N, heads, query_len, key_len)
        attention_scores = queries @ keys.transpose(-2, -1)
        attention = torch.softmax(attention_scores / (self.head_dim ** 0.5), dim=-1)

        # weighted sum of values -> (N, heads, query_len, head_dim)
        out = attention @ values

        # merge heads back -> (N, query_len, embed_size), then mix with W^O
        out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(N, query_len, self.heads * self.head_dim)
        return self.fc_out(out)

Now, though a lot of this is similar to code we’ve already seen, multi-head attention is really THE key mechanism of the transformer, and as we’ll see through sections 3 and 4, gets re-used repeatedly when building the full architecture. So we’ll take a beat here to make sure we understand precisely what each line does.
The setup (__init__).
We start by setting up the dimensions of our MHA implementation. We need to define the embed_size (the dimension of the embedding actually going into the model - which is n_embeds, but as we discussed also d_model as this number is held constant) and the number of heads we want.
Then, we calculate the dimension of the heads from this number, and of course, must check that they are actually divisible.
def __init__(self, embed_size, heads):
    super(MultiHeadAttention, self).__init__()
    self.embed_size = embed_size
    self.heads = heads
    self.head_dim = embed_size // heads

    assert (self.head_dim * heads == embed_size), "Embedding size must be divisible by heads"
Then, we define the learned projections - W_Q, W_K, W_V, and the output projection W^O. Two things are worth noticing:

We do a single matrix multiplication, embed_size → embed_size, not embed_size → head_dim We are doing multi-head attention, so you might expect one projection per head. But as it turns out, since it’s mathematically identical to do all heads’ projections at once, in a single embed_size × embed_size matrix, then split the result afterward, and much more computationally efficient to do so, that’s what we’ll do. We’ll see this split happen later.
bias=False on all of Q/K/V These are meant to be pure linear projections. We use the nn.Linear built in to do these, which accepts a bias. But we just need the “regular” matrix multiplies here. A bias would add a constant offset that, in practice doesn’t buy anything, so it’s conventionally dropped. (fc_out, by contrast, keeps its bias, the default, which we’ll get to at the end.)

    self.values  = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
    self.keys    = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
    self.queries = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
    self.fc_out  = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
The forward signature.
Next, we need to define what a forward pass will do. The forward function takes values, keys, and query as three separate inputs, each shaped (N, seq_len, embed_size). N, the batch size, is something relatively new that we’re introducing here, which we’ll talk more about later. But we make sure we know what it is, and need it because we want to process multiple inputs at once.
Another thing to note here - this code tracks the sequence lengths: value_len, key_len, and query_len separately. While in our self-attention implementation, n_seq was always the same, because Q, K, and V were always being constructed for the same sequence, nothing requires that this be true. In fact, later in this tutorial, we’ll see an implementation of attention where that is explicitly not true - so this definition of different lengths just keeps that open. But more on that later!
def forward(self, values, keys, query):
    N = query.shape[0]  # batch size
    value_len, key_len, query_len = values.shape[1], keys.shape[1], query.shape[1]
Applying the projections.
The next step is then to apply the projections that we defined above. The first step of this, is then to simply use the Q,K,V projections on the queries, keys, and values we’ve passed in.
    values  = self.values(values)    # (N, value_len, embed_size)
    keys    = self.keys(keys)        # (N, key_len, embed_size)
    queries = self.queries(query)    # (N, query_len, embed_size)
Next, we do the “multi-head” split, which as we discussed, happens with pure reshaping. We take the embed_size vector, as if it were heads contiguous chunks of size head_dim. Then, head 0 gets the first head_dim numbers, head 1 the next, and so on. After these lines, each of values, keys, and queries have a new heads axis, so that for the remaining computations, the head slices travel through the computations on their own.
    values  = values.reshape(N, value_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
    keys    = keys.reshape(N, key_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
    queries = queries.reshape(N, query_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
Computing the attention scores.
Next, we need to compute attention scores. This is the first time that we’re doing more “real” math on our matrices, so let’s pause on two key syntax pieces first.


@ is matrix multiplication. For two 2D matrices it’s the ordinary matrix product: an (m × k) times a (k × n) gives an (m × n), and the inner dimensions, k, must match. For tensors with more than two axes, @ treats everything except the last two axes as a batch: it lines those leading axes up and does an independent matrix multiply on each (last two × last two) slice. So,

(N, h, q, d) @ (N, h, d, k)  ->  (N, h, q, k)
For every one of the N × h combinations, multiply the (q × d) matrix from the first input by the (d × k) matrix of the second input. The (N, h) just come along unchanged, and only the last two axes actually get multiplied. (The leading (N, h) axes must match on both sides - or be broadcastable - but here they’re always identical. It’s the inner matrix dimensions, the shared d, that have to line up for the multiply itself.)

transpose(a, b) swaps two axes. The two arguments are which axes to swap, by their index, with every other axis staying as-is. So for a tensor of shape (N, s, h, d):

x.transpose(1, 2)   # swaps axes 1 and 2  ->  (N, h, s, d)
As with all indexing, negative indices count from the end, so -1 is the last axis, and -2 the second-to-last.

So, at this point in the calculation, each of queries, keys, values has shape (N, seq_len, heads, head_dim). If we want to matrix multiply along the correct axes (the last two), we first move the heads axis to the front via a transpose. This means swapping the two middle dimensions (we ultimately want (N, heads, seq_len, head_dim)), so we start with a transpose.
    values  = values.transpose(1, 2)    # (N, heads, value_len, head_dim)
    keys    = keys.transpose(1, 2)      # (N, heads, key_len,   head_dim)
    queries = queries.transpose(1, 2)   # (N, heads, query_len, head_dim)
Now, we can easily calculate the scores with a single batched matrix multiply:
    attention_scores = queries @ keys.transpose(-2, -1)
    # (N, heads, query_len, head_dim) @ (N, heads, head_dim, key_len)
    # -> (N, heads, query_len, key_len)
The transpose that happens here is a “regular” transpose - the math asks that we swap the final two dimensions. Then, we use the “@” operator to matrix multiply, over just the final two dimensions of those larger, batched matrices.
So, for a fixed batch item and head, queries is a (query_len × head_dim) matrix, with one row per query position. keys is transposed to (head_dim × key_len), so that multiplying gives a (query_len × key_len) matrix whose entry (i, j) is the dot product of query row i with key row j. Because the leading (N, heads) axes are just kept, treated as a batch, this matrix multiply happens independently for every item in the batch and every head, but gets to occur all at once.
Scaling and softmax.
Softmax is a very common function in machine learning, and thus also has an easy built-in with torch. We first divide by √head_dim, as that’s the dimension the dot product is really acting over and thus needs to be scaled by. Then, we apply the softmax, making sure to pass dim=-1, as we want to softmax over the last axis, the key_len axis. That turns each query’s row of scores across the keys into weights that sum to 1.
    attention = torch.softmax(attention_scores / (self.head_dim ** 0.5), dim=-1)
Applying the weights to the values.
The next step is to apply the attention weights to the values.
    out = attention @ values
    # (N, heads, query_len, key_len) @ (N, heads, value_len, head_dim)
    # -> (N, heads, query_len, head_dim)
Per head, this multiplies the (query_len × key_len) weight matrix by the (value_len × head_dim) value matrix.
Note that here, key_len and value_len are the same number, so the inner dimensions line up. This actually is a generally true property of attention - because this multiply has to happen, K and V, at least, must be asking about the same sequence. (We’ll see in Section 4, that Q doesn’t - and talk more about the implications there!)
Recombining the heads.
Now, the heads have been treated separately during most of the attention math. We recombine them here by putting the “original” dimension back together.
This starts with a transpose to “fix” the dimensions back to normal, returning them to (N, query_len, heads, head_dim). Then, we reshape, returning the heads x head_dim dimensions back into a single dimension of size embed_size.
    out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(N, query_len, self.heads * self.head_dim)  
    # (N, heads, query_len, head_dim) -> (N, query_len, heads, head_dim)
    # -> (N, query_len, embed_size)
Then, finally, fc_out is that multiply by the final matrix, W^O. This of course is the final of the projections that we defined in __init__.
    out = self.fc_out(out)
So, what does this all mean for how we actually call and use this MultiHeadAttention class? A few things.

Because the function takes values, keys, and query as three independent inputs, self-attention is just the case where we pass the same sequence as all three, so that all of Q, K, and V operate on the same thing.
Writing it in this way, using the pytorch built-ins means that pytorch handles a lot of the math behind the scenes for us.

Number (1) we’ll touch more on in the decoder section. But (2) is worth discussing in a little more detail here, because it can make the math and code a little more difficult to line up with one another.
If you’re not used to reading class-based code like this, the key thing to note is that each nn.Linear isn’t a function - it’s an object that holds a weight matrix inside it. That’s why when we defined the projections in __init__ like this:
self.values = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
We could apply them later. Those definitions told torch to create an object, filled with a randomly-initialized embed_size × embed_size matrix, and stash it under the name self.values. That matrix is W_V, and we can look at it with self.values.weight.
So in the forward pass, when we do self.values(values), we’re asking to apply that matrix stored in self.values to the values matrix we’re feeding in. These objects also keep track of which weights belong to which layer - since each layer is a separate object, each object owns its own weights. Each distinct nn.Linear object holds an independent matrix, and each MultiHeadAttention object we’ll define when we build the encoder holds its own independent instances of those calls. So these objects are keeping everything separate for us “for free”.
It’s also of course what will make training very easy for us. Because we built MultiHeadAttention as an nn.Module and assigned those layers as attributes, PyTorch automatically registers every inner matrix as a learnable parameter. So when it comes time to actually do backpropagation and tweak those weights, PyTorch also handles figuring out how those weights all need to move.
Of course, if you want to make every single bit of the math totally transparent, you can write every single thing yourself. In practice, even a “highly custom” architecture won’t do that, and will use PyTorch instead.
Finally, we can see how we’d actually use this MultiHeadAttention we just built, and be sure that it gives us the output we expect in the self-attention case below:

embed_size = 4   # Embedding size (d_model)
seq_length = 3   # Sequence length
heads = 2        # (with embed_size=4, heads=2 gives head_dim=2)

# Simulate input embeddings - NOTE the batch dimension: (batch=1, seq_length, embed_size)
x = torch.rand((1, seq_length, embed_size))

attention_model = MultiHeadAttention(embed_size=embed_size, heads=heads)

# self-attention: Q, K, and V all come from the same input, so we pass x three times
O = attention_model(x, x, x)

print("Input shape: ", tuple(x.shape))
print("Output shape:", tuple(O.shape), " <- same shape in and out")
print("\nInput Embeddings (X):", x.numpy())
print("Output Matrix (O):", O.detach().numpy())

Input shape:  (1, 3, 4)
Output shape: (1, 3, 4)  <- same shape in and out

Input Embeddings (X): [[[0.37555784 0.5225613  0.57295054 0.61858714]
  [0.69621414 0.5299501  0.25603563 0.7365945 ]
  [0.02037555 0.20364666 0.37483507 0.25644332]]]
Output Matrix (O): [[[-0.44758716  0.14991242 -0.48490107  0.05346444]
  [-0.44845763  0.15030378 -0.48452932  0.05426714]
  [-0.4486941   0.14936079 -0.48329026  0.05332798]]]






A residual connection (also called a skip connection) is an incredibly simple but important idea that ensures that information gets passed through a model without too much loss of what it originally contained. Instead of just passing input through a layer and using the output:
\[\text{output} = f(x)\]
You add the original input back to the output:
\[\text{output} = x + f(x)\]
In the case of the attention sublayer, this means concretely:
\[X_1 = X + O\]
where \(X\) is the input to the attention layer (our embedded + positionally encoded tokens) and \(O\) is the attention output we just computed. \(X_1\), the sum of both, is what gets passed forward.
That’s it. The layer’s output gets added to its input, element-wise, so that even though you do a bunch of useful transformations to the input via the attention section, you also keep what you already knew. In a transformer, this is applied around each sublayer - both the attention mechanism and the feed-forward network (which we’ll cover shortly). So after multi-head attention, for example, the actual output is:
\[\text{output} = x + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(x)\]
where \(x\) is the input that went into the attention sublayer.


This idea comes from the 2015 paper “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition” (He et al.), which was originally developed for very deep convolutional networks. But the problem it solves is so universal and fundamental to training deep networks of any kind, including transformers, that it’s applicable here as well.
The Degradation Problem
You might expect (and indeed, it’s a typical assumption) that making a network deeper always makes it more powerful. More layers means more capacity to learn complex functions, more parameters to create more complex relationships, etc. But in practice, researchers found the opposite: beyond a certain depth, adding more layers actually made performance worse, even on the training data. This wasn’t overfitting (which would hurt test performance but NOT training performance). The deeper network was genuinely worse at learning.
This is strange if you think about it. A deeper network contains the shallower one - in theory, the extra layers could just learn to be identity functions (pass the input through unchanged), and you’d match the shallower network’s performance at worst. But of course, in practice, how a network learns is not so obvious, and learning the identity through a stack of nonlinear transformations is surprisingly difficult for gradient-based optimization.
What Residual Connections Change
With a residual connection, the layer doesn’t need to learn the full desired transformation. It only needs to learn the difference between the desired output and the input - the “residual”:
\[f(x) = \text{desired output} - x\]
If the best thing to do is pass information through unchanged (which is common - not every layer needs to dramatically transform every token to do something useful), the layer just needs to output something close to zero. Learning “do approximately nothing” is much easier than learning “reproduce the input exactly through a chain of matrix multiplications and nonlinearities.”
This connects to initialization, too. At the start of training, each block’s \(f(x)\) often starts out small relative to \(x\). With a residual connection, that means the whole network begins as approximately an identity function, with the input passing through relatively unchanged. Each layer then gradually learns to make useful refinements from that starting point, rather than having to reorganize from a random transformation.
And, there’s an additional intuition here specific to attention. Attention creates a weighted average of value vectors, where each position becomes a blend of information from other positions. After many layers, without residual connections, this repeated blending could cause individual token representations to converge toward a generic “average of everything,” losing token-specific information. The residual connection ensures that each position always retains its original representation, with contextual information added on top rather than replacing it.
Gradient Flow
Finally, residual connections also provide a direct path for gradients to flow backward through the network during training. Consider backpropagation through \(\text{output} = x + f(x)\). The gradient of the output with respect to \(x\) is:
\[\frac{\partial \text{output}}{\partial x} = 1 + \frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x}\]
That “\(1\)” does a lot of work. It enforces that, no matter what \(f\) does - even if its gradient is very small (the vanishing gradient problem) - the gradient through the residual is always exactly 1. This gives the training signal a “highway” to travel back through many layers without degrading. If \(f\)’s gradient gets very small, you still have a signal, which is essential for training the deep stacks of layers that transformers use.



In a transformer, residual connections wrap around every sublayer that makes up a transformer block. Each transformer block has two of such sublayers - attention and a feed-forward network - and each gets its own residual connection:
\[x_1 = x + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(x)\] \[x_2 = x_1 + \text{FeedForward}(x_1)\]
The intuition here is simple. Since each sublayer makes its own incremental refinement to the representation, we allow each of those refinements to be a difference via residuals. The attention sublayer adds contextual information from other positions. The feed-forward sublayer adds nonlinear transformations. The original information is preserved through both via the skip connection, and what exactly the attention and feed-forward need to change can be kept as separate components.



The implementation is as simple as the concept, no new parameters or layers, just a simple addition. It’s typically implemented inside an attention or feedforward block because it’s so straightforward it’s not really worth separating out.
Inside a transformer block’s forward pass, each sublayer is wrapped in a residual connection, just adding the sublayer’s input back onto its output. For that reason, this is the pseudocode for it, but this won’t run on its own because, as we said, it really just makes sense to be within the layer, not its own thing.
# Attention sublayer with a residual connection
attention_output = self.attention(x)
x = x + attention_output          # keep the input, add the change

# Feed-forward sublayer with a residual connection
ff_output = self.feed_forward(x)
x = x + ff_output                 # residual again, around the FFN




Layer normalization is a very standard technique (established even a year before the advent of the transformer architecture) that stabilizes training by normalizing the values flowing through the network. The idea is straightforward: for each token’s representation, we normalize across the feature dimensions so that the values have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
For token \(t\) with representation \(X_t\) (a vector of \(d_\text{model}\) values), layer normalization computes:
\[\text{LayerNorm}(X_t) = \gamma \cdot \frac{X_t - \mu_t}{\sqrt{\sigma_t^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta\]
where:

\(\mu_t = \frac{1}{d_\text{model}} \sum_{i=1}^{d_\text{model}} X_{t,i}\) is the mean across token \(t\)’s feature vector
\(\sigma_t^2 = \frac{1}{d_\text{model}} \sum_{i=1}^{d_\text{model}} (X_{t,i} - \mu_t)^2\) is the variance across token \(t\)’s feature vector
\(\epsilon\) is a tiny constant (like \(10^{-6}\)) to prevent division by zero
\(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable parameters (both of size \(d_\text{model}\))

Each token gets its own mean and variance, computed only from its own features, so this operation happens on a row by row basis.
The \(\frac{X_t - \mu_t}{\sqrt{\sigma_t^2 + \epsilon}}\) part centers and scales the values to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Then \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) let the model learn to shift and scale the normalized values to whatever range is actually useful. This means normalization doesn’t force the values to be mean-zero, it just makes mean-zero the default starting point that the model can adjust from.


As values propagate through many layers of a deep network, their magnitudes can drift - some values might grow very large while others shrink toward zero. This is a problem because:

Unstable gradients: If activations become very large, gradients can explode. If they become very small, gradients can vanish. Either way, training becomes unreliable.
Sensitivity to initialization and learning rate: Without normalization, the behavior of deeper layers depends heavily on the exact scale of activations coming from earlier layers. This makes the network fragile - small changes to the learning rate or weight initialization can cause training to diverge, making optimal values for those much harder to find.
Internal covariate shift: Each layer’s inputs are the outputs of the previous layer, which are constantly changing during training. Normalization ensures that regardless of what the previous layer is doing, each layer receives inputs in a consistent, well-behaved range.

Layer normalization addresses all of these by repeatedly resetting the scale of activations. It’s a simple operation, but it’s one of the things that makes training deep transformers stable and practical.



As I mentioned when we first introduced this building block - normalization isn’t unique to transformers. It shows up in virtually every modern deep learning architecture. The underlying motivation is always the same - we want to keep the values flowing through the network in a stable, well-behaved range so that training converges reliably. What varies is which dimensions you normalize across, and the choice depends on the structure of your data.

Input Normalization / Feature Scaling: Before data even enters a model, it’s common practice to normalize input features to have zero mean and unit variance (or scale them to a fixed range like [0, 1]). Here, you just compute statistics across your dataset and rescale. This prevents the model’s gradients from being dominated by the largest-scale features.
Batch Normalization: Introduced for CNNs (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015), this normalizes across the batch dimension. For a given feature (in this case, one channel), it computes the mean and variance of that feature across all examples in the current mini-batch, then normalizes. This works well because convolutional filters are applied identically across spatial positions and across images, so normalizing a filter’s activations across a batch is normalizing “measurements from the same instrument,” keeping them on a consistent scale.
Group Normalization, Instance Normalization, RMS Normalization: Other variants exist that normalize across different subsets of dimensions, each designed for specific architectural needs. RMS Norm, for instance, is a simplified version of layer norm (it skips the mean-centering step) that has become popular in recent LLMs like LLaMA for its computational efficiency.

However normalization is done, the common thread and purpose remains the same: wherever activations might drift in scale during training, insert a normalization step to reset them. The differences are just about what you average over to compute the statistics.
Why Layer Norm for Transformers?
Like filters in a CNN, transformers also share weights across positions. But attention creates a complication: each token’s representation after attention becomes a content-dependent blend of information from every other token in the sequence. Two tokens at the same position in different examples can have wildly different representations because they had wildly different context.
What a transformer’s downstream computations - the dot products in the next attention layer, the matrix multiplications in the feed-forward network - care about is whether the features within a single token’s representation are well-scaled relative to each other. These \(d_\text{model}\) numbers are about to interact with each other through matrix multiplications, and if some dimensions have drifted to large magnitudes while others have shrunk, those interactions become dominated by whichever dimensions happen to be largest, regardless of whether they’re the most informative.
So, layer normalization addresses this by normalizing each token’s feature vector independently, resetting all \(d_\text{model}\) dimensions to a common scale before the next computation. It doesn’t matter what other tokens in the sequence are doing, or what other examples in the batch look like. Each token’s internal geometry is kept well-behaved on its own terms.
There are practical advantages too. Layer normalizations don’t care about variable sequence lengths, work identically regardless of batch size, and behave the same at training and inference time. So they are the choice.



In the original transformer paper, layer normalization is applied after the residual addition (“post-norm”):
\[x_1 = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(x))\]
However, most modern implementations use “pre-norm”, where normalization is applied before the sublayer:
\[x_1 = x + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))\]
Pre-norm tends to train more stably, especially for very deep models, because the residual path stays completely true to its original purpose. The raw \(x\) flows through without any modification. With post-norm, the normalization sits on the residual path itself, which can interfere with the gradient highway we discussed in Section 2.3. In our implementation, we’ll use pre-norm, which is the more common modern choice.
So after the attention sublayer with pre-norm, the full computation is:
\[X_1 = X + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(\text{LayerNorm}(X))\]
That is: we normalize our input \(X\), run it through attention to get \(O\), then add the original (un-normalized) \(X\) back. \(X_1\) then becomes the input to the feed-forward sublayer (which we discuss in detail next!), where the same pattern repeats:
\[X_2 = X_1 + \text{FFN}(\text{LayerNorm}(X_1))\]
But, one consequence of that residual \(X\) never getting normalized is that at the end of an encoder layer, the final output actually won’t be normalized. To fix this, we’ll add one final LayerNorm at the very end of each, to make sure what comes out is properly normalized. When it comes time to actually build the encoder, we’ll revisit this.



# PyTorch provides LayerNorm out of the box:
layer_norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

# Usage inside a transformer block (pre-norm style):
# Attention sublayer
attention_output = self.attention(self.norm1(x))
x = x + attention_output

# Feed-forward sublayer
ff_output = self.feed_forward(self.norm2(x))
x = x + ff_output
Notice how with pre-norm, the pattern becomes very clean: normalize, transform, add back. The residual connection always adds the un-normalized input, keeping the skip path simple.




Each transformer block contains, in addition to the multi-head attention sublayer, a feed-forward network (FFN) that is applied independently to each token’s representation. It’s a simple architecture - two linear layers with a nonlinearity in between:
\[\text{FFN}(x) = \text{ReLU}(X \cdot W_1 + b_1) \cdot W_2 + b_2\]
This introduces two new weight matrices:

\(W_1\) is of size \(d_\text{model} \times d_\text{ff}\)
\(W_2\) is of size \(d_\text{ff} \times d_\text{model}\)

Here, \(d_\text{ff}\) is the inner dimension, typically \(4 \times d_\text{model}\) (so for \(d_\text{model} = 512\), \(d_\text{ff} = 2048\)), but of course can be different.
The input and output are both \(d_\text{model}\)-dimensional (so the residual connection still works), but internally the representation expands to a larger space and then contracts back down.
The paper calls this ‘position-wise’ to emphasize that it operates on each token independently - but that’s just the natural behavior of matrix multiplication, not a special mechanism. Naturally, in the operation above, you get token 1’s output depending only on token 1’s input, token 5’s depending only on token 5’s, etc. It’s more that an FFN was chosen because it’s position-wise, not that anything special needs to be done to make this FFN position-wise.


The paper is called “Attention is All You Need”. The attention mechanism has learnable weights. It has a nonlinear function. So it might not be obvious why you’d bother with a “plain” feedforward network in the mix. We just did attention, which is the main mechanism of the transformer.
The answer is that attention, despite its power, is fundamentally still a linear operation over the value vectors. Look at what attention actually computes for each token:
\[o_i = \sum_j a_{ij} \cdot v_j\]
That’s a weighted sum - a linear combination of the value vectors, with the attention weights choosing how to blend them. The softmax introduces nonlinearity in computing the weights \(a_{ij}\), but the operation that produces the output (multiplying those weights by V) - is linear. If you stacked multiple attention layers without anything else in between, the composition of linear operations over V is still fundamentally doing weighted averaging.
The FFN adds the nonlinear transformation capacity that attention lacks. The ReLU (or GELU, in many modern implementations) between \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) means the FFN can compute nonlinear functions of its input. It can suppress some features, amplify others, and create entirely new combinations that a linear transformation simply cannot produce.
The two sublayers have complementary roles:

Attention gathers information from across the sequence, deciding what information each token should collect from other tokens.
FFN processes that information, transforming each token’s now context-enriched representation through a nonlinear function.

You might wonder - if it’s just about nonlinearity, why not apply a ReLU directly to the attention output? You could, but a pointwise ReLU on a \(d_\text{model}\)-dimensional vector is limited - all it can do is zero out negative values.
The FFN’s power comes from the expand-then-contract structure: \(W_1\) projects into a \(4\times\) larger space, ReLU selectively activates features in that larger space, and then \(W_2\) combines those selectively-activated features back into \(d_\text{model}\) dimensions. The expansion is what gives the FFN the capacity to compute rich, nonlinear transformations - not just “add nonlinearity” but “create new feature combinations that didn’t exist before.”
Similarly, adding more parameters to attention itself wouldn’t fill this role. Attention’s parameters control which tokens to gather information from and what to extract. Making those bigger improves the gathering, but the output is still a weighted average of value vectors - and still linear. The FFN’s job is fundamentally different: not gathering information across positions, but transforming it within each position.



The inner dimension \(d_\text{ff}\) is typically \(4 \times d_\text{model}\). This expand-then-contract pattern might seem arbitrary, but there’s intuition behind it.
\(W_1\) projects from \(d_\text{model}\) up to \(d_\text{ff}\), then ReLU zeroes out the negative values. If roughly half the neurons are zeroed out (which is typical for ReLU), you’re left with about \(2 \times d_\text{model}\) active features - a richer representation than the original \(d_\text{model}\) dimensions but computed sparsely. \(W_2\) then compresses this back to \(d_\text{model}\) for the rest of the network.
The \(4\times\) factor was chosen empirically by the original authors and has proven to be a reliable default. Some modern architectures adjust this (LLaMA uses \(\frac{8}{3} \times d_\text{model}\) with a different activation function), but the expand-then-contract pattern is essentially universal.



Simple as it gets - two linear layers, a ReLU in the middle. Applied identically and independently to every token position.

class FeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff):
        super(FeedForward, self).__init__()
        self.linear1 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x shape: (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
        x = self.linear1(x)   # (batch_size, seq_len, d_ff)
        x = self.relu(x)      # (batch_size, seq_len, d_ff)
        x = self.linear2(x)   # (batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
        return x




Here’s a fact that might surprise you: the FFN contains the majority of a transformer’s parameters. For a standard configuration with \(d_\text{model} = 512\) and \(d_\text{ff} = 2048\):

\(W_1\): \(512 \times 2048 = 1,048,576\) parameters
\(W_2\): \(2048 \times 512 = 1,048,576\) parameters
Total FFN: ~2.1 million parameters (plus biases)

Compare that to multi-head attention with \(\text{h} = 8\):

\(W^Q, W^K, W^V\): \(3 \times (512 \times 512) = 786,432\) parameters
\(W^O\): \(512 \times 512 = 262,144\) parameters
Total attention: ~1.05 million parameters

The FFN has roughly twice as many parameters as the attention mechanism. The part of the transformer that gets all the attention (pun intended) is actually the smaller component. The FFN is where most of the model’s learned knowledge is stored. It’s something to keep in mind as you appreciate the evolution from “regular” neural networks to transformers. The attention mechanism is, don’t get me wrong, a brilliant addition - it’s what allows information to flow between tokens and sequences to be efficiently treated as a whole. But the majority of a transformer’s parameters, and much of its representational power, still lives in the humble feedforward network!





So that’s all of the core theoretical components that go into building a transformer!
Now, it’s time to start seeing it in action - how these things come together to form the full transformer architecture, we’ll start with the Encoder.
We’ve basically already seen a single encoder block come together as we went over the last few of our building blocks in Section 2. As we discussed, a transformer layer is really just comprised of two sublayers in sequence, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization (using pre-norm):
\[X_1 = X + \text{MultiHeadAttention}(\text{LayerNorm}(X))\] \[X_2 = X_1 + \text{FFN}(\text{LayerNorm}(X_1))\]
That’s it. Normalize, attend, add back. Normalize, feed forward, add back.

📌 Note on terminology: A single unit of these two sublayers together is > called both a “block” and a “layer” interchangeably in the literature. Within > each block/layer, attention and the FFN are each called a “sublayer.” The full encoder is a stack of N of these blocks. In the original transformer, every block is identical in structure and size. This means same \(d_\text{model}\), same number of heads, same \(d_\text{ff}\). The only things that differ between blocks are the learned weight values.

Reminder: you can see all of the dimension details in Appendix 0. But here, let’s do a quick recap tracing through the full computation for an input \(X\) of shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\):

Layer Norm: Normalize each token’s features. Each row of \(X\) is normalized independently using its own mean and variance (no mixing between tokens). → shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)
Multi-Head Attention: This is where tokens interact. Each token’s output row is a weighted combination of information from every token’s value vector. This is the only step where information flows across rows of the matrix! → shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)
Residual Add: Add the original \(X\) back to the attention output, element-wise. → \(X_1\), shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)
Layer Norm: Normalize each row of \(X_1\) independently, same as step 1. → shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)
Feed-Forward Network: Transform each token’s row independently through the same two-layer network - no mixing between tokens. → shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)
Residual Add: Add \(X_1\) back, element-wise. → \(X_2\), shape \((n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model})\)


So, the information is transformed many times, but the input and final output to the encoder block always have the same shape. This means we can additionally stack encoder blocks, making the output of one the input into the next.
The original transformer used 6 encoder blocks, but of course, this is a hyperparameter, and deeper, larger networks will stack many more!


Now, let’s build an encoder block in code.
This will look incredibly simple! That’s because we already built these components, and all that’s left is just assembly.



class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(EncoderBlock, self).__init__()
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.feed_forward = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, X):
        # Sublayer 1: Multi-Head Attention
        norm_X = self.norm1(X)
        attention_output = self.attention(norm_X, norm_X, norm_X)  # Q, K, V all come from same input
        X_1 = X + self.dropout1(attention_output)

        # Sublayer 2: Feed-Forward Network
        norm_X_1 = self.norm2(X_1)
        ff_output = self.feed_forward(norm_X_1)
        X_2 = X_1 + self.dropout2(ff_output)

        return X_2

You’ll notice we’ve snuck in dropout - this is a standard regularization technique that randomly zeroes out a fraction of values during training. It’s applied after each sublayer (before the residual addition) to prevent overfitting. We won’t dwell on it since it’s not specific to transformers, but it’s worth noting that it’s typically there.
Also note that in the attention call, we pass norm_X as all three arguments (Q, K, V). This is what makes it self-attention - the queries, keys, and values all come from the same source. In the decoder, we’ll see a case where Q comes from one source and K, V come from another.



We can confirm that this block does what we expect by actually choosing some dimensions, and looking at what each part of this encoder block does to the input shapes.

# Using the classes we built in Section 2:
d_model = 64
heads = 4
d_ff = 256
n_seq = 5
batch_size = 1

# Create an encoder block
encoder_block = EncoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff)

# Simulate input: 5 tokens, each a 64-dimensional vector
X = torch.randn(batch_size, n_seq, d_model)
print(f"Input X:              {X.shape}")

# Trace through each step manually:
norm_X = encoder_block.norm1(X)
print(f"After LayerNorm:      {norm_X.shape}")

attn_out = encoder_block.attention(norm_X, norm_X, norm_X)
print(f"After Attention:      {attn_out.shape}")

X_1 = X + attn_out
print(f"After Residual Add:   {X_1.shape}")

norm_X_1 = encoder_block.norm2(X_1)
print(f"After LayerNorm:      {norm_X_1.shape}")

ff_out = encoder_block.feed_forward(norm_X_1)
print(f"After FFN:            {ff_out.shape}")

X_2 = X_1 + ff_out
print(f"After Residual Add:   {X_2.shape}")

print(f"\nInput shape:  {X.shape}")
print(f"Output shape: {X_2.shape}")
print(f"Same shape:   {X.shape == X_2.shape}")
