    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout=0.1):
        super(InputEmbedding, self).__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        pe = torch.tensor(get_positional_encodings(max_len, d_model), dtype=torch.float)
        self.register_buffer("pos_encoding", pe) # store the positional encodings
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):                       # x: token IDs, (N, seq_len)
        seq_len = x.shape[1]
        x = self.embedding(x) + self.pos_encoding[:seq_len] # add the fixed PE to the embedding
        return self.dropout(x) # dropout at the END - right before the next layer

A few things to point out here:

The positional-encoding function is implemented here with the get_positional_encodings that we wrote before, but stored with register_buffer. This makes it a part of the module - moved to the GPU and stored there alongside it without being a learnable parameter, since sinusoidal positional encodings have nothing to learn.
nn.Embedding is a torch built-in layer, like the nn.Linear we discussed before. This special kind of layer is exactly the lookup table we described back when we first talked about embeddings. It contains a learnable weight matrix of shape \(n_{\text{vocab}} \times d_{\text{model}}\), with one row per token in the vocabulary, that returns row \(i\) for a token index \(i\). It does the exact same thing as the “one-hot vector times the embedding matrix” calculation that we talked about in Section 1, just done as a direct row-lookup instead of an actual matrix multiply. The nn.Embedding layer is a special layer that knows to do this instead of the full matrix multiply.
nn.Dropout is slipped into here again, just like we did with every encoder and decoder block so far. It might be obvious why dropping random activations helps the model from over-relying on certain features, but dropping parts of an embedding might seem like a stranger choice. But it’s still for the exact same reason. Regularizing here means that the next layer, the first layer of the encoder or decoder, doesn’t get every single feature of the embedding vector, and thus can’t learn to over-rely on certain features of that vector.




Next, we’ll assemble the encoder. But first, actually, we need to rewrite our original EncoderBlock code. At the time that we wrote that code, we didn’t yet understand the need for masking, and so we left it out. Now that we’ve covered the role of the source mask, we need to just make a tiny edit to that code to be sure that it can take in and handle that.
The two line changes are pointed out with comments.

class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(EncoderBlock, self).__init__()
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.feed_forward = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, X, mask=None):                                   # <- added mask=None by default
        norm_X = self.norm1(X)
        attention_output = self.attention(norm_X, norm_X, norm_X, mask=mask)  # <- attention is already wired for a mask, but pass it through here
        X_1 = X + self.dropout1(attention_output)

        norm_X_1 = self.norm2(X_1)
        ff_output = self.feed_forward(norm_X_1)
        X_2 = X_1 + self.dropout2(ff_output)
        return X_2

Then, building up the encoder is just a few lines, since it just means stacking encoder blocks, which contain all of the relevant operations, on top of each other.

class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(Encoder, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [EncoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(num_layers)]
        )
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)       # <- new addition: final LayerNorm (needed with pre-norm)

    def forward(self, x, mask):                 # x: (N, src_len, d_model), already embedded
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, mask)
        return self.norm(x)                     # <- normalize once more on the way out

So as you can see, really all this does is just puts num_layers encoder blocks all in a row. Just a few things to point out:

nn.ModuleList is a new piece of PyTorch. It’s meant for cases exactly like stacking our already made encoder modules: it’s really just a list that holds sub-modules, but unlike a regular Python list, everything gets registered with PyTorch so all weights are properly tracked, and will show up in model.parameters(). It just tells PyTorch “here’s a bunch of trainable things”.
We do wrap it around a “normal” list, with the list comprehension: python   [EncoderBlock(...) for _ in range(num_layers)] simply making num_layers separate EncoderBlock objects. Since each is a distinct object, it’ll have its own \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) and \(W_{\text{ff}}\) weights.
In forward, the loop is where the “stacked” behavior really comes to fruition. We go through each layer in that list, run x through it, take the x that comes out of it, and put it into the next one. The same mask is handed to every block, because the same batch passes through all blocks to get the final output.
Remember here that the first x is going to arrive already embedded. We’ll see when we build the full transformer object.
num_layers is the stack depth N, a hyperparameter - the original transformer used 6; we’ll pick something small for our toy task.
We snuck in an “extra” nn.LayerNorm. Remember that with pre-norm, each sublayer normalizes its input, but the residual stream that runs through the whole stack never gets normalized itself - it’s just added onto, block after block. So the last block hands back an un-normalized \(x\). This would leave one “missing” at the end - our final encoder output wouldn’t be normalized, if we didn’t add one more norm to the end.




The Decoder structurally matches the encoder almost exactly - a lot of the work already went into building our DecoderBlock object back in the Decoder Section, so now all that’s left is stacking a bunch of them together.

class Decoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(Decoder, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [DecoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(num_layers)]
        )
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

    def forward(self, x, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask):   # x: (N, trg_len, d_model), already embedded
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask)
        return self.norm(x)

So what is different from the encoder?

It stacks DecoderBlocks instead of EncoderBlock’s, of course.
forward must take four arguments instead of two, for the same reasons that our DecoderBlock’s forward needed 4 arguments. On top of x (the target sequence, already embedded), it also receives:

enc_out - the encoder’s output.
src_mask - the mask for the encoder output, for handling padding of different sequence lengths, and
trg_mask - the causal mask to block the future.

These masks will get defined in the Transformer object.
Just like the encoder, we loop through the layers in the forward definition. Same as the encoder, x changes from one block to the next. But those extra inputs: enc_out, src_mask, and trg_mask stay fixed, handed identically to every block.
Also just like the encoder, we end with a nn.LayerNorm on the output, because pre-norm doesn’t normalize the final output as-is.

So structurally, they’re really the same, and the differences just come down to how we had to construct the encoder vs decoder block differently, which we already covered extensively.



Now, finally, we really put it all together.

class Transformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len,
                 src_pad_idx, trg_pad_idx, dropout=0.1):
        super(Transformer, self).__init__()
        # Define all of the sections we just made
        self.input_embedding = InputEmbedding(vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout)
        #ONE Input block, that we'll share since our source and target share a vocabulary. Otherwise, we'd define two here!
        self.encoder = Encoder(d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout)
        self.decoder = Decoder(d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout)
        self.output_projection = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size)   # the "Output" / prediction layer is so simple, it just gets defined right here
        self.src_pad_idx = src_pad_idx # padding for the SOURCE - input
        self.trg_pad_idx = trg_pad_idx # padding for the TARGET - output

    def make_src_mask(self, src):
        # 1 where the token is real, 0 where it's padding
        # shape (N, 1, 1, src_len) so it broadcasts over heads and query positions
        # we get this DIRECTLY from the source padding!
        return (src != self.src_pad_idx).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2)

    def make_trg_mask(self, trg):
        N, trg_len = trg.shape
        # lower-triangular causal mask, shape (N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)
        trg_mask = torch.tril(torch.ones((trg_len, trg_len), device=trg.device))
        return trg_mask.expand(N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)

    def forward(self, src, trg):
        # 1) build the masks
        src_mask = self.make_src_mask(src)       # (N, 1, 1, src_len)
        trg_mask = self.make_trg_mask(trg)       # (N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)

        # 2) embed both inputs, with the SAME embedding object
        src_emb = self.input_embedding(src)      # (N, src_len, d_model) for the input (source)
        trg_emb = self.input_embedding(trg)      # (N, trg_len, d_model) for the output (target)

        # 3) pass through the encoder
        enc_out = self.encoder(src_emb, src_mask)                     # X_enc: (N, src_len, d_model)

        # 4) pass through the decoder
        dec_out = self.decoder(trg_emb, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask)  # X_out: (N, trg_len, d_model)

        logits = self.output_projection(dec_out)  # (N, trg_len, vocab_size)
        return logits

All things considered, it’s relatively brief. And of course that’s one of the big advantages to building up these building blocks as their own objects. Now that we have a full encoder, we just have to say “go through the encoder” - we can look to that specific object for the encoder architecture.
The forward pass is the entire architecture - the full flow of an input through the entire process, so let’s make sure we understand every line there to see how everything we’ve talked about finally comes together.

📌 Note: Recall in the above code, and what we’re about to discuss that \(N\) is referring to batch size. Where before we’ve talked about “N” layers in the encoder/decoder stacks, in code, that has become num_layers to be more explicit.

The main components to this forward pass are:

The first thing we do is build the masks.


make_trg_mask is the causal torch.tril which simply constructs a triangular mask from the target length. Remember that this kind of triangular mask, and the size it needs to be, is just exactly determined by what the current sequence length is, so this needs no other information than “what is the current target sequence”.
make_src_mask is the padding mask we make from the source. Remember that, similarly, this mask just needs to assign a 1 where a real token was placed, and 0 where a padding token was placed. So this also needs no extra information other than what the current source is - it marks which source positions are real (src != pad_idx), and it’s shaped to broadcast across heads and query positions so a single mask covers the whole score matrix. All that we’ll need to do is tell it what the padding token looks like, what its ID is, which we’ll pin down when we get to actually passing in data.


Then, we embed the sequences with the same InputEmbedding object. Both self.input_embedding(src) and self.input_embedding(trg) call the same object, because as we discussed, in this case, the vocabulary is shared - with tokens always meaning the same thing on both sides. After embedding, both come out as (N, seq_len, d_model).
We run the full encoder first. It gives us enc_out, which is what we’ve been calling X_enc - the fixed, fully contextualized output from the encoder, that we hold fixed after the forward pass and use in the decoder. Its shape coming out is (N, src_len, d_model). It’s computed once, then handed to the decoder in the next step.
The decoder runs after, using that enc_out. This gives us dec_out, which is what we’ve been calling X_out, the contextualized target representation that we use to get the next token. It has shape (N, trg_len, d_model).
The output projection picks the next token. Finally, we give that X_out to the output layer, which projects each position from d_model up to vocab_size, giving logits of shape (N, trg_len, vocab_size)

Then, even though we aren’t quite ready to train yet, we can put this together, and make sure that it all runs forward, giving back the correct shape, at least with dummy numbers:

# a small toy config
vocab_size = 15          # something small - e.g. digits, '-', eos, bos, pad, unk
d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len = 64, 3, 4, 256, 32
src_pad_idx = trg_pad_idx = 0

model = Transformer(vocab_size, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len,
                    src_pad_idx, trg_pad_idx)

N, src_len, trg_len = 2, 18, 11       # batch of 2; a padded source, a target
src = torch.randint(1, vocab_size, (N, src_len))   # fake token IDs
trg = torch.randint(1, vocab_size, (N, trg_len))

logits = model(src, trg)
print("src:   ", tuple(src.shape))
print("trg:   ", tuple(trg.shape))
print("logits:", tuple(logits.shape))

src:    (2, 18)
trg:    (2, 11)
logits: (2, 11, 15)







So we’ve done the full assembling - we literally have the Transformer defined. But looking at the forward, a few things probably feel conspicuously absent. Some of these are things we’ll cover right now: how to make sure that our targets really only learn from positions they should be able to see, what signal actually determines if we’re getting the answer right or wrong, the actual learning of the weights, and how to do it all when data comes in as a batch.
Other things that we had discussed - like the autoregressive loop that produces one token at a time, appends it, and feeds it back in - will come down to how we use the model, after it’s trained. We’ll cover those as their own set of topics, in Section 9, once we’ve trained this model on a real task in Section 8.
So this Section is just all about the theory and practicalities of training. We have a full Transformer architecture, we can pass in a tensor, it’ll get multiplied by all of the weights, and we get a set of logits back out. How, then, do we set it up with data so those weights shift to produce correct outputs? How do we measure correctness? How do we know how much to change the model by? These are all training time considerations.


The first important concept that we need because things are different at training time vs. at generation time is something called teacher forcing. Basically, it’s how we mimic autoregressive generation - making just one token at a time, conditioned by what comes before - when during training, we actually already have the whole answer.


Maybe the most obvious way to train a model that wants to run autoregressively is to train it autoregressively: just give it the input, have it generate token 1, feed that back in to generate token 2, and so on, and every time you look at the correct answer and ask if it was right or wrong.
That would work, but it’s a bad idea and not done in practice for two huge reasons:

Sequential generation like that is painfully slow. Generating the output one step at a time means doing an entire forward pass, through the whole big decoder, with a whole new pass per token. You can’t parallelize, run through whole batches at once, or take real good advantage of knowing what the whole sequence should be ahead of time.
Early in training, the model is terrible. If you rely on what the model generates at step \(i\) to determine step \(i+1\), it’s likely to be wrong at \(i+1\) if it was wrong at \(i\). It will compound its own errors over the sequence and likely just produce garbage, especially early on. But as those errors compound, the model can struggle to even get started on actually good trajectories.

Teacher forcing fixes both. And the core idea is to exploit the feature that we’ve already mentioned here a few times: during training, you have an entire correct sequence, and you know what the next token should be given the truth so far at every step. Teacher forcing just does exactly this - instead of running the “real” autoregressive loop, where the model gets its own previously generated tokens back, we only ever give it the ground-truth for a given position. We say “what would you generate for j…. given this is what {a….i} actually was”. The teacher “forces” the correct history at every step.
And remember, this is actually the whole reason we built the causal mask! As we discussed in Section 4 and then proved in Appendix 4, causal masking keeps previous tokens in the sequence frozen, not allowing them to look ahead. We did this so that the current position we’re looking at is the only one that has “full access” to see everything. But if we trained autoregressively, where we pick off the last row to predict the next token anyway, then who cares if a previous position’s embedding changes - we’re only looking at the most recent one anyway. It’s precisely because we want to feed the model the entire target sequence at once, and see how every token position does with the true prefix, that we need the causal mask - it allows us to predict the next token at every position at once in a single parallel forward pass.
(I encourage you to visit Appendix 4 if you haven’t already and need to see this play out with the exact matrix math. We work out there that, with masked self attention, for a sequence of length 2 vs. length 3, the rows that correspond to the 1 and 2 position don’t change. So they don’t change for an n-length sequence, either. Masked attention lets us put in the whole sequence at once, and still get a prediction “as if” the tokens ahead didn’t exist)



Ok, so conceptually, it’s simple. And the masked self attention almost gives it to us without any extra effort. Mechanically, the one thing that we have to add is just a one-position shift.
Say the full target we want is:
\[\text{target} = [\texttt{<bos>}, \,y_1,\ y_2,\ \dots,\ y_n,\ \texttt{<eos>}\,]\]
Then to see if the decoder actually produces that, we need to give that sequence as input. Except because there’s nothing to predict at the end of the sequence, we drop the <eos>:
\[\text{decoder input} = [\,\texttt{<bos>},\ y_1,\ y_2,\ \dots,\ y_n\,]\]
And then the label, the thing we actually want to predict, is simply the target sentence, shifted one to the left with the start <bos> removed:
\[\text{truth label} = [\,y_1,\ y_2,\ \dots,\ y_n,\ \texttt{<eos>}\,]\]
Think about what this gives us and why this works. When we pass an input into the decoder, we get, as each row of the output, a prediction of what the next token will be.
\[\text{input} = [\texttt{<bos>},\ y_1]
\\
\\
X_{\text{out}} = \begin{bmatrix} X_{\text{out, 1}} \\ X_{\text{out, 2}} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{matrix} \leftarrow \text{prediction for} \ y_1 \\ \leftarrow \text{prediction for} \ y_2 \end{matrix}
\]
Then for a given input, what we want out is the next token for every token of that input. It’s why we just need to do that single shift to get labels. Both are constructed from the truth, but the relative shift means then we get to grade what the input says will come next.
This is also why the causal mask gets to be so simple - since we pass in the whole sequence like this, the causal mask is just sized to remove the later tokens, decreasing what’s blocked one-by-one. That means exactly the triangular mask we talked about.
In code, trg is the full target sequence. Then the actual input to the decoder is just the target with the last token removed. The label, as we said, is just the target, shifted by one after removal of the <bos> token:
decoder_input = trg[:, :-1]   # everything except the last token
labels        = trg[:, 1:]    # everything except the first (<bos>)



There is one more thing to mention here, just quickly before we move on. Teacher forcing means that the model always trains on correct prefixes. At each step, all of the tokens coming before are from the ground truth. So the model only makes mistakes for one token at a time - we can correct it towards the right token, but only given it messes up based on something previously correct.
Of course, at generation time, the model will have to build on its own outputs. But these can be wrong, meaning mistakes can compound - and each one can lead to the whole downstream trajectory of the generated sequence being wrong.
This mismatch is called exposure bias, and it’s a known limitation of teacher forcing. Basically, the model can become out of distribution - in a state that it doesn’t know what to do with, that it’s never seen before, just because of a mistake it made earlier on, that it never would’ve encountered during training. That’s where the name comes from: the model was only ever exposed to clean, correct histories, so the distribution of prefixes it trained on is biased away from the messier, sometimes-wrong ones it actually faces when generating.
In practice, this is often tolerable and a fairly small effect, given you train with enough data to generalize and are starting with a capable model. If so, the model will likely mostly produce its own good prefixes anyway, and errors will rarely cascade catastrophically. So teacher forcing is still the standard approach, and the one we’ll use here. But just know that this is a potential concern, and indeed, one that people in the field are thinking about. (There are some tricks that deliberately feed the model some of its own predictions during training to close the gap, like scheduled sampling, but we will not cover that here!)




So, we use teacher forcing to generate our outputs all at once:

run the decoder_input through the model
get logits of shape (N, trg_len, vocab_size), which contains a score for every vocabulary token at every position
look at labels, which has shape (N, trg_len), and contains the single correct token ID at each position

Then, we just need to compare logits to labels.
Compare…. how? That, of course, is the job of the loss function - it quantifies just how wrong the model was compared to what we wanted it to produce, in a way that we can optimize for, to try to make it smaller next time.


Before we talk about the specific one that we use, let’s take a minute to remind ourselves what a loss function is in general, and what it needs to do.
A loss function’s core job is to take the model’s output and the correct answer and returns a single number that says how wrong it was. Even though that might seem like a relatively simple task, it’s the thing that ends up determining all learning. Training the model is just literally tweaking the model’s weights to make the loss smaller.
So while its role might be pretty simple, that doesn’t mean the loss function itself can just be anything. It needs to satisfy some properties:

It must produce a single scalar. That is a core property. Whatever the model outputs - a whole grid of logits in the case we’re discussing here, the loss needs to boil down to one number that gives an unambiguous notion of the current model’s “quality”.
It needs to be lower when the model is better. The loss should be such that it’s smallest when the prediction matches the truth and larger as the prediction gets more wrong. Training’s job is to minimize it, so “small loss” has to mean “good model.”
It has to be differentiable. This is where we start to get into the weeds of the math, which, for all we’ve done here, is going to be beyond the scope of this notebook. But training only works by computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, so that we can determine how the weights need to move to make the loss smaller. That means the loss must be a smooth function of the model’s outputs.
It should be graded, not just right/wrong. A good loss which gives good training signal should reflect how wrong the model is, not merely whether it’s wrong. This is crucial for stable learning and for our gradients to lead to meaningful improvement.

Those last two points are precisely why we don’t just train on pure accuracy, literally if the output is right or wrong. Accuracy is a step function: 1 if right, 0 if wrong, and flat everywhere in between. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere, so it can’t tell you how to improve a wrong answer. Instead, we choose a smooth, graded stand-in that rewards getting closer to the right answer even before it’s exactly right.



The standard choice of loss function in language modeling tasks is the cross-entropy, which you may actually know as the standard choice in classification tasks. It’s powerful, but incredibly simple, and we’ll see why it’s the perfect choice here.
Consider what the model actually gives us as its output. For every single token that we put into the decoder, we get a score of likelihood for every token in the vocabulary, that that token is the one that comes next.
\[
X_{\text{out}} = \begin{bmatrix} X_{\text{out, 1}} \\ X_{\text{out, 2}} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{matrix} \leftarrow \text{prediction for} \ i \\ \leftarrow \text{prediction for} \ i+1 \end{matrix}
\]
\[
\text{output}(X_{\text{out, 1}}) = \begin{bmatrix} p_1 \ \quad \quad p_2 \ ... \ \quad p_n \end{bmatrix} \\
\quad \quad \quad \quad  \quad \quad\begin{matrix} ⇑ \ \quad \quad ⇑ \ \quad \quad ⇑ \end{matrix} \\
\quad \quad \quad \quad  \quad \quad \begin{matrix} \text{prob}(1) \ \ \ \text{prob}(2) \ \ \ \text{prob}(n)\end{matrix}
\]
We get a probability, for every token in the vocabulary. But we also have exactly one correct answer. So it really is a classification problem in the end, for which the standard loss is cross-entropy. The reason that cross-entropy is so good for a case like that, is that we can also think of the correct answer as a probability distribution with all of its mass on the correct token, then comparing the distributions comes down to answering the question: “how much does the probability mass you gave to the correct answer match the correct probability mass for that answer - 1?”
So cross-entropy for any position works like this. First, take the output for that position coming out of the decoder, and pass it through the output layer to get the probability distribution over the whole vocabulary. Then, the loss is just the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the correct token:
\[\text{loss} = -\log\, p(\text{correct token})\]
The “negative log” part of this does some real work.

If the model gives the correct token a probability of 1, perfectly correct, then \(-\log(1) = 0\) - no loss, nothing to fix.
If the model gives the correct token a probability near 0, then \(-\log(0) \to\) \(\infty\) (in practice, we don’t let it be literally 0 because of this), and you get a massive penalty for being confidently wrong
If the model is in a reasonable range, the loss is a nice, reasonable range too.

The log helps punish being confidently wrong more severely. The difference between predicting 0.8 and 0.9 for the correct token is: \[ -\log(0.9) + \log (0.8) = -0.118 \] a small amount more loss for the slightly less confidence in the right answer. But the difference between predicting 0.2 and 0.3 for the correct token is: \[ -\log(0.3) + \log (0.2) = -0.405 \] The same lost probability on the right answer costs far more when you were already wrong. The \(−log\) ensures that: the penalty accelerates as the correct answer’s probability heads toward zero.
This is also of course, evident in the very shape of the function, which we can see here:

p = np.linspace(0.02, 1.0, 500)
loss = -np.log(p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(p, loss, color=LINE, linewidth=2.6)

ax.set_xlim(0, 1.02); ax.set_ylim(0, 4.2)
ax.set_xlabel("probability on correct token", fontsize=12, color=TEXT)
ax.set_ylabel("loss   =   \u2212log(p)", fontsize=12, color=TEXT)
ax.tick_params(colors=TEXT); ax.grid(color='#ececec', linewidth=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








So, then to turn each of these predictions into total loss over all of our data, we simply compute this:

at every position,
for every example in the batch,

and average them into a single scalar to summarize how wrong the model was across the whole batch.
The last thing that we need to do though, is just make sure that we ignore the padding. We talked about this during the decoder section, but when we batch, all of our sequences need to get padded to deal with the differing sequence lengths. Those pad positions mark those positions with meaningless filler. But as we also discussed in Section 6.2, the easiest thing to do is still let the model produce logits for them, and then just be sure to ignore them later. Well here, in the loss calculation, is the “later” where you need to ignore them.
It’s easier to do here - we just tell the loss to skip them. And in code, PyTorch’s built-in nn.CrossEntropyLoss handles that for us. We pass ignore_index, which just says what the indices were that we padded on the target sequences, and it keeps them out of the loss calculation:
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=pad_idx)

# logits: (N, trg_len, vocab_size)  ->  (N * trg_len, vocab_size)
# labels: (N, trg_len)              ->  (N * trg_len,)
loss = loss_fn(logits.reshape(-1, vocab_size), labels.reshape(-1))
The things to note here about CrossEntropyLoss:

It expects a 2D (num_items, vocab_size) tensor of logits and a 1D (num_items,) tensor of labels, so we flatten the batch and position axes together. Every (example, position) pair becomes one classification item.
It takes raw logits, not softmaxed probabilities, because it applies the log-softmax internally. So we actually just feed it the output of output_projection directly. Our built Transformer already outputs logits, so this is just a step we need to be sure to avoid, not something extra we’ll need to do
ignore_index=pad_idx drops every item whose label is the pad token, so they contribute nothing to the average. We simply remember what we padded, and pass it in!




Cross-entropy is the natural fit here because of what our output is: at each position the model produces a distribution over a discrete vocabulary, with exactly one correct token, which as we’ve already discussed is a classification problem. Cross-entropy is the canonical loss for that, and for next-token language modeling it’s nearly universal. And it isn’t an arbitrary pick, either. Minimizing cross-entropy is the same thing as maximizing the probability the model assigns to the true data, so it forces the correct tokens to be as likely as possible, which means it’s exactly the behavior we want.
But, it’s worth asking: is there another loss that could be a good fit? Is there ever a time we’d want a different one? The answer is really just that the right loss depends on the task, and specifically, on what the model outputs.

Classification means the model chooses one of K discrete options - exactly our case here, and the general case for language modeling. Cross-entropy is a good, universal choice.
Regression, though, would mean the model predicts a continuous value (a price, a coordinate, a temperature, a pixel value), and there, you’d have to choose a different loss, maybe something like MSE (mean squared error), the squared distance to the true value.

So while everything we’ve talked about here has focused on language specifically, the basic transformer architecture is not required to output probabilities over tokens. And in a case where your transformer produces a continuous values per position instead, you’d choose an entirely different loss.
All of that being said, though cross-entropy is the standard choice, we didn’t strictly have to pick it. Remember, all we had to make sure of was that the loss satisfied the key rules we laid out above.
So even within next-token prediction, what else could you choose? Well, actually in the original Transformer, they used label smoothing, where instead of asking the model to put all the probability on the single correct token, you actually do build a probability distribution for the correct answer that has most, but not all of its mass on the correct token. Compared to what we just did, it might sound counterproductive, but it can keep the model from becoming overconfident and help it generalize better.
Of course, some setups change the objective entirely, for instance if you train your model with reinforcement learning which brings its own, very different loss. But that would be WAY too much to dig into here, so we’ll leave it at that.
The critical point is that the loss is a flexible thing to choose, but should always be chosen in a way that genuinely encodes what “good” means, as best as it can, for the specific task. Cross-entropy is a good choice here, and usually a good choice for language modeling, so it’s definitely the one to know for this task.




So, we have a loss function, and we use it to calculate how “wrong” the model is in its current state. We glossed over it, but we know that the loss is something that’s differentiable such that it produces gradients that tell us how to tweak every weight. The last thing is to decide how much to tweak by.
The loss does tell us this - the gradients have values which are larger when the model needs to change more and smaller when it needs to change less. But in learning, stability is of critical importance. If we just listened to how much the loss told us to change the weights by, for some weights that might be HUGE and swing the model to a very different place, sometimes tiny and barely change at all. It’s too much burden on just the loss to decide all of that. So instead, we define an optimizer, which tells you what to do with the signal coming from the loss, to update in the right direction, but keep things more stable.


The loss you get, while calculated from comparing the model’s produced answer to the truth, in reality depends on every weight in the model, since those all work to produce the output. In a real model, that can be billions of individual numbers.
For each one, we can compute a gradient of the loss with respect to that weight. The gradient for every weight points uphill, toward higher loss. So to “correct” that weight in a way that reduces the loss, you take a step the opposite way - downhill in slope - for every weight at once:
\[\text{weight} \leftarrow \text{weight} - (\text{its gradient})\]
If you keep doing this every time you see data, the loss will trend downward. This is gradient descent, the engine under essentially all neural-network training.
(Computing all those gradients efficiently, in one backward sweep through the whole network, is backpropagation. PyTorch handles this for us, so we won’t cover it in any depth here. But if you want the full mechanics, see my Basic Neural Network tutorial. The exact same principles apply to the transformer, so we just need to understand at a high-level here that that’s what happens.)



The thing about gradients though, is that they can be very large. If you just subtract the gradient, you might take a huge step downhill for that weight - maybe too far of a step. So in reality, what we do is set a learning rate, which just lessens the amount that we update by:
\[\text{weight} \leftarrow \text{weight} - (\text{learning rate}) \times (\text{its gradient})\]
The learning rate is really just a step size. The direction of update, and even the relative strength, is still coming from the gradient, which directly comes from the loss. But the learning rate lets you keep updates more gentle. It’s just one number, but because it literally determines how much the model can update, it’s one of the most important knobs in all of training:

If you make it too large, you can overshoot the corrections every time. The loss can bounce around trying to fix itself with huge updates, sometimes even diverging (the loss explodes).
But, if you make it too small, training can slow to a halt - effectively barely changing the model at all.

Just setting a learning rate, and letting the model go based off of that is “plain” gradient descent. It’s a little crude, but it will work ok if you get the learning rate right. In practice though, optimizing weights to reduce a loss is a hard problem, especially when the model is massive. So an optimizer does a few extra things that modulate this learning rate and help the model learn better over its whole training trajectory.



For a large model with many weights, the optimizer is just an algorithm that essentially helps determine how much to actually update the weight, still based off of the gradients, based on how training is going. This is especially important because training is not an inherently stable thing.

When you just start training, the model has been initialized with random weights - it will be terrible at the task, and so updates will be massive because the model will be so far from the optimum.
But later in training, when you’re close to a really good model, a lot of the weights just need to move a little to make the model a little bit better. Sometimes a boost can help ensure they move enough.

The standard choice for transformers is the Adam optimizer, which tries to tackle these issues with a few additional parameters:

Momentum. Instead of using only the current gradient, Adam keeps a running average of recent ones. This means that updates “build up speed”. If a lot of your recent updates have been moving in one direction, you’re allowed to take a bigger step, since likely that weight really does need to move significantly. But if your updates have been bouncing around, the update isn’t allowed to be as large - there isn’t a firm direction that we know we need to move in.
A per-parameter learning rate. Adam also tracks how large each weight’s gradients have typically been, and scales the weight’s step accordingly. Weights that are consistently getting large updates have those updates dampened a little - making sure the steps they’re taking aren’t too big. Weights that are only getting tiny tweaks get boosted a bit - making sure that the weight is really getting an update instead of sitting there unchanged. Every weight gets an appropriately-sized update automatically, instead of forcing one global learning rate to suit all of them.

Concretely, Adam keeps two running averages per weight, one of the gradient (m, the momentum) and one of the squared gradient (v, the typical magnitude), governed by decay rates β₁ (typically ≈0.9) and β₂ (typically ≈0.999).
\[
\begin{aligned}
m &\leftarrow \beta_1\, m + (1-\beta_1)\, g && \text{(1st moment: momentum)}\\
v &\leftarrow \beta_2\, v + (1-\beta_2)\, g^2 && \text{(2nd moment: typical magnitude}^2\text{)}\\
\end{aligned}
\]
Then,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{m} &= \frac{m}{1-\beta_1^{\,t}}, \quad \hat{v} = \frac{v}{1-\beta_2^{\,t}}
\end{aligned}
\]
And our final weight update actually looks like this: \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{weight} &\leftarrow \text{weight} - (\text{lr})\cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \varepsilon}
\end{aligned}
\]
With some small \(\varepsilon\) to prevent divide by 0. So those two properties that we mentioned above are showing up as:

Momentum is the numerator \(\hat{m}\). It’s the running average of the actual gradient, updated at each step to include the current gradient. \(\beta_1\) (default 0.9) is its decay rate, how much to weight past-gradient memory it keeps. A high \(\beta_1\) means a long memory.
Per-parameter learning rate is the division by \(\sqrt{\hat{v}}\) in the denominator. \(\hat{v}\) is the running average of the squared gradient, which is an estimate of how big this weight’s gradients typically are. Dividing by it shrinks steps for consistently-large-gradient weights and boosts quiet ones. Its decay rate is \(\beta_2\) (default 0.999)




In PyTorch, the optimizer is one object, created over the model’s parameters:
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
This does take values for all of the parameters we just talked about - \(β_1\), \(β_2\), and \(ɛ\) - but if you don’t set them, it uses the defaults we discussed above (.9, .999. \(10^{-8}\)), which in practice are universally good parameters for Adam, so you don’t usually change them.

📌 Note: The original Transformer paper actually used .9, .98, and \(10^{-9}\) as its Adam parameters. It’s a pretty small change, and the defaults are known to be good, so we’ll go with defaults even though that’s not technically what the original did exactly.

Notice, again, that this just needs to take model.parameters(). The optimizer understands both to use and to update every weight registered through the module tree.
Then each training step on a batch can happen in just three lines:
optimizer.zero_grad()   # 1. clear the gradients left from the last batch
loss.backward()         # 2. backprop: get the gradient of the loss from every weight
optimizer.step()        # 3. update every weight using those gradients
The things to note:

zero_grad() comes first because PyTorch accumulates gradients by default. If we don’t have this, this batch’s gradients pile on top of the last batch’s.
loss.backward() handles all backpropagation, and gives back a .grad for every parameter.
optimizer.step() runs the update we just discussed above. Using the gradient the loss gives us, and the actual weight value, calculate the internal Adam parameters, and update the weight.





One more thing. Even with Adam, which helps smooth how the gradients behave, we still had a fixed learning rate. This, actually, is a whole separate thing that is usually dynamic over training via learning rate scheduling.
The idea goes back to what we already mentioned: at the very start, the weights are random and the gradients are wild, and a large learning rate can make updates too large and destabilize training. Not even Adam totally fixes this, as especially at the beginning, there isn’t a big gradient history to use.
So, the standard thing to do is to warm up the learning rate - essentially, take a few hundred to a few thousand of the first steps to grow the learning rate from something very small to its “full size”, so that the first few sets of updates aren’t huge. It also will then slowly decay it once it reaches its full size, making sure that tweaks are smaller when you get closer to a good model, as you also don’t want to risk big updates messing it up.


The exact schedule the original Transformer used is:
\[\text{lr}(\text{step}) = {d_{\text{model}}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min\!\left(\text{step}^{-0.5},\ \text{step} \cdot \text{warmup}^{-1.5}\right)\]
So a few things to unpack there.
First, you might be wondering: Why is the learning rate a function of \(d_{\text{model}}\)? The job of that factor is just to set the overall scale. Wider models tend to produce larger-magnitude activations and gradients (actually, we do this for the same reason attention divides by \(√d_k\) - because sums over more dimensions grow like \(√d_{\text{model}}\)), so the learning rate is scaled down to compensate. Baking it into the formula just means the same schedule works across model sizes without needing to re-tune what the peak will be by hand.
The other two terms inside the \(min\) are the two phases made explicit:

while \(\text{step}\) is small, \(\text{step}\)· \(\text{warmup}^{-1.5}\) is the smaller term, and grows linearly,
once \(\text{step}\) passes \(\text{warmup}\) , \(\text{step}^{-0.5}\) takes over and the rate decays as \(1/√\text{step}\).
they are equal exactly at \(\text{step}\) = \(\text{warmup}\) , which is the peak.

We can see exactly what this looks like:

d_model, warmup = 512, 4000
steps = np.arange(1, 20001)
lr = d_model**-0.5 * np.minimum(steps**-0.5, steps * warmup**-1.5)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
plt.plot(steps, lr, color="#5B8FB9", linewidth=2.2)
plt.xlabel("training step")
plt.ylabel("learning rate")
plt.title("Transformer learning-rate schedule (warmup then decay)")
plt.show()











In PyTorch, of course, you don’t need to compute this by hand for each step, as there’s a way to simply set what the learning rate scheduler will be. LambdaLR takes a function of the step number and uses it to scale the learning rate:
d_model      = 512     # same as the model's d_model
warmup_steps = 4000

def lr_lambda(step):
    step = max(step, 1)                               # avoid step=0 blowing up
    return d_model ** -0.5 * min(step ** -0.5, step * warmup_steps ** -1.5)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1.0)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lr_lambda)
If we set the optimizer’s base lr=1.0, the schedule is the learning rate - LambdaLR multiplies the base lr by whatever lr_lambda returns.
Then the training loop needs one more addition, where after each weight update, you step the scheduler too.
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
scheduler.step()      # <- advance the learning rate



Of course, as with all decisions made in model training, we don’t have to pick that exact scheduler. And while we’ve chosen inverse square root for our training for its simplicity and because it’s what the original transformer did, modern training has mostly moved to different decay shapes. The warmup part, though, has stuck around almost universally - nearly every other modern choice still ramps the learning rate up at the start.
So, what are people usually using now instead? The most common modern choice is cosine decay, which warms up, then has the learning rate follow the shape of a cosine curve. Not oscillating - just gliding smoothly from its peak down to near zero as a cosine does. It’s a bit smoother than the \(1/√\text{step}\) decay and reliably ends very low, which tends to help the model settle into a good minimum. It’s what GPT-3 and many modern LLMs use.
But, there are also other common shapes:

Linear decay is a straight ramp down to zero after warming up. Simple and very common (BERT and many Hugging Face defaults use this).
Constant with warmup just holds the rate flat after warming up. Very simple, and often does work perfectly fine.

So whatever shape you choose, there are really only a few knobs to set:

Peak learning rate - whatever the maximum value you’ll ever reach is. It’s still the single most important number.
Warmup length - how long it will take you to reach peak. Usually a few hundred to a few thousand, or a small fraction of total training.
Final learning rate - whether you’ll decay all the way to zero or stop at some small floor.

But almost all of them will warm up in some way, reach some peak, and then decide by how much to decay after. This general shape is where you get the benefits, and exactly how you implement it is a choice you can make.




Across this section we’ve made a complete, working set of training choices, and flagged where some alternatives exist. Nothing that we’ve set up here, which is how we’ll proceed with training, is wrong, but still, modern training has some genuinely new additions, and some minor tweaks, to the choices we’ve made that are worth at least mentioning so that you’re aware of them, even though we won’t cover them in any depth here.
So before we go on, here’s a quick rundown of a handful of things that modern, large-scale training does differently.

Weight decay. A common additional regularizer is added to the weights themselves with something called weight decay. Its job is to gently shrink every weight toward zero on each step. The idea is that large weights tend to signal an overfit, brittle model, so nudging them all slightly downward each update discourages that - again, requiring no single weight to ever be too large or too important. How it’s actually done is by subtracting a small fraction \(\lambda \cdot \text{weight}\) from each weight every update, where \(\lambda\) sets the strength. It’s an optional addition to the optimizer step that’s fairly standard.
Adam vs. AdamW. However, if you do want weight decay, how you add it into the optimizer step matters. Our implementation will not use weight decay, but standard Adam adds in weight decay like this: when you go to update the gradient, folds it in right there, by using \(g + \lambda w\) in place of \(g\). You just apply it right to the gradient you’re about to run Adam on. But that means that the \(\lambda w\) term rides through everything, including the division by \(\sqrt{\hat v}\). That ends up distorting it - weights with large, active gradients get decayed less and quiet ones more, instead of all uniformly. AdamW just “corrects” this by applying weight decay in a place where it’s more stable. It applies the decay directly to the weight update, outside of the \(\sqrt{\hat v}\) scaling: \[\text{weight} \leftarrow \text{weight} - (\text{lr})\left(\frac{\hat m}{\sqrt{\hat v} + \varepsilon} + \lambda\,\text{weight}\right)\] so all weights get an identical decay rate. It’s a one-line change, but because of it, AdamW is the default optimizer for essentially all transformers.
(Note that with no weight decay, Adam and AdamW are actually identical, so the choice only matters if you’re doing weight decay at all.)
Gradient clipping. Gradients can still be overly large during training. To prevent this, gradient clipping simply caps the overall size allowed (via the norm of the gradient) at some threshold, commonly 1.0, to scale it down if it’s too big. This is done before the optimizer, and just stops unlucky batches with enormous gradients from making a single catastrophic update that wrecks training. This is also now nearly universal.
Mixed-precision training. Because modern models are large, rather than 32-bit floats everywhere, most modern training runs the bulk of the math in 16-bit. 16-bit floats are smaller and faster, but they have far less precision and (for fp16) far less range than 32-bit. “Mixed” precision means running the parts that can tolerate that in 16-bit while keeping the parts that can’t in 32-bit. The big matrix multiplies of the forward and backward pass run in 16-bit - it’s where nearly all the compute is, so that’s where the speed and memory savings come from. Other crucial parts, that can benefit from more precision, stay in 32-bit. These are:

The master copy of the weights, and the optimizer step that updates them. The update \(\text{lr}\cdot\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}\) is often tiny next to the weight itself (maybe \(10^{-7}\) added to a weight of order \(10^{-1}\)). In 16-bit, a number that small is below the precision available at the larger weight’s magnitude, so it can round away to nothing. So a “real” copy of the weights is kept in 32-bit and updated in full precision, with a 16-bit copy used for the forward/backward compute.
Any reductions or sums over many values. Operations like softmax, LayerNorm, and the loss require adding up many numbers. Doing this in 16-bit loses precision as small terms get swallowed by a large running total, so these accumulate in 32-bit. Adam’s moment estimates are in 32-bit as well, for the same reason.

(fp16 actually has one extra wrinkle: its range is so small that gradients can underflow straight to zero, so training scales the loss up before the backward pass and scales the gradients back down after. bf16 has the same range as 32-bit, just with less precision, so it skips that step. This is why it’s often preferred when the hardware supports it!)
Gradient accumulation. Often in compute-limited situations, the batch size you want won’t fit in memory, but dropping a batch size has consequences for generalization and stability. In this case, you instead run several smaller batches, not changing the model after each but instead add up their gradients, and only step the optimizer once. It simulates a large batch without paying its memory cost.

It’s worth noting that so much of what modern models do also has a lot to do with scale. Frontier models run their training loops across many GPUs at once (data and model parallelism), over vastly more data, and often in multiple stages. So a lot of what has been developed in modern modeling has been to help in cases where the training scale and model size is truly massive, and designed to be multi-step.



Ok, so now that we’ve talked about all of the pieces of the training loop, let’s put it together. The fortunate thing, is that we basically already built the core workhorse of it as we’ve gone through this section.
Here’s what it ends up looking like. We define a few components at the start. A couple of these will still depend on our data, so we won’t write them into code quite yet.
model     = Transformer(...).to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1.0)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lr_lambda)
loss_fn   = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=pad_idx)
But once those are defined, the loop that runs the training just takes those as arguments:

def train_epoch(model, data_loader, optimizer, scheduler, loss_fn, device,
                global_step, target_set, save_ckpt):
    model.train()                                  # put the model in training mode (dropout ON)
    total_loss = 0.0

    for src, trg in data_loader:                   # src: (N, src_len), trg: (N, trg_len), the data
        src, trg = src.to(device), trg.to(device)

        # --- teacher forcing: shift the target by one ---
        decoder_input = trg[:, :-1]                # [<bos>, y1, ..., yn]
        labels        = trg[:, 1:]                 # [y1, ..., yn, <eos>]

        # --- run the forward pass from the model we built before ---
        logits = model(src, decoder_input)         # (N, trg_len-1, vocab_size)

        # --- compute the loss: flatten as input, give to loss_fn ---
        loss = loss_fn(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)),  # (N*(trg_len-1), vocab_size)
                       labels.reshape(-1))                    # (N*(trg_len-1),)

        # --- go through all of the update steps ---
        optimizer.zero_grad()                      # clear last batch's gradients
        loss.backward()                            # backprop to compute new gradients
        optimizer.step()                           # update every weight
        scheduler.step()                           # advance the learning rate

        total_loss += loss.item()

        # --- save a checkpoint off, in STEPS not EPOCHS - we'll use later ---
        global_step += 1                           # global_step keeps track of where we are
        if global_step in target_set:
            save_ckpt(global_step)                 # save if it's a predefined saving step

    return total_loss / len(data_loader), global_step         # average loss over the epoch

Notice that this loop just runs for one epoch. One epoch is one pass over all of the data, which we do in batches that are much smaller than the size of all of the data. So we accumulate the loss and then average it over the number of batches that we have at the end. One epoch takes many steps. (Inside this function, we’ve snuck in a way to save checkpoints on steps not epochs, because we want to use that granularity later.)
Running for many epochs, then, just means wrapping this in another loop, which again, I still won’t write into a real code cell yet, since some of this is waiting to be defined.
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    avg_loss = train_epoch(model, train_loader, optimizer, scheduler, loss_fn, device)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:2d} | loss {avg_loss:.4f}")
But that’s it! A few decisions to be made, but it still comes together into something very brief and readable.
The training loop is really just a few key steps:

The model is defined, and model.train() just puts it into training mode, turning dropout on (model.eval() by contrast, turns it off so we can actually use the model)
We shift for teacher forcing, using exactly the same code we called out earlier in this section.
model(src, decoder_input) runs the forward pass of the whole architecture we built in Section 6. And notice we don’t build any masks here: the Transformer’s forward constructs src_mask and trg_mask internally from the inputs, because it’s well understood how to structure them based on that.
The loss is exactly the code we used earlier in the loss section. We must flatten batch and position together, set the ignore_index to drop the padding, and make sure we give it raw logits.

It all ends in the optimizer update that we defined. Clear out old gradients, calculate the new ones, give them to the optimizer, then advance the learning rate scheduler.




Ok. So everything we’ve set up so far has actually been fairly task-agnostic - we said what we would do with data when it came in, and how that data would matter, but so far everything about this setup could still apply to a variety of different encoder-decoder tasks. We’ve made some choices based on the type of task (like whether or not the input to the encoder vs decoder share a vocabulary), but that’s still broad, not based on specific task we’re training for.
In this section, we’re going to make it real. Choose a real task, build data, make our vocabulary, batch it, and watch our transformer train to do something it actually is good at learning.


We’ve talked about how the encoder-decoder architecture is good for tasks like translation, where really, you want to produce an outgoing piece of text, based on your understanding of some separate, other sequence. Date formatting is a good example of a (very simple, so we can train it quickly) version of this task.
Our goal is going to be to construct a small dataset of dates in standard variations of “human” formatting:
\[\text{sept 04 2015 ; 22 may 2026 ; october 19, 1950}\]
And we’ll want to translate them into a standardized YYYY-MM-DD (ISO) formatting:
\[ \text{2015-09-04 ; 2026-05-22 ; 1950-10-19}\]
That’s it! Now, could this task be done more simply with a classic lookup table? Absolutely, yes. But a transformer can also learn to do it perfectly, which means we’ll get to see real training happen. So no, this isn’t some kind of breakthrough task, but we can easily generate large amounts of data here, and train a model in a few minutes, so it’s what we’ll go with.
So, let’s write a quick function to generate the data. We pick random dates, render each into one of several human-readable formats for the input, and pair it with its standardized target string:

INPUT_FORMATS = [
    "%d %B %Y",        # 03 march 2019
    "%B %d, %Y",       # march 03, 2019
    "%d %b %Y",        # 03 mar 2019
    "%b %d %Y",        # mar 03 2019
    "%A, %B %d, %Y",   # sunday, march 03, 2019
    "%d/%m/%Y",        # 03/03/2019  (always day/month/year)
]

def random_date(start_year=1950, end_year=2049):
    start, end = date(start_year, 1, 1), date(end_year, 12, 31)
    return start + timedelta(days=random.randint(0, (end - start).days))

def make_example():
    d = random_date()
    human = d.strftime(random.choice(INPUT_FORMATS)).lower()
    iso   = d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    return human, iso

random.seed(0)
dataset = [make_example() for _ in range(50000)]

A few small design choices worth calling out:

The inputs vary in length, the outputs don’t. Across the dataset the human inputs run from about 10 to 29 characters (15 may 1976 vs tuesday, december 13, 1994). Every ISO target, though, is exactly 10 (YYYY-MM-DD). This is deliberate because it makes the need for padding real - we’ll have to pad the shorter inputs when we batch them. The fixed-length target means no target padding, though that was the less interesting case (it’s all handled internally for us), so that’s ok.
We’ll lowercase everything. In my above example, I capitalized months. But keeping both capital and lowercase is extra vocabulary, for no benefit - march is the same as March, and both get turned into 03 anyway, so it’s the kind of choice that just makes sense for a task like this. We’ll see this lowercasing pay off in the next part when we make the vocabulary.
Every format is unambiguous. We chose a variety of input formats to make the task a little more interesting, but none of them are missing information, and none of them could mean anything else. In practice for dates especially, that means choosing one purely numeric format (DD/MM/YYYY, day-first). If we’d also included MM/DD/YYYY, then a string like 03/04/2019 would have two valid answers and no way to know the intended formatting. So we choose just one so that every input→output mapping is well-defined.




So, the next step is to build a vocabulary from all of our data. Since we’re going to work at the character level (the model needs to produce one character at a time for dates), and the source and target share an alphabet, we just need one, pretty small vocabulary.
(For that reason… we aren’t going to build it up from BPE like we had talked about at the start of this notebook. BPE makes a lot of sense when you’re building up from a large corpus of data where you don’t know, or it’s impossible to know, exactly what’s in it and what pieces are most common. The task we’ve chosen here is a rare case where we want to work on the character level, so making the vocabulary is just “what are all the different characters that show up”. We don’t need to build statistics-based bindings of tokens - our total vocabulary is going to have like 40 items to begin with.)

# every character that appears, in inputs or targets
chars = set()
for human, iso in dataset:
    chars.update(human)
    chars.update(iso)

# special tokens FIRST, so that <pad> gets ID 0
special = ["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>"]
vocab = special + sorted(chars)

char_to_id = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(vocab)}
id_to_char = {i: c for i, c in enumerate(vocab)}

pad_idx = char_to_id["<pad>"]   # 0
bos_idx = char_to_id["<bos>"]   # 1
eos_idx = char_to_id["<eos>"]   # 2
vocab_size = len(vocab)

print("VOCAB SIZE:", vocab_size)
print("TOTAL VOCAB:", vocab)

So, just a tiny 39-token vocabulary. And it’s a nice sanity check actually that k, q, x, or z, never appear, because no month or weekday name ever uses them. So it still is genuinely built from the data, as it should be.
Two things just got decided here, which all through sections 6 and 7 we said would “need to come from the data”:

pad_idx is now 0. We listed all of the special tokens first, and <pad> was the first of them. That means that the token ID 0 will always mean “padding”.
vocab_size is 39. We of course need to give this number to the output projection and the shared embedding table, and now we know it.

Then tokenizing is just a lookup to the right index, and we tokenize the source and target the same, except that the target will need the special start/end tokens:

def encode_src(s):
    return [char_to_id[c] for c in s]                          # just the characters

def encode_trg(s):
    return [bos_idx] + [char_to_id[c] for c in s] + [eos_idx]  # needs to also wrap in <bos> and <eos>

So we see it works exactly how we want. The target sequence has <bos>=1 at the front, and <eos>=2 at back. Besides that, the sequences match their number of characters since we encode character-by-character. The ISO-format is exactly the length we expect (12: <bos> + 10 ISO chars + <eos>). So these functions give our tokenized sequences, ready to go.



Now, it’s time to put the data together into a batch, and this is where padding also comes into play. Remember, we need to pad the shorter sources in our batch out to match the length of the longest one in the batch, filling with <pad> (which is ID 0).
In PyTorch, we build our dataset to do this with a Dataset object. This handles the fact that batches constructed of different sources will need different amounts of padding (you always pad to the longest in the batch, not globally, to save compute). This will also handle the tokenizing via those functions we just defined.

class DateDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, pairs):
        self.pairs = pairs
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.pairs)
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        human, iso = self.pairs[idx]
        return (torch.tensor(encode_src(human), dtype=torch.long), # use the functions we just wrote
                torch.tensor(encode_trg(iso),  dtype=torch.long))

# finish constructing the batch by padding when needed
def collate(batch):
    srcs, trgs = zip(*batch)
    # pad each side to the longest sequence in this batch, filling with pad_idx
    src = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(srcs, batch_first=True, padding_value=pad_idx)
    trg = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(trgs, batch_first=True, padding_value=pad_idx)
    return src, trg

train_loader = DataLoader(DateDataset(dataset), batch_size=16,
                          shuffle=True, collate_fn=collate)


DateDataset’s job is just to turn (human, iso) pairs into the two token-ID tensors
collate is where the padding happens. The DataLoader is what gathers batch_size examples and hands them to collate to fill them as needed. Within collate, batch_first=True just says to put the batch dimension first, giving the \((N, n_{\text{seq}})\) shape our model expects.
DataLoader ties it together. It shuffles the data each epoch and yields padded (src, trg) batches.

Now, our example here was really simple, so we also could have done this without the DataLoader, without too much trouble. But the Dataset/DataLoader pair is the standard PyTorch way that you’d realistically use and see in almost every implementation. The only hard requirement for using it is that the Dataset must implement two methods:

__len__ (how many examples), and
__getitem__(i) (get the i-th one)

That’s why our DateDataset implements exactly those two. The collate function is technically optional, but you do almost always have to supply it, because PyTorch’s default batching will assume every example is already the same size.



So the data is ready. The final thing is to construct the model with the specific choices for its configuration. This includes all things we get to choose and could tune: the model sizes, the optimizer parameters, and feeding in the information we collected while generating our data.
We’ll define them in the cell below, first thing, so you can see plainly all of the choices we get to make.

# ---- Define hyperparameters ----
d_model      = 128      # the original paper used 512 - we scale down to keep small
num_layers   = 3        # the original paper used 6 -  we keep small with 3
heads        = 8        # this is what the original paper used, confirm d_model is divisible by heads
d_ff         = 512      # the FFN inner size (we choose 4 x d_model, as in the paper)
dropout      = 0.1      # 0.1 is fairly standard
max_len      = 40       # most the model is allowed to generate. must exceed our longest sequence (source max ~29)
warmup_steps = 3000      # scaled down from the paper's 4000 - we expect to train fast
num_epochs   = 10

# will be blazing fast if you can get a GPU!
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# ---- Set up the model----
# this is where all of those choices above come to actually shape what this model looks like!
model = Transformer(
    vocab_size  = vocab_size,     # 39
    d_model     = d_model,
    num_layers  = num_layers,
    heads       = heads,
    d_ff        = d_ff,
    max_len     = max_len,
    src_pad_idx = pad_idx,        # 0, decided when we built the vocabulary
    trg_pad_idx = pad_idx,        # 0, decided when we built the vocabulary
    dropout     = dropout,
).to(device)

# ---- Put together the training pieces ----
# we've seen this code before, but only wrote it within markdown
# here, we define it so it's usable.
def lr_lambda(step):
    step = max(step, 1)
    return d_model ** -0.5 * min(step ** -0.5, step * warmup_steps ** -1.5)

# define the optimizer, scheduler, and loss
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1.0, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8) #defining them here to be clear, but these are exactly the defaults for beta/eps.
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lr_lambda)
loss_fn   = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=pad_idx)

A few of the choices I’ll point out:

Our model is a scaled-down version of the original. Where the original paper used d_model=512, 6 layers, and d_ff=2048, we use 128 / 3 / 512. Our task is easy, and our data is small, so a small model will learn it quickly.
max_len must exceed our longest sequence. It determines our positional encoding, so it needs to be at least as big as the longest sequence we’ll ever feed. Our sources top out around 29 characters, so 40 is just comfortable headroom.
warmup_steps is scaled down from 4000 to 3000. The original paper used 4000. But warmup should be chosen based on the number of training steps you’ll do, because it’s determined by the data size, batch size, and number of epochs. For us, ≈ 50,000 examples ÷ 16 per batch ≈ 3125 steps per epoch, × 10 epochs ≈ 31,250 steps. So we need to warm up for a number of steps reasonable for our model size - here, over the first ~epoch.

Now it’s time to actually set the training going! It’s what we’ve been building up to, but at this point the code to actually do it is anticlimatic: it’s actually the exact same code we saw earlier this section, just now made “real” instead of in markdown since there’s now a real model behind it, and with one additional saving step.
So the last little piece of setup we need to do first is get set up to save checkpoints of our model. We already added some infrastructure needed for this into our train loop, but here we’ll define when to actually save. For this model, we’re going to save checkpoints often (you’ll see why later - we are going to use them for something), but in a normal implementation you would not save so frequently, especially not early on.
In general, though, saving some checkpoints is always a good idea. It helps us have multiple points to reload our model from (saving the last few is a good idea, since in general sometimes one or two before the last is actually the best model), and allows any results you get to be exactly reproducible.
This model is small enough, that simply retraining only takes a few minutes. But still, every version of the newly trained model will have its own nuances and behaviors, so saving your model protects from that.

targets, k = {0}, 0

    targets.add(int(1.5 ** k)); k += 1

target_set = {t for t in targets if t <= total_steps}

And there you have it - our date translation model is trained!
There are a few things we can glean from that loss trajectory.

It starts “high”. Even if you’ve re-run this notebook, you probably see this start at around 0.3. An untrained model, with no idea which token comes next, spreads its probability roughly evenly over all 39 vocabulary tokens, so it gives the correct token about 1/39 probability, and the cross-entropy loss should start near −ln(1/39) ≈ 3.66. So by the end of even the first epoch, when that 0.3 reports, it’s already learned how to do the task much better than random. A big part of that is that this task is deterministic and easy, so the model picks up the pattern fast.
By epoch 3, it’s basically trained. The loss falls steeply and then flattens out near zero, with loss values of \(0.00xx\). That flattening is the model essentially nailing the mapping, and like we said, it gets there pretty fast because the task is so easy.

But that second point is actually worth digging into a little more, because you might be thinking, if the task is literally deterministic - trivial - why does it bounce around down near 0 at all? Why not just hone in on the answer and stay there - being literally perfect every time? And it’s worth pointing out, because really it’s a feature of training, coming from several different places, that means we never truly get perfect.

The loss literally can’t be zero. Cross-entropy is −log(p) on the correct token, which is zero only if the model gives that token probability exactly 1. But since the probabilities come from a softmax over finite logits, they can’t actually reach \(1.0\) - that would take an infinitely large logit. So even a flawless model on a perfectly deterministic task has a tiny positive floor it can only ever approach, never touch.
Training is inherently stochastic. Each step’s gradient comes from a different random batch, which is different every epoch, and each batch pulls the weights in the direction that’s best for it specifically. It’s likely that essentially the same weights are good for this task regardless of batch (that’s what generalization is), but you still expect a little bit of push and pull based on the randomness of the batches.
The learning rate is still nonzero. Something has to move in some direction every time. Even with small steps, you have to move a little bit around the exact perfect solution just by virtue of being forced to take some kind of step at all. A learning rate decayed all the way to near zero would shrink those updates to zero, but ours here stays small but positive.
Dropout introduces randomness. During training, dropout randomly zeroes different activations on every forward pass. Even if the current forward pass’s weights were literally perfect, next time, the set of weights allowed to contribute would be slightly different. So really, the network computing the loss is a slightly different network each batch. It helps no specific configuration of weights matter too much, but it also means the training loss can’t be perfectly minimal or perfectly smooth.

None of this matters for whether the model works: the loss ending up at around \(0.00x\) means that the model is putting essentially all its probability on the right character every time. But that little bit of randomness exists due to many of the exact mechanics we’ve been laboring over this whole time, so it’s worth a moment. And this little bit of randomness is a good thing! Yes, on this task, you could find a very exact mapping with a lookup table. But most tasks are not so exactly deterministic, and all of this randomness helps protect against overfitting and forces the model to learn something more general. For almost every use case, that’s exactly what’s desired.
Now, of course, a model can be perfectly performing on the training data, and still not have learned any general mapping. So the thing to do next is to actually give this model examples it has never seen before, and see if it still performs. We’ll dive deep into all of that next!




Now, we have a trained model. The next thing you of course want to do is use it - give it a date, and see if it actually knows what to do.
And beyond that, you might want to know how well it does its job. Not just what one answer looks like - but measuring accuracy on some evaluation set, checking what it does on edge cases, or even on pieces of data that you haven’t exactly shown it before.


The first thing we need to do, then, to see how the model performs, is to be able to run it! And that means use it to generate one token at a time. Back in Section 5 we described generation as a loop, where we start with <bos> token, run it through the decoder, read off the last row, pick a token, append it, feed the longer sequence back in, and repeat until <eos>.
That’s exactly the loop we now need. And we’ll write it into code so that we can actually call it, and then see what it makes for a test sequence.

def generate(model, src_str, max_len=12):
    model.eval()                                           # turns dropout OFF
    src = torch.tensor([encode_src(src_str)], device=device)   # tokenize it with our encode_src
    trg = torch.tensor([[bos_idx]], device=device)             # start with just <bos>

    with torch.no_grad():                                  # no gradients needed at inference
        for _ in range(max_len):                           # generate until max_len is reached
            logits    = model(src, trg)                    # get the logits from the model. size (1, current_len, vocab_size)
            next_id   = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(dim=-1)    # take ONLY the last row only. Greedily pick next token
            trg       = torch.cat([trg, next_id.unsqueeze(0)], dim=1)   # append to the running target sequence
            if next_id.item() == eos_idx:                  # stop if the model emits <eos>
                break

    out_ids = trg[0].tolist()[1:]                          # drop the leading <bos>
    if eos_idx in out_ids:
        out_ids = out_ids[:out_ids.index(eos_idx)]         # cut at <eos>
    return "".join(id_to_char[i] for i in out_ids)         # turn tokens back into characters

So, what exactly is going on here?

First, model.eval() to turn dropout off.
Seed trg with [[bos_idx]] - always signaling the start of generation.
Run it through the model, and get logits[:, -1, :] - just the last row.
Use .argmax for greedy decoding. We could sample here, but the task isn’t really suited to that.
Append the chosen token with torch.cat([trg, next_id ...]) so the next time the loop comes around, trg now includes it.
Break if we produce an end token. if next_id == eos_idx: break is when the model tells us it’s done.
Strip the <bos>, cut at <eos>, and map the IDs back to characters.

One honest inefficiency with writing it like this: calling model(src, trg) runs the whole model every step, so the encoder re-processes the same source each time, even though (as we said in Section 4.5), it never actually changes. A real implementation would encode once and reuse enc_out. We keep it this way so generate uses the exact same forward we built. (The decoder has the same kind of waste, as it re-processes its own earlier tokens every step, even though they never change. But fixing that requires the more complex KV cache that we touched on in Appendix 4.)
We can use this function to see what our model actually generates:

generate(model, test_date)

… on one example. Testing your model and seeing the output you want is encouraging, of course, but a working model should work on many, many examples. More than you can just try by changing what that test_date string is manually and re-generating over and over again. That’s why when measuring model performance, we want to be able to quantify how well the model does on a real set of examples it’s never seen before. We want to be sure it didn’t just memorize the specific dates we gave it, but actually learned a pattern.
So let’s test this model on some hold-out data. We’ll freshly generate new examples that are guaranteed not to be in the training set, and then see how often we get those right.
For this task, we’ll define “correct” with exact-match accuracy. In our case, the entire ISO string has to be correct, character for character. A date that’s off by a number is wrong, not “80% right”, so this is a good metric to use.
Let’s see how our model does on this hold-out set:
