In Section 1.2 we ran BPE by merging characters. And in that section, we saw that we needed a special <unk> token to accommodate anything that wasn’t a known letter from our vocabulary. You can imagine, real text scraped from the internet would have the opportunity to have tons of things represented by an <unk>, especially if we didn’t have an ideal, complete, representative corpus to begin with.
But as we’ve also discussed, there’s nothing really special about letters other than that they’re the symbols of which words are comprised. But are letters really the best symbols you can use to represent words? Well, just words, maybe, but real life text is full of all sorts of non-word things.
Real tokenizers choose a different symbol to represent words and other text - bytes. It’s the reason they can handle emojis, Chinese characters, code snippets, or any random string of pure garbage, all without ever needing to actually rely on that <unk>.


Everything on a computer is ultimately stored as numbers, and text is no exception. The system for deciding which numbers represent which characters is called Unicode - a giant, agreed-upon table that assigns a unique number to essentially every character in every writing system humans use: the English alphabet, every other alphabet, mathematical symbols, emojis. Unicode just assigns an ID per character - say, 界 is number 30028, 🙂 is number 128578, and so on - for ~150,000 characters and counting.
It’s sort of like starting with a 150,000-character alphabet. Which is useful, but very extensive and large numbers are difficult to store. That’s where UTF-8 comes in. It’s the standard way of writing Unicode characters as sequences of bytes. A single byte is a single value from 0 to 255 that takes up the smallest unit of memory on a computer. Since 0 to 255 isn’t enough to hold all of the different Unicode options, UTF-8 uses a variable number of bytes per character: the common ones (ordinary English letters) take a single byte, while rarer characters take two, three, or four. Let’s see how a few words actually get encoded:

for s in ["hi", "café", "世界", "🙂"]:
    b = s.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{s!r:8} -> {len(b)} bytes -> {list(b)}")

'hi'     -> 2 bytes -> [104, 105]
'café'   -> 5 bytes -> [99, 97, 102, 195, 169]
'世界'     -> 6 bytes -> [228, 184, 150, 231, 149, 140]
'🙂'      -> 4 bytes -> [240, 159, 153, 130]


So “hi” is 2 bytes, 2 letters, while an emoji takes 4 bytes for the single character.
But in this way, we’ve actually reduced our “alphabet” to 256. The unit of the “letter” or “character” is now no longer the smallest unit - some will take more than 1 byte to represent, but everything can be represented by the set of numbers between 0 and 255. Everything.
And every possible new thing, not even in our dictionary, can be represented by a series of bytes. With how we did things in Section 1.2, having the vocabulary contain all of the individual letters means some non-real word like “blacapeptopotamus” could still be represented, at worst by all of its letters. With bytes, everything that can be typed into a computer can be represented by bytes - the <unk> is all but completely unnecessary.



The nice thing is that it doesn’t! Everything about how we worked through BPE works exactly the same. You count adjacent pairs, glue the most frequent, repeat. It’s just that the starting alphabet is 256 byte-values instead of all of the letters. Frequent byte-sequences get merged into single tokens exactly as frequent character-sequences did - so naturally multiple bytes in a row that make up a single letter probably get merged early on. Common English words still likely build up as whole tokens (their byte sequences are everywhere in the corpus). And other common byte sequences, like a very common emoji, might get merged into a single token too. The algorithm is completely indifferent to what a byte represents, it works just the same.
For that reason - I’ll skip reworking the example here over bytes. It’s not really intuitive to watch bytes connect, or build up a vocabulary and really it all does come together the same way. The intuition is still best developed using an example like we did in Section 1.2.



Two final little things worth noting on the BPE discussion (one specific to bytes and one not), because some real model behaviors can be explained by tokenizing this way.
Consequence 1 is general to tokenization. Tokens are usually bigger than letters. So a word like “strawberry” won’t be treated as ten letters - BPE will merge it into a couple of chunky tokens, maybe straw + berry. Each of those is a single ID pointing to a single learned vector. The token for berry relates inherently not at all to the tokens for b, e, r, or y. So the famous case, asking “how many r’s in strawberry?”, is something models will be bad at, for a reason coming all the way from how they understand words at all. Being able to do this task must come from specifically memorizing that berry contains two r’s, and straw contains one. This can be held in the embedding of the tokens “straw” and “berry” themselves, but it’s NOT going to come from knowing to divide either component back down into its letters. Models are famously so bad at spelling and letter-counting because all access to that level of word construction is really gone unless it gets baked back into the embedding during training.
Consequence 2 does come from specifically using bytes, and it’s that doing BPE on bytes can mean you end up with tokens that contain sub-characters. Take ‘🙂’ -> [240, 159, 153, 130]. BPE could merge just the first two of those bytes into a unit, and leave the other two. A token can end up as a fragment of a single character - a couple of bytes that don’t complete any single letter on their own. Literally, half an emoji. And this can complicate things at decode time, because the model can now also theoretically output half of an emoji… which is invalid UTF-8 that can’t be turned back into anything at all (UTF-8 is constructed smartly enough that two bytes of what was a 4-byte string simply map to nothing at all). In practice, this really won’t happen, the model won’t learn to print out the first half of 🙂 without the second half. But if it gets cut off for some reason, reaches an output limit before it could finish, we can end up with a � after decoding - the universal symbol for “I don’t know what those bytes are”.
So, the mismatch between tokens and characters can run in both directions. Sometimes a token can encompass many letters and lose sight of what those letters were, and sometimes a single character gets split in half. Either way, the clean “characters” we take for granted are not the units the model actually operates on. Fortunately, both lead to just small quirks, not critical failures.



In your study of modern architectures, you may find that tokenizers use some common alternates to BPE. They all share the same goal of building a vocabulary of common subword pieces, but they differ in the exact rules for how to choose which pieces to form. We won’t cover these in depth, but here are some of the common ones you might see, and what’s different.
WordPiece (used by BERT). This is a common alternate that’s very close to BPE. It also merges pairs, but instead of merging the most frequent pair, it merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training text. In practice that means scoring each candidate pair by roughly: \[
\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\,\text{count}(b)}
\] and favoring pairs that co-occur more than their individual frequencies would predict rather than pairs that are merely frequent. It also tokenizes new words a bit differently. Instead of replaying merges in order (as we did), it greedily takes the longest vocabulary piece that matches at each step (which we actually discussed as a potential way to tokenize in the main tutorial). WordPiece also marks pieces that continue a word with a ## prefix, so “playing” becomes play + ##ing.
Unigram / SentencePiece (used by T5, mBART, and many multilingual models). This employs a truly different algorithm, in that rather than building up by merging small pieces, it starts with a large candidate vocabulary and prunes down by repeatedly removing the tokens that “don’t matter” in a probabilistic model of the text - basically asking, “if I removed this piece, could I still come up with essentially the entire corpus anyway?”. It’s also probabilistic at tokenization time - a word can have several valid segmentations, each with a probability. In normal use, it just takes the single most likely one (so it’s used deterministically), but it can sample among the alternatives, for instance, to add variety during training. (One note: “SentencePiece” is technically the library that usually runs this, but it can also run BPE.)
So how does a team building a real model pick one? Why would someone use BPE vs WordPiece? It really is less about quality, as most of these schemes have been shown to perform pretty similarly, and more about some practical implications.

The biggest factor is language coverage. Approaches like SentencePiece run on raw text with no assumptions about spaces, which matters enormously for languages like Chinese, Japanese, and Thai that don’t separate words with spaces, so multilingual models tend to favor it.
Another factor is robustness. Byte-level fallback (like we have with byte-level BPE) guarantees anything can always be encoded and represented, with truly no unknowns.
Finally, there’s of course the very practical consideration of ecosystem. The tokenizer is a fundamental choice to the model that can’t be changed, so teams often just inherit whatever tooling they already have and whatever the models they build on have already used.

But really, the above considerations are fairly small, and tweaks can help accommodate them, so truly all of the above choices for algorithm here will work well. In modern times, the choice is converging, and most recent frontier models have landed on using byte-level BPE with large (100k+) vocabularies.




As we saw in the positional encoding section, the cosine similarity between all consecutive positional encoding vectors is exactly the same value: approximately 0.9691 (for \(d_\text{model}=100\)). The similarity between positions 1↔︎2 is identical to 200↔︎201.
This isn’t a coincidence, and it hints at a deep structural property of sinusoidal encodings. Let’s work through why this happens mathematically, and then uncover the more fundamental property underneath - the one the transformer actually exploits.


Recall that a positional encoding vector for position \(pos\) has \(d_\text{model}\) entries, arranged in sin/cos pairs. For frequency index \(j\) (where \(j = 0, 1, ..., \frac{d_\text{model}}{2} - 1\)):
\[\text{Column } 2j: \quad \sin\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right), \qquad \text{Column } 2j+1: \quad \cos\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\]
where \(\omega_j = 10000^{2j/d_\text{model}}\) sets the scale of that frequency-specific band (whose wavelength is \(2\pi\omega_j\)).
So we can think of each PE vector as \(d_\text{model}/2\) pairs of (sin, cos) at different frequencies:
\[PE(pos) = \left[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_0}\right),\ \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_0}\right),\ \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_1}\right),\ \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_1}\right),\ \ldots\right]\]
Step 1: The Norm is Constant
The squared norm of any PE vector is:
\[\|PE(pos)\|^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \left[\sin^2\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos^2\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\right]\]
By the Pythagorean identity (\(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\)), every term in the sum equals 1:
\[\|PE(pos)\|^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} 1 = \frac{d_\text{model}}{2}\]
Therefore:
\[\|PE(pos)\| = \sqrt{\frac{d_\text{model}}{2}} \quad \text{for all } pos\]
Every positional encoding vector has exactly the same length, regardless of position. This already tells us something: positions are distinguished purely by direction, not magnitude. They all live on the surface of a hypersphere of radius \(\sqrt{d_\text{model}/2}\).
Step 2: The Dot Product Depends Only on the Offset
Now, consider the dot product between two PE vectors at positions \(pos\) and \(pos + k\) (for any offset \(k\)):
\[PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k) = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \left[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\right]\]
The cosine difference identity states:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
So if \(\alpha = \frac{pos}{\omega_j}\) and \(\beta = \frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\), each pair collapses:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j} - \frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{-k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
Since \(\cos\) is an even function (\(\cos(-x) = \cos(x)\)):
\[PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k) = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
The absolute position \(pos\) has completely cancelled out. The dot product depends only on the offset \(k\).
Step 3: Therefore, Cosine Similarity is Constant at Fixed Offset
Cosine similarity is defined as:
\[\text{CosSim}(PE(pos),\ PE(pos+k)) = \frac{PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k)}{\|PE(pos)\| \cdot \|PE(pos+k)\|}\]
We’ve shown:

The numerator = \(\sum_{j} \cos(k/\omega_j)\), which depends only on \(k\)
The denominator = \(\sqrt{d/2} \cdot \sqrt{d/2} = d/2\), which is the same for all positions

So:
\[\boxed{\text{CosSim}(PE(pos),\ PE(pos+k)) = \frac{1}{d_\text{model}/2}\sum_{j=0}^{d_\text{model}/2-1} \cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) \quad \text{for all } pos}\]
This is a constant that depends only on the offset \(k\) and the model hyperparameters (\(d_\text{model}\) and the base 10000).



For our case (\(d_\text{model} = 100\), \(k = 1\)):
\[\text{CosSim} = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{j=0}^{49} \cos\!\left(\frac{1}{10000^{2j/100}}\right) = 0.969108...\]
We can verify this in code:

d_model = 100
k = 1
def cosine_sim(d_model, k):
    return sum(np.cos(k / (10000 ** (2*j / d_model))) for j in range(d_model // 2)) / (d_model / 2)

print(f"Predicted: {cosine_sim(d_model, k)}")

Predicted: 0.9691077369162043


This matches the flat line in our cosine similarity plot exactly. Of course, the usefulness of this is much more than just the fact that two neighboring positions have the exact same offset. The usefulness is that any two positions separated by an offset k have the same value as any other two positions separated by that same k.



Let’s talk about why this really happens. We’ve proven that cosine similarity is constant at fixed offset. But cosine similarity is a scalar summary - it collapses the relationship between two 100-dimensional vectors down to a single number. And the model doesn’t actually compute cosine similarities between PE vectors - it operates on the full vectors through learned linear projections. So cosine similarities being the same is not a useful property in and of itself. Rather, it’s a visible symptom of something deeper: shifting position by a fixed offset \(k\) is a rotation in embedding space.
In their paper, Vaswani et al. state a much more generalized property of sinusoidal positional encodings:

“We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset \(k\), \(PE_{pos+k}\) can be represented as a linear function of \(PE_{pos}\).”

If that doesn’t make immediate intuitive sense to you - it didn’t to me, either. So let’s dig into what exactly they meant, and why that leads to the downstream property we saw.
What This Means
Consider a single frequency band \(j\), which contributes a (sin, cos) pair to the PE vector. When we move from position \(pos\) to position \(pos + k\), these two entries transform as:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \longrightarrow \sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\] \[\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \longrightarrow \cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
Applying the trigonometric addition formulas:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
\[\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) - \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
This is a matrix equation:
\[\begin{bmatrix} \sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) \\[4pt] \cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(k/\omega_j) & \sin(k/\omega_j) \\ -\sin(k/\omega_j) & \cos(k/\omega_j) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \\[4pt] \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \end{bmatrix}\]
That transformation matrix is a 2D rotation matrix \(R_j(k)\), rotating by an angle of \(k/\omega_j\) radians. A rotation matrix is a transformation that changes the direction a vector points without changing its length. This is consistent with what we showed earlier, that all positional encoding vectors have the same norm. They’re distinguished purely by direction, and moving between positions is just a rotation. Since each frequency band transforms independently, the full PE vector transforms as:
\[PE(pos + k) = M_k \cdot PE(pos)\]
where \(M_k\) is a block-diagonal matrix:
\[M_k = \begin{bmatrix} R_0(k) & & & \\ & R_1(k) & & \\ & & \ddots & \\ & & & R_{d/2-1}(k) \end{bmatrix}\]
Each 2×2 block rotates its frequency band by an angle that depends on \(k\) and that band’s wavelength (\(2\pi\omega_j\)), but is completely independent of \(pos\). Shifting by \(k\) positions is a fixed linear transformation, regardless of where you start.

So cosine similarity is constant because rotations preserve geometry. A rotation doesn’t stretch, shrink, or distort vectors. It preserves all norms and all angles. So the angle between \(PE(pos)\) and \(PE(pos+k)\) is determined entirely by the rotation \(M_k\) that connects them, which depends only on \(k\). Cosine similarity measures the cosine of that angle, hence it’s constant. That is an outcome of how rotational transformations operate.




This rotational property is really what Vaswani et al. were referring to. Here’s why it’s so important. The attention mechanism computes:
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]
where \(Q = XW_Q\) and \(K = XW_K\) are linear projections of the input. If the input \(X\) includes positional encodings, then the attention score between positions \(pos_a\) and \(pos_b\) involves, among other things, the interaction between \(PE(pos_a)\) and \(PE(pos_b)\) through these learned weight matrices.
Suppose the model needs to learn “attend to the word 3 positions back.” That means it needs the attention score to be high when \(pos_a - pos_b = 3\). Since:
\[PE(pos_a) = M_3 \cdot PE(pos_b)\]
The relationship between the two PE vectors is captured entirely by the fixed matrix \(M_3\). The model’s learned projections \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) can compose with \(M_3\) through ordinary matrix multiplication, so the same \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) that detect “3 positions back” at position 10 will automatically detect “3 positions back” at position 200. The model learns this pattern once and then, (in theory), it could generalize everywhere.
If the positional encoding didn’t have this rotation structure and moving by \(k\) positions involved a different transformation depending on where you started, then the model’s fixed \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) couldn’t capture relative position as a general concept. It would need to learn separate attention patterns for every absolute position, which scales terribly with sequence length.
Ok, one more thing though. Because the keen eye might have noticed - we DO have fixed cosine similarities between fixed positions k, great. And typically distinct cosine similarities for any k. And we have rotational transformations as a general property.
But we do not have monotonically decreasing cosine similarities for increasing k, and we made a statement earlier that we want close positions to have similar embeddings as one another. So, does that matter?

ks = np.arange(1,101,1)
def cosine_sim(d_model, k):
    return sum(np.cos(k / (10000 ** (2*j / d_model))) for j in range(d_model // 2)) / (d_model / 2)

cossims = [cosine_sim(d_model, k) for k in ks]

plt.scatter(ks, cossims); plt.show()








Short answer, not totally, but a little. We know that cosine similarity is a lossy scalar summary of a rich high-dimensional relationship - so the number itself isn’t important.
BUT… it is a useful property that nearby positional encodings are similar, because it can help the model learn relationships more easily. This is actually up to that choice of frequency - the “10000” that we sort of shrugged off before.
In truth, sinusoidal positional encodings have been largely replaced in modern transformers by methods like Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), which apply the same frequency-based rotation idea inside the attention mechanism rather than as an additive encoding. Because, as it turns out, while the rotational properties of sinusoidal encodings are present, the model can have issues fully exploiting them. But before we get into every single little detail here about positional encodings, I’ll instead save the full story - including why sinusoidal PE fell out of favor, how RoPE works, and why the base frequency turns out to be one of the most actively studied hyperparameters in modern LLMs - for a future, dedicated positional encodings notebook. For now, the sinusoidal version gives us exactly the right intuitions to understand the rest of the transformer architecture. And just know - it was still a good, calculated choice!
Take me back to the main tutorial




As we worked through what the encoder produced, we saw a very key observation about the architecture come into play. That while attention is the mechanism that allows for complex information retrieval and word relationships, an MLP is still necessary for learning, because attention is fundamentally a layer of linear transformations, and non-linearity is a requirement for learning complex relationships.
In fact, this is one of the most consequential insights in all of modern machine learning, so worth digging deep into. If this isn’t your first introduction to neural networks, this concept is probably familiar, but we’ll go over again here, in detail, why non-linearity is such an essential feature.


First we have to be precise, because non-linearity being so important rests on what a linear function can and cannot give us. A function \(f\) is linear if it satisfies one property:
\[
f(a\mathbf{x} + b\mathbf{y}) = a\,f(\mathbf{x}) + b\,f(\mathbf{y})
\]
for inputs \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\) and scalars \(a, b\).
There are two valuable properties in this definition.

First, this means that the inputs are additive - any way that the inputs can be broken up into an addition of parts, the function can be applied independently to those parts, and added later, to get the same result.
Second, it means that the function scales linearly. If you scale the input, the output scales by the exact same amount - putting “20” through the function is exactly equivalent to putting “5” through the function, then multiplying the result by 4.


📌 Note: You might wonder if these two properties are redundant. Over strictly rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q})\), additivity actually forces scaling to work automatically. And physically speaking, digital computers only use rational numbers (finite floating-point fractions). However, because we design neural networks under the theoretical, continuous framework of real numbers \((\mathbb{R})\) so that calculus and gradients work, we must explicitly include both properties in our definition, as over real numbers, they are completely distinct.

Simply put, a linear function preserves addition (and therefore subtraction) and scalar multiplication (and therefore division).



A matrix multiply \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}W\) is the canonical linear function, as “linear algebra” as a field deals with this class of transformations. Any matrix multiply (as we’ve seen work out many times in this tutorial) is just a combination of products - multiplies between row and column values, summed. Since addition and multiplications themselves of course satisfy the property of “preserving addition and multiplication” - any matrix multiply with a matrix constructed of numbers is a linear function.
(Strictly speaking, adding a bias, \(\mathbf{x}W + \mathbf{b}\), to a matrix multiply, as is typical in neural networks, makes it affine - shifted on the origin - rather than linear, but the same conclusions follow, so we’ll use “linear” loosely to include it, as everyone does.)
The core insight that will lead to nonlinearity being necessary is this: a composition of linear functions is itself a linear function. Or basically, it doesn’t matter how many matrix multiplies you do in a row - since a matrix multiply is a linear combination, as many as you stack will always also be a linear combination.
Consider two linear layers:
\[
\mathbf{f(x)} = \mathbf{x}W_1, \qquad \mathbf{g(x)}  = \mathbf{x}W_2
\]
If we stack them, doing them one after another, we get:
\[
\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{g ( f(x) )} = (\mathbf{x}W_1)W_2
\]
But remember the property above. Since f(x) and g(x) are both linear functions, and matrix multiplication is associative, we have:
\[
(\mathbf{x}W_1)W_2 = \mathbf{x}(W_1 W_2)
\]
But \(W_1 W_2\) is itself just a matrix. If we call it \(W' = W_1 W_2\), then we can simply write:
\[
\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}W'
\]
So two stacked layers is exactly equal to one with some other weight matrix \(W'\). And this doesn’t stop at two. Stack a hundred linear layers, or a thousand, and the same argument collapses every one of them:
\[
\mathbf{x}W_1 W_2 W_3 \cdots W_{1000} = \mathbf{x}W', \qquad W' = W_1 W_2 \cdots W_{1000}
\]
What this means is that two, three, four, thousands of stacked linear layers are exactly equivalent to a single linear layer (with different numbers, of course, but always still expressible as just a single matrix). Since linear functions don’t care how many ways you decompose the input as a series of multiplies and adds, you get the exact same answer doing the math as 100 operations as you would just doing one.
Now, linear combinations can of course learn something. A vector, for instance, is interpretable as a combination of unit vectors, and how to combine those unit vectors is a learnable combination. That’s why linear layers are still useful in some layers of the network. But the other issue here is just that: that a linear function can only learn linear relationships.
The important geometrical interpretation is that linear functions can only separate their space with straight lines, or in higher dimensions, flat planes. Its decision boundaries are hyperplanes, and nothing it does can bend them. Geometrically, any linear mapping can rotate, scale, shear, and reflect space, but only uniformly - moving all of the points by the same amount, at once. This means that any decision boundary that can’t be divided by a hyperplane, cannot be learned by a purely linear function. But as we just saw, no matter how many layers of linear functions we stack, we can never get out of that trap.



An incredibly simple example where we can observe the linear function being unable to learn is the simple XOR (“exclusive or”) function. Consider four points and labels we want a model to produce for each of them:
\[
(0,0) \to 0, \qquad (1,1) \to 0, \qquad (0,1) \to 1, \qquad (1,0) \to 1
\]
The output is 1 when exactly one input is 1, and 0 otherwise. Plot the four points: the two 0-labeled points sit on one diagonal (bottom-left and top-right), and the two 1-labeled points on the other (top-left and bottom-right).
Now try to separate them the only way a linear classifier can: with a single straight line, 1’s on one side, 0’s on the other. In the demo below, we’ll plot the points, and you can freely tweak all parameters that a linear function has available to fit the data.
The below code makes the demo - unhide if you want to see it

# @title
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider

# 1. Define the XOR dataset
X = np.array([[0,0], [1,1], [0,1], [1,0]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])

def xor_challenge(w1, w2, bias):
    # Set up the plot canvas
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.5)
    ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

    # Generate the decision line: w1*x + w2*y + b = 0 -> y = -(w1*x + b) / w2
    x_vals = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 100)
    if abs(w2) > 1e-3:
        y_vals = -(w1 * x_vals + bias) / w2
        ax.plot(x_vals, y_vals, color='purple', linewidth=2.5, label='Decision Boundary')

        # Color the spaces to show the model's predictions (Positive vs Negative space)
        # We check the sign of the center point to determine shading direction
        if w2 > 0:
            ax.fill_between(x_vals, y_vals, 2, color='blue', alpha=0.05)
            ax.fill_between(x_vals, y_vals, -2, color='red', alpha=0.05)
        else:
            ax.fill_between(x_vals, y_vals, 2, color='red', alpha=0.05)
            ax.fill_between(x_vals, y_vals, -2, color='blue', alpha=0.05)

    elif abs(w1) > 1e-3:
        # Handle perfectly vertical line scenario
        ax.axvline(-bias / w1, color='purple', linewidth=2.5, label='Decision Boundary')

    # Calculate live classification accuracy
    # Model predicts 1 if w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b > 0, else 0
    raw_outputs = X[:, 0] * w1 + X[:, 1] * w2 + bias
    predictions = (raw_outputs > 0).astype(int)
    correct_mask = (predictions == y)
    accuracy = np.mean(correct_mask) * 100

    # Plot the XOR points (Green if model gets it right, Orange/Red if it fails)
    for i in range(4):
        marker = '^' if y[i] == 1 else 'o'
        edge_color = 'green' if correct_mask[i] else 'crimson'
        linewidth = 4 if not correct_mask[i] else 2

        # Plot point colored by its true class, outlined by its correctness
        ax.scatter(X[i, 0], X[i, 1],
                   color='blue' if y[i] == 1 else 'red',
                   s=250, marker=marker, zorder=3,
                   edgecolors=edge_color, linewidths=linewidth)

        ax.text(X[i, 0] + 0.05, X[i, 1] + 0.05, f"Label: {y[i]}", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

    # Status box
    status_text = f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.0f}%\n"

    ax.text(-0.4, -0.4, status_text,
            bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.9, boxstyle='round,pad=0.5'), fontsize=11)

    ax.set_title("XOR Linear Classifier", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    plt.show()


# 2. Build the interactive sliders and launch the challenge
interact(
    xor_challenge,
    w1=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=-3.0, max=3.0, step=0.1, description='W1'),

The best any linear model can do is 75% - it’s impossible to draw a line to cleanly separate XOR. And since we just proved that any depth of linear layers collapses to a single linear map, no linear network of any size, however deep or wide, can solve XOR.
In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons, which laid out exactly this limitation of single-layer linear models - and XOR was the canonical issue. The simple perceptron, which was the leading neural model of the day, provably would never be able to learn this simple four-point function. This finding contributed to a long decline in neural-network research, part of what’s now called the first “AI winter”.
The resolution, when it came, was precisely the architecture we use today: stack layers, with a differentiable non-linear function between them, then use backpropogation to learn. This insight saved the field, as it’s fundamental to the ability for any NN-based architecture to learn.



We already discussed how linear transformations can only move points rigidly, by rotating, scaling, shearing, or reflecting, but can never change which points a straight line can separate, since all transformations move all points rigidly, the same way.
A non-linearity escapes this because it can move points non-rigidly. Some points can change their position a lot while others remain in roughly the same spot. The ReLU,
\[
\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)
\]
is an incredibly simple non-linear function that does this by simply clamping every negative value to zero. Geometrically, a whole half of the space gets flattened onto a wall at zero. Crucially, what this means, is that different points that were spread out can get pressed onto the same spot. Just that simple idea of “forcing values below the threshold to 0”, gives us enough of a nonlinearity that we can shift the coordinates and the points as we need, into a configuration where a line now can separate them.
The key way to think of this is as a transformation of the coordinate space. A neural network has hidden units, and each hidden unit computes a new coordinate for every point (first via a linear combination, then the clamp). A full hidden layer moves all of the points into a new room, with a new coordinate space of transformed axes \((h_1, h_2)\). Where the original room was a Euclidean space - all lines are parallel and shifts uniform, ReLU’s clamp allows this new coordinate space to have creases that collapse points together as it relocates them.
If this isn’t feeling intuitive, because humans really don’t find folded spaces intuitive, let’s also see how running our four XOR points through one ReLU layer transforms them mathematically.



Let’s go through the math of the simplest neural network we can make.
A neural network processes a spatial transformation in three distinct stages. First, the linear projection, then, the nonlinear activation, and finally, the final linear readout.
Let’s say our network takes a two-dimensional input coordinate vector \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2]\) and passes it to a hidden layer containing two hidden units. In standard matrix notation, this layer is expressed as:
\[
\mathbf{h} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{x}W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)
\]
To see exactly what happens to a coordinate, we can unpack these matrices into their structural components:
\[
W_1 = \begin{bmatrix} w_{11} & w_{12} \\ w_{21} & w_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 & b_2 \end{bmatrix}
\]
If we break this matrix multiplication down into individual scalar equations, we can see the exact independent recipe used to calculate each new hidden coordinate (\(\text{h}_1\) and \(\text{h}_2\))
1. The Linear Projection


The first step of this layer is to calculate a raw linear score (\(z_1\)) by scaling and adding the inputs (doing a linear transformation) on the original coordinate set. \[
z_1 = x_1 w_{11} + x_2 w_{21} + b_1
\]



Simultaneously, the second unit calculates its own independent linear score (\(z_2\)): \[
z_2 = x_1 w_{12} + x_2 w_{22} + b_2
\]
So each hidden unit starts with a linear combination of the original coordinates - a shift, shear, or rescaling, of the original coordinate.
2. The Nonlinear Activation
After the linear combination, we have a new set of points, \((z_1, z_2)\), that are each some linear combination of the original points. We have moved the points within the Euclidean coordinate space with this transformation, but have not been able to fundamentally change their relative layout in the space. The next step, the nonlinear activation, is where we can actually move the points in the space non-uniformly, by clamping one side. This draws a bend, or wall, in the new coordinate space where points on one side of the boundary are pushed and points on the other side are left alone.
\[
h_1 = \max(0, \, z_1)
\]
\[
h_2 = \max(0, \, z_2)
\]
These final outputs \([h_1, h_2]\) are our brand-new coordinate vector \(\mathbf{h}\), which now exist, for each of our original points, in this hidden state space, and no longer in the original coordinate system.
3. The Final Readout Line
Then, we can draw a decision boundary line in this new coordinate space that attempts to separate the points. This is an output layer, and it takes the hidden vector \(\mathbf{h} = [h_1, h_2]\) and applies one final linear combination:
\[
\text{Output Score} = \mathbf{h}W_2 + b_{\text{out}}
\]
Expressed as a plain scalar equation, the final readout is simply:
\[
\text{Output Score} = h_1 w_{\text{out1}} + h_2 w_{\text{out2}} + b_{\text{out}}
\]
The network then applies a strict threshold to this score to determine the final classification prediction:

If \(\text{Output Score} > 0 \implies \text{Predict } 1\)
If \(\text{Output Score} \le 0 \implies \text{Predict } 0\)





The incredibly simple XOR / two hidden unit network is a rare case that’s small enough that we can put actual numbers in and reason about why each weight has the value it does. So just to really hammer in the point, let’s look at a specific set of weights that solves XOR, and how exactly these computations proceed to transform the values.
If:
\[
W_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{b}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
W_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b_2 = 0
\]
Then, this will solve XOR.
First, notice what XOR actually depends on. Look at the four points by the sum of their inputs, \(s = x_1 + x_2\):

The label is 1 exactly when the sum is 1, and 0 otherwise. The issue is that drawing a boundary between both 0 and 1 and 1 and 2, is impossible. Any way that you linearly combine those coordinates, there will not be able to be this clean separation.
\[
\underset{\text{label 0}}{0} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \underset{\text{label 1}}{1} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \underset{\text{label 0}}{2}
\]
Now, let’s look at what the two hidden units actually do. With these weights, both units compute a linear combination of the inputs. With the weights that we chose above for \(W_1\)’s, rows both \([1,1]\), both hidden units do just compute the sum (\(s\)), differing only in bias:
\[
z_1 = x_1 + x_2 = s, \qquad z_2 = x_1 + x_2 - 1 = s - 1
\]
\[
\text{h}_1 = \max(0,\, s), \qquad \text{h}_2 = \max(0,\, s-1)
\]
Unit 1 is just the raw sum (it never goes negative here, so the ReLU never needs to clamp the values), so \(\text{h}_1 = s\). On its own, \(\text{h}_1\) cannot be thresholded to draw a decision boundary between the values, like we just saw above.
\[
\text{h}_1:\quad s {=} 0 \to 0, \qquad s {=} 1 \to 1, \qquad s {=} 2 \to 2
\]
But Unit 2 has a bias of \(-1\), shifting the line so that \(z_2 = s - 1\): negative at \(s=0\), zero at \(s=1\), positive at \(s=2\). The ReLU then hinges at \(s = 1\) - it clamps everything up to the sum-of-1 flat to zero, and only lets \(s=2\) rise above it:
\[
\text{h}_2:\quad s{=}0 \to 0, \qquad s{=}1 \to 0, \qquad s{=}2 \to 1
\]
So \(\text{h}_2\) is essentially a detector of values over one. This is precisely what was needed - we could draw a boundary between 0 and 1, but not also between 1 and 2. Hidden unit 2 allows us to find, easily, all of the values > 1.
But the second unit is also not able to capture all of the information we need on its own. When we combine them, we get the benefit of how both hidden units divided the space. The readout is \(\text{out} = \text{h}_1 - 2\text{h}_2 = s - 2\text{h}_2\):

Essentially, ReLU has allowed us to turn that 2 back into a 0, without changing the value of the “1”. We still use the original sum to identify values that exceed our threshold of “1” and need a label of “0”, but we can re-transform it to “0” using the output of the second hidden unit, without affecting our sums of “1” that we needed, because ReLU let us put a fold in the space that lets us manipulate numbers only above 1. After this transformation, now a threshold (\(\text{out} > 0.5\)) cleanly isolates the middle, and XOR is solved.
You can imagine these numbers to be something different. Even keeping the weights the same, shifting that bias term will move which values get clamped. So as you also can see, these particular weights are just one particular solution, of which XOR has many! This was just a particularly clean one that lets us build up good intuition about how ReLU helps solve the problem. Gradient descent, left to its own devices, usually finds a much messier set of weights. The point isn’t that this is the answer - it’s that a nonlinearity makes it possible to find an answer because it allows transformation into a new hidden space.
Below, here’s a simple demo that shows the hidden space mapping and the boundary line we drew through it, starting with the weights we just worked through above. But the values are adjustable - if you want to try and think of a different potential solution, feel free to try it out below! import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider

relu = lambda z: np.maximum(0, z)
X = np.array([[0,0], [1,1], [0,1], [1,0]], float)
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
col = {0: '#2166ac', 1: '#b2182b'}   # blue = label 0, red = label 1
mk  = {0: 'o',       1: '^'}

def xor_playground(w11, w12, w21, w22, b1a, b1b, wo1, wo2, bo):
    # --- hidden layer: relocate the points ---
    W1 = np.array([[w11, w12], [w21, w22]])
    b1 = np.array([b1a, b1b])
    H  = relu(X @ W1 + b1)                 # the four points' new coordinates

    # --- readout line: try to separate them ---
    w = np.array([wo1, wo2])
    score = H @ w + bo
    pred  = (score > 0).astype(int)
    acc   = (pred == y).mean()

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.6))

    # LEFT: input space, fixed reference
    for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
        ax1.scatter(*xi, c=col[yi], s=250, marker=mk[yi], edgecolor='k', lw=1.5, zorder=3)
    ax1.set_title("Input space (fixed)")
    ax1.set_xlim(-0.6, 1.7); ax1.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.7)
    ax1.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax1.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3); ax1.set_aspect('equal')

    # RIGHT: hidden space - points move here, and the readout line tries to split them
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-0.6, 3.2, 300), np.linspace(-0.6, 2.6, 300))
    region = ((np.stack([gx, gy], -1) @ w + bo) > 0).astype(int)
    ax2.contourf(gx, gy, region, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5],
                 colors=['#2166ac', '#b2182b'], alpha=0.08)   # shaded predicted regions
    if abs(wo2) > 1e-6:                                       # draw the boundary line
        xs = np.array([-0.6, 3.2]); ax2.plot(xs, -(wo1*xs + bo)/wo2, 'g-', lw=2)
    elif abs(wo1) > 1e-6:
        ax2.axvline(-bo/wo1, color='g', lw=2)

    seen = {}
    for h, yi, pi in zip(H, y, pred):
        key = tuple(np.round(h, 3))
        k = len(seen.get(key, [])); seen.setdefault(key, []).append(1)
        o = 0.06 * k                                          # jitter coincident points
        edge = 'green' if pi == yi else 'crimson'
        lw   = 2 if pi == yi else 3.5                         # thick red edge = misclassified
        ax2.scatter(h[0]+o, h[1]+o, c=col[yi], s=260, marker=mk[yi],
                    edgecolor=edge, lw=lw, zorder=5)
    ax2.set_title(f"Hidden space $(h_1, h_2)$   -   accuracy: {acc*100:.0f}%")
    ax2.set_xlim(-0.6, 3.2); ax2.set_ylim(-0.6, 2.6)
    ax2.set_xlabel("$\text{h}_1$"); ax2.set_ylabel("$\text{h}_2$")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3); ax2.set_aspect('equal')
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    w21=s(1, -2, 2, 'W1[2,1]'), w22=s(1, -2, 2, 'W1[2,2]'),
    b1a=s(0, -2, 2, 'bias h1'), b1b=s(-1, -2, 2, 'bias h2'),

So we just proved that non-linearity is necessary, AND exactly how a non-linearity gets around the issues that pure linearity cannot. As it turns out, a remarkable theorem shows just how sufficient this simple non-linear function is, and states an even more general property more cleanly. The universal approximation theorem as it was originally stated (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991; sharpened by Leshno et al., 1993) says:

A feedforward network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a closed and bounded domain to arbitrary accuracy - provided its activation function is not a polynomial.

Every bolded part is an important qualifier, so let’s step through them.

“Single hidden layer.” Note here that this is not a statement about depth. The theorem is instead about width. One hidden layer, with enough units, summed together, can do the job. Going back to our folds in the space analogy - you might need a whole ton of folds, but you can always make enough folds to divide the space how you need to. (As it turns out, depth - stacking layers - which most modern neural nets rely on, will learn much more efficiently, which is why real models are deep. But that is separate from this fundamental theorem’s result.)
“Continuous function on a closed and bounded domain.” Not literally any underlying function can be learned this way. The target has to be continuous, have good approximation over a reasonably bounded portion of input space, not out to infinity. As long as that’s satisfied though, the relationship between inputs and outputs can be as complicated as you want. You’ll note that this is true for any real case we use neural nets for. We presume some true underlying relationship between our inputs and outputs, over reasonable values we can really put into a computer, and roughly that other inputs that mean the same sort of thing can go through the same process to get the same answer. That’s really all you need.
“To arbitrary accuracy.” This is really saying, no matter how accurate you want to be, there exists a network that stays within your error tolerance everywhere on the domain, for all of the points.
“Not a polynomial.” This is the condition, that we just spent all of that time explaining the importance of. The activation can take many, many different forms (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, …) as long as it isn’t a polynomial. This condition is actually the general version of our multiple linear layers always becoming a single linear layer. That earlier “linear collapses to linear” observation wasn’t a special quirk of linearity - it is a case of the more general rule that any polynomial activation fails to be universal.


Basically, if the activation were a polynomial of degree \(d\), then any combination of our hidden units is also a polynomial of degree at most \(d\). Since polynomials can’t arbitrarily bend - how they bend is limited by their degree, a polynomial activation is not able to generally and arbitrarily divide the space - similar to the linear instance, there are very particular, rigid ways in which it can transform the space, which will not in general be sufficient.

Two very important things to point out:

This is an existence result, meaning, it guarantees a good network exists, not that gradient descent will actually find it, or that the version that was found to fit the training data will universally generalize. In practice, this “true” underlying function is never really found.
“Enough units” can be enormous. Just because enough units could approximate, doesn’t mean you can build a network that has enough units. This can be an arbitrarily enormous number, well beyond practical limits.

So the takeaway isn’t “one hidden layer is all you need”. It’s that linear (and polynomial) machinery is limited to approximating only a very small class of functions. But even a single nonpolynomial nonlinearity makes the entire space of continuous functions theoretically within reach.



We used ReLU in our example, partly because it’s so simple and easy to understand. But actually, it’s a reasonable default (even though it’s mostly been replaced in modern implementations), and worth mentioning why it’s still is so useful despite being so simple.
Historically, sigmoid and tanh were more standard. They are smooth, curved non-linearities. They work well, but are easy to saturate, meaning that large positive or negative inputs, their slope flattens to nearly zero. This causes a classic issue where gradients flowing backward through them shrink toward nothing (the “vanishing gradient” problem), slowing or stopping entirely the training of a network.
ReLU looks almost embarrassingly simple by comparison. But its simplicity provides many benefits:

It’s sufficiently non-linear. As we just saw above, the non-linear function doesn’t have to be complicated to allow learning, just non-linear at all. The tiny break in ReLU is totally sufficient to satisfy that property.
The fact that for any positive input, its slope is exactly 1, means that those gradient issues pose no problems - gradients pass through undiminished, and deep networks train far faster and more reliably.
It’s trivially cheap to compute. A simple clamp is about the computationally cheapest function you can do, which matters when the activation function has to be applied repeatedly in the already onerous math of a neural network.

The fact that any nonlinearity is sufficient isn’t to say that the choice doesn’t matter at all. As we just discussed, gradients flow through this calculation, so there are certainly other considerations, and in fact, typically other activations are used in modern models. GELU, essentially a smoothed version of ReLU, is used in many modern transformers. And there are many other options, chosen for many other reasons, which we will not get into here! But even if not perfect, ReLU has repeatedly been found to still be a pretty good choice in a lot of cases, for the reasons explained above.
And at its core, it’s all that’s needed. That small ReLU operation is the only nonlinearity that acts on each token’s own features, allowing the model to transform them into something new. So while it might look like a tiny little filter on the numbers, hopefully you’ve seen now how it’s the crux of all learning!
Take me back to the main tutorial




When we were in Section 5, talking about the output, we made a claim: That the final row of the output from the decoder is all that you need to predict the next token, because that’s its job. Without pausing on that for a bit, that might seem strange. We get a whole matrix out of the decoder that represents the full sequence, and then we just use the last row to predict the next token. It seems wasteful on compute, and on information.
Then, I pointed out that it’s sort of neither. That we only use the last row, because everything else will be identical and therefore of no new use to us, and that this repetitive nature of the matrix coming out leads to something we can exploit to speed up generation.
In this appendix, we tackle both of those claims. First proving, what exactly is new and what is the same when you feed the same sequence over and over again through the decoder, and then talking about how we can use this property in something called the KV Cache.


Before we can talk about how to exploit this property, let’s prove that it’s true. That after each pass through the decoder, the only part of the matrix that is different is the new final row corresponding to the most recently added token.
Rather than do that abstractly, it’s easiest to see working through exactly the math for a simple, small example. We’ll take a sequence of 2 tokens, write out literally every matrix in the masked self-attention step of the decoder, then append a 3rd token, and write everything out again. To keep it simple, we’ll use just one attention head, but by now you should be convinced that more heads will behave exactly the same way.


Coming into the decoder, let’s say that our input sequence is: \[
\text{[I, love]}
\] which gets tokenized cleanly into the two tokens: \[
\text{inp} = [x, y]
\]
with a \(d_\text{model}\) of say, 3, after we embed this input, we would end up with:
\[
X = \begin{bmatrix}{x_i \ x_j \ x_k \\ y_i \ y_j \ y_k}\end{bmatrix}
\]
The first step of attention is to construct \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) matrices, from \(W_Q\), \(W_K\), and \(W_V\). Remember that these are all constructed by multiplying \(X\) by a \(W\) matrix of size \(d_\text{model} \times d_\text{model}\). Looking at just, for example, the final query matrix, \(Q\):
\[
Q = X  W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}{x_i \ x_j \ x_k \\ y_i \ y_j \ y_k}\end{bmatrix} \times
\begin{bmatrix}q_{1,1} \ q_{1,2} \ q_{1,3} \\ q_{2,1} \ q_{2,2} \ q_{2,3} \\ q_{3,1} \ q_{3,2} \ q_{3,3}\end{bmatrix}
\]
Just to be super explicit, let’s write out the final matrix:
\[
Q = \begin{bmatrix}
(x_i q_{1,1} + x_j q_{2,1} + x_k q_{3,1}) \ \ \ (x_i q_{1,2} + x_j q_{2,2} + x_k q_{3,2}) \ \ \ (x_i q_{1,3} + x_j q_{2,3} + x_k q_{3,3}) \\
(y_i q_{1,1} + y_j q_{2,1} + y_k q_{3,1}) \ \ \ (y_i q_{1,2} + y_j q_{2,2} + y_k q_{3,2}) \ \ \ (y_i q_{1,3} + y_j q_{2,3} + y_k q_{3,3})
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Calling the elements of \(Q\) by just \(Q_n\), notice something.
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
Q_{x1} \ Q_{x2} \ Q_{x3} \\
Q_{y1} \ Q_{y2} \ Q_{y3}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{matrix} ← \text{depends only on x} \\ ← \text{depends only on y} \end{matrix}
\]
And this is true for K and V as well, as they’re constructed the same exact way as Q, just with different W:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}K_{x1} \ K_{x2} \ K_{x3} \\ K_{y1} \ K_{y2} \ K_{y3} \end{bmatrix} ,
\begin{bmatrix}V_{x1} \ V_{x2} \ V_{x3} \\ V_{y1} \ V_{y2} \ V_{y3} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{matrix} ← \text{depends only on x} \\ ← \text{depends only on y} \end{matrix}
\]
So row 1 of \(Q, K,\) and \(V\) each depend only on token 1; row 2 only on token 2. Appending a 3rd token at the end creates a row 3 to each of these matrices, that has nothing to do with token 1 or token 2 at all. Each row of \(Q, K,\) and \(V\) corresponds to exactly one token in the sequence.
Well, does that change when we use them? Let’s see.
The next step of the attention calculation is to compute attention scores, \(S\), from \(Q\) and \(K^\top\)
\[
S = Q K^\top = \begin{bmatrix}
Q_{x1} \ Q_{x2} \ Q_{x3} \\
Q_{y1} \ Q_{y2} \ Q_{y3}
\end{bmatrix}
\times
\begin{bmatrix}K_{x1} \ K_{y1} \\ K_{x2} \ K_{y2} \\ K_{x3} \ K_{y3} \end{bmatrix}
\ = \
\begin{bmatrix}
(Q_{x1} K_{x1} + Q_{x2} K_{x2} + Q_{x3} K_{x3}) \ \space \
(Q_{x1} K_{y1} + Q_{x2} K_{y2} + Q_{x3} K_{y3}) \\
(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3}) \ \space \
(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3}) \end{bmatrix}
\]
So in S, things are now mixed, writing s in terms of what tokens it mixes from this above calculation, we see:
\[
S =
\begin{bmatrix}
s_{xx} \ s_{xy} \\
s_{yx} \ s_{yy}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
But, remember what happens next specifically at generation time in the decoder. We have to mask this sequence, because there’s no reasonable way that x could be asking about y - \(s_{xy}\) doesn’t really make sense. So we apply the causal mask, saying query \(i\) may not look at key \(j\) when \(j > i\), so those entries become \(-\infty\):
\[S_{\text{masked}} = \begin{bmatrix} s_{xx} & -\infty \\ s_{yx} & s_{yy} \end{bmatrix}\]
Then, we softmax each row (over the keys). Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\):
\[
\text{row 1:}\quad \left[\frac{e^{s_{xx}}}{e^{s_{xx}}+e^{-\infty}},\ \frac{e^{-\infty}}{e^{s_{xx}}+e^{-\infty}}\right] = [\,1,\ 0\,]
\] \[
\text{row 2:}\quad \left[\frac{e^{s_{yx}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}},\ \frac{e^{s_{yy}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}}\right] = [\,a_{yx},\ a_{yy}\,]
\]
The attention-weight matrix is then:
\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ a_{yx} & a_{yy} \end{bmatrix}\]
Finally, we multiply this back by V to get the final output
\[
O = A V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ a_{yx} & a_{yy} \end{bmatrix}
\times
\begin{bmatrix}V_{x1} \ V_{x2} \ V_{x3} \\ V_{y1} \ V_{y2} \ V_{y3} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{x1} \ V_{x2} \ V_{x3} \\ (a_{yx} V_{x1} +  a_{yy} V_{y1}) \ (a_{yx} V_{x2} +  a_{yy} V_{y2}) \ (a_{yx} V_{x3} +  a_{yy} V_{y3}) \end{bmatrix}
\]
So mixing still happens, but only backwards mixing. Looking more closely at the second output row (the more interesting one), just at what that very first entry in the output is, explicitly:
\[
(a_{yx} V_{x1} +  a_{yy} V_{y1}) =
\frac{e^{s_{yx}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}} V_{x1} + \frac{e^{s_{yy}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}} V_{y1} = \\
\frac{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}}{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}+e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}} V_{x1} + \frac{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}}{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}+e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}} V_{y1}
\]
I know it’s quite the doozy to write out like that, but just keep it in mind and we’ll come back after working through the example with 3!



We’ll go through this one just a little faster. When we add a third token to the sequence, so \(X = [x,y,z]\), we now have for \(Q,K,V\):
\[
\begin{bmatrix}Q_{11} \ Q_{12} \ Q_{13} \\ Q_{21} \ Q_{22} \ Q_{23} \\ Q_{31} \ Q_{32} \ Q_{33}\end{bmatrix}  ,
\begin{bmatrix}K_{11} \ K_{12} \ K_{13} \\ K_{21} \ K_{22} \ K_{23} \\ K_{31} \ K_{32} \ K_{33}\end{bmatrix} ,
\begin{bmatrix}V_{11} \ V_{12} \ V_{13} \\ V_{21} \ V_{22} \ V_{23} \\ V_{31} \ V_{32} \ V_{33}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{matrix} ← \text{depends only on x} \\ ← \text{depends only on y} \\ ← \text{depends only on z}\end{matrix}
\]
When the S calculation comes around to mix these, we get:
\[S = \begin{bmatrix} s_{xx} & s_{xy} & s_{xz} \\ s_{yx} & s_{yy} & s_{yz} \\ s_{zx} & s_{zy} & s_{zz} \end{bmatrix}\]
Then, this time when we apply the triangular causal mask for \(j > i \Rightarrow -\infty\):
\[S_{\text{masked}} = \begin{bmatrix} s_{xx} & -\infty & -\infty \\ s_{yx} & s_{yy} & -\infty \\ s_{zx} & s_{zy} & s_{zz} \end{bmatrix}\]
Notice something immediately. The 2x2 matrix that exists in the top left of this is the identical matrix to the one we had above in the 2 token case. Adding a third token added a third row, with real values, but only an extra \(-\infty\) to the existing rows which we know becomes 0 in the next step.
Indeed,
\[
\text{row 1:}\quad \frac{[\,e^{s_{xx}},\ e^{-\infty},\ e^{-\infty}\,]}{e^{s_{xx}}+e^{-\infty}+e^{-\infty}} = \frac{[\,e^{s_{xx}},\ 0,\ 0\,]}{e^{s_{xx}}+0+0} = [\,1,\ 0,\ 0\,]
\] \[
\text{row 2:}\quad \frac{[\,e^{s_{yx}},\ e^{s_{yy}},\ e^{-\infty}\,]}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}+e^{-\infty}} = \frac{[\,e^{s_{yx}},\ e^{s_{yy}},\ 0\,]}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}+0} = [\,a_{yx},\ a_{yy},\ 0\,]
\] \[
\text{row 3:} \quad \text{(I will spare you the math)} \quad  = [\,a_{zx},\ a_{zy},\ a_{zz}\,]
\]
\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a_{yx} & a_{yy} & 0 \\ a_{zx} & a_{zy} & a_{zz} \end{bmatrix}\]
And then, the final output here ends up being:
\[
O = A V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a_{yx} & a_{yy} & 0 \\ a_{zx} & a_{zy} & a_{zz}\end{bmatrix}
\times
\begin{bmatrix}V_{x1} \ V_{x2} \ V_{x3} \\ V_{y1} \ V_{y2} \ V_{y3} \\ V_{z1} \ V_{z2} \ V_{z3}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{x1} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad V_{x2} \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad V_{x3} \\
(a_{yx} V_{x1} +  a_{yy} V_{y1}) \ \quad \quad \ (a_{yx} V_{x2} +  a_{yy} V_{y2}) \ \quad \quad \ (a_{yx} V_{x3} +  a_{yy} V_{y3}) \\
(a_{zx} V_{x1} +  a_{zy} V_{y1} +  a_{zz} V_{z1}) \ \ (a_{zx} V_{x2} +  a_{zy} V_{y2} +  a_{zz} V_{z2}) \ \ (a_{zx} V_{x3} +  a_{zy} V_{y3} +  a_{zz} V_{z3}) \\
\end{bmatrix}
\]
We can write out row 2 column 1, the first output for the second token explicitly again, tracing exactly what contributes to each of the elements that comprise it, but spoiler: it’s exactly the same as it was in the 2 token case:
\[
(a_{yx} V_{x1} +  a_{yy} V_{y1}) =
\frac{e^{s_{yx}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}} V_{x1} + \frac{e^{s_{yy}}}{e^{s_{yx}}+e^{s_{yy}}} V_{y1} = \\
\frac{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}}{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}+e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}} V_{x1} + \frac{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}}{e^{(Q_{y1} K_{x1} + Q_{y2} K_{x2} + Q_{y3} K_{x3})}+e^{(Q_{y1} K_{y1} + Q_{y2} K_{y2} + Q_{y3} K_{y3})}} V_{y1}
\]
It doesn’t pull in any z elements. The causal mask makes sure of it - because tokens can only look behind, never ahead, the mixing they do is only over tokens before them. Every time we add a new token, and new rows, that mask makes sure that no information from that new token comes into play. We could add a fourth, fifth, hundredth token to the sequence, and never will any of their Q, K, or V come to incorporate into that row 2 output - it’s completely fixed.




So, hopefully you’re convinced that masked self-attention leaves previous rows unchanged. But a decoder stack has two more sublayers that operate on it before we get to our final output. So of course the next question is: do they matter?
Of course, the point of this whole appendix is to assure you: no. The good news is that self-attention was the hard case of the three to run through. So we’ll hopefully not need to go through quite as much effort here to be sure the other two don’t matter, either.
Cross-attention
Recall how cross-attention differs from self-attention: the query comes from the decoder, but the key and value come from the encoder’s output, let’s call it \(E\), which are computed a single time and then are frozen. Whatever \(E\) is at the end of the encoder stack, it always is.
Then, recall how the score matrix mixes information. Every entry of S is a row of queries - corresponding to our decoder’s current sequence, multiplied by a column of keys, which will correspond to the frozen encoder information. Let’s say our encoder encoded the sequence:
\[ [a, b, c]\]
and we’re back to the 2 token case in the decoder, where our current output sequence is
\[ [x, y]\]
then:
\[
S = Q K^\top = \begin{bmatrix}
Q_{x1} \ Q_{x2} \ Q_{x3} \\
Q_{y1} \ Q_{y2} \ Q_{y3}
\end{bmatrix}
\times
\begin{bmatrix}K_{a1} \ K_{b1} \ K_{c1} \\ K_{a2} \ K_{b2} \ K_{c2} \\ K_{a3} \ K_{b3} \ K_{c3} \end{bmatrix}
\ = \
\begin{bmatrix}
(Q_{x1} K_{a1} + Q_{x2} K_{a2} + Q_{x3} K_{a3}) \ \ \
(Q_{x1} K_{b1} + Q_{x2} K_{b2} + Q_{x3} K_{b3}) \ \ \
(Q_{x1} K_{c1} + Q_{x2} K_{c2} + Q_{x3} K_{c3}) \\
(Q_{y1} K_{a1} + Q_{y2} K_{a2} + Q_{y3} K_{a3}) \ \ \
(Q_{y1} K_{b1} + Q_{y2} K_{b2} + Q_{y3} K_{b3}) \ \ \
(Q_{y1} K_{c1} + Q_{y2} K_{c2} + Q_{y3} K_{c3})
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The first row is still all about how token x queries about all of the other keys.
\[
S^{c} = \begin{bmatrix} s_{x,a} & s_{x,b} & s_{x,c} \\ s_{y,a} & s_{y,b} & s_{y,c} \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{matrix} \leftarrow \text{decoder token x asking about encoder tokens a, b, c}\\ \leftarrow \text{decoder token y asking about encoder tokens a, b, c} \end{matrix}
\]
When we add a new token to what the decoder is processing, we add a new row to this: token \(z\) asking about encoder tokens \(a, b, c.\) Because the encoder tokens are never changing, we also here never change rows about tokens that come before. In particular, because we just proved that the output from masked self attention always has existing rows frozen, then that \(Q\), the only thing in cross attention that cares about what’s coming in from self attention, also has existing rows frozen. We just proved in the 2-token self attention walkthrough that \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) themselves only ever mix within row. So cross-attention’s \(Q\), the only thing constructed by the output of self-attention \(O\), just re-mixes rows again. But those rows are frozen. The encoder output is frozen, so there’s nowhere in this cross-attention for mixing either.
This is true even as we press forward. We know the softmax and scaling only operate on the rows, so A must also just be the same kind of mix:
\[
A^{c} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{x,a} & a_{x,b} & a_{x,c} \\ a_{y,a} & a_{y,b} & a_{y,c} \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{matrix} \leftarrow \text{decoder token x asking about encoder tokens a, b, c}\\ \leftarrow \text{decoder token y asking about encoder tokens a, b, c} \end{matrix}
\]
And finally, just to really hammer it home:
\[
O = A^{c} V = \begin{bmatrix} a_{x,a} & a_{x,b} & a_{x,c} \\ a_{y,a} & a_{y,b} & a_{y,c} \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix}V_{a1} \ V_{a2} \ V_{a3} \\ V_{b1} \ V_{b2} \ V_{b3} \\ V_{c1} \ V_{c2} \ V_{c3} \end{bmatrix}
\]
I can hopefully prove to you without writing this all the complete result, that the first row of this output is the only place \(x\) will show up, and the second row is the only place \(y\) will.
The feed-forward network, layer norm, and residual adds.
These are easy to write off, without doing any math at all, because all of these operations are explicitly position-wise - each one is processing over a single row as a fundamental assumption. It’s not that they happen to never mix - nothing about those operations would ever allow any mixing at all.

The FFN applies the same two-layer network to each row independently: row \(x\)’s output depends only on row \(x\)’s input.
LayerNorm normalizes each row using only that row’s own mean and variance.
The residual add is element by element, so every position is added to its own position - every row to its own row.

Since none of them can reach over to another row, none of them can pull \(z\) information into row \(x\) or row \(y\).
So, the whole block is safe. All three sublayers give the same result for the same position, every time. Masked self-attention mixes each decoder row only with earlier decoder rows, cross-attention mixes each decoder row only with the fixed encoder, and the FFN, norms, and residuals handle each row entirely on its own. There is no way by which the newly appended token’s information enters an earlier row. The earlier rows pass through the entire decoder block exactly as they were.



Just to finally relate back to the original point, that’s exactly why we just take the final row of the decoder output for next token prediction. When we say “the previous rows have already been used”, we really mean exactly that. The previous rows were used already, and since they literally do not change at all with every pass, they have nothing new to offer us. The information about those previous tokens do come into play for the current one, and help it come together as a rich mix of everything in the past, but the actual information we read off of a previous row is a fixed thing.
And it’s really all down to that causal mask. Because we don’t allow any looking forward, of course adding a token ahead of an existing one doesn’t tell us anything. That was the whole point of masking out the future, so that previous tokens can’t cheat and look ahead. The way that we do that is exactly what we’ve seen play out here: by making sure that none of the new token’s information ever changes what we would predict without it.



Now, the glaring thing to think here is that the whole decoder stack seems like a huge waste of compute. Imagine when the output sequence is hundreds, thousands, tokens long. We’re holding multiple thousand-dimension matrices in memory just to read off the very last line as the thing we actually use. Seems like a total waste!
And it is. Of course, modern techniques are very clever, and have found a way to exploit this to drastically speed up inference times with something called the KV Cache.
The basic idea is this: When we have a new token come into the sequence, the only way an earlier position participates is as an attention target. The new token’s query just needs to know how to attend to the earlier positions’ keys and values. But those keys and values depend only on the earlier positions’ representations, which we just meticulously proved don’t change.
So, instead of doing it all over again, just compute each position’s keys and values once, and cache them. Then each generation step becomes:

Run forward only the new token through the stack.
Append its key and value to the cache, and let its query attend over the whole cache.
Project its final vector to get the next token.

Instead of re-processing a growing sequence every step, you process exactly one new token per step. Every modern autoregressive LLM does this, and it’s a huge part of what allows generation to be blazing fast.
Of course, it isn’t free. The cache now has to hold the keys and values for every past position, at every layer. So how to manage the cache, share it where possible, access it quickly, are all active concerns for those working on large, modern models.
If you’re interested in much more detail about KV Caching, I have a whole tutorial about it! You can find it here: KV Caching Tutorial
Take me back to the main tutorial

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
We’ll build the full transformer from the original paper, which includes both an encoder, which reads and understands an input sequence, and a decoder, which generates an output sequence from it, one token at a time. The core model architecture then just needs an input to process the data, those two parts, and an output to give the final predictions:

Of course, a lot happens inside those individual pieces, which we’ll fill as we go. But those 4 main components are the core of the architecture.
And while this encoder-decoder design is the original, complete form of the architecture, modern models also come in encoder-only and decoder-only flavors. We’ll discuss those once we fully understand the “complete” version.
As we go, we’ll use the original paper is our blueprint, but this notebook isn’t a line-by-line reproduction of it. In the time since 2017, the field has settled on a clearly better choice for some parts of the model, so where those choices are obvious and settled, we’ll choose them instead rather than sticking faithrfully to the paper and choosing something deprecated. When that happens, I’ll point out what the paper did differently and why things changed. The goal is a strong understanding of the core architecture, built the way you’d reasonably build it today.
We’ll build up to actually assembling and training a transformer on a small, simple task. The paper’s training task was translating between languages, which needs far more data and compute than we’d want here. So we’ll give our model a miniature version of translation: converting human-written dates into a standard format.
"15 june 2017" \(\rightarrow\) "2017-06-15"
It’s small enough to train quickly, but still has all of the same core considerations as the original task, which we’ll get to see really matter in how we make decisions about setting up our model.

Major Sections
This notebook is divided into 11 core sections, each covering some major block of the architecture, training, evaluating, or modern extensions.

Inputs - how text becomes numbers: tokenization, byte-pair encoding, embeddings, and positional encodings.
The Building Blocks - attention, multi-head attention, residual connections, layer normalization, and feed-forward networks.
The Encoder - assembling the blocks into the half that understands the input.
The Decoder - causal masking and cross-attention, for the half that generates.
The Output - turning vectors back into tokens.
Assembling the Full Transformer - putting it all together in one model.
Training - teacher forcing, the loss, the optimizer, and learning-rate scheduling.
Training on a Real Task - our date-translation model, trained from scratch.
Using the Model - generating outputs, and testing how far it generalizes.
Inspecting the Model - attention maps and embeddings: what did it actually learn?
Transformers in the Wild - how modern models build on (and depart from) this architecture.

A handful of deeper tangents live in the Appendices, where I link to the appropriate one wherever it comes up.

📌 Note: This notebook assumes you’re comfortable with the basics of neural networks - layers, weights, and training by gradient descent. If you aren’t - I suggest a brief introduction there first!
