Either way, it seems the embeddings, like everything else we’ve looked at, just mirror what the model needed to know.




Similar to Section 9, where we could’ve looked at thousands of outputs, you can keep going forever with attention maps. We’ve looked at them every which way, and even peeked at the embeddings. So while we can keep going, I think we’ve proved how and when those things are useful, and when they’re not. They can tell us many things, but are also not the full story.
So you might wonder, how do we get the full story? But that answer is a very, very long list of things involving editing the model, picking it apart thoroughly, and very complex visualizations. So we’ll just mention a few more things you could do, but then wrap up looking at the model’s internals for any more answers.
Most of these things try to get at exactly the wall we kept hitting in this Section - attention helps us understand what the model decided to look at, but not what it decided to do with that information. A lot of that exists in the output projections and the feedforward networks, which are a lot harder to investigate. But, if you wanted to, here are some of the ways you’d do that:

The logit lens. The model’s final step turns a position’s vector into a next token by running it through the output layer. The logit lens does that early, taking the half-finished vector from an intermediate layer and pushing it through that same output layer, to see what the model would say if it only had part of the information. If you do it at every layer, you can watch the guess sharpen from nonsense into the final answer.
Ablations and activation patching. Rather than just looking at what the model did and inferring, these methods actively intervene. You prove that a part of the model matters by changing it, and seeing what happens. During ablations, you delete a component to see if the model needed it. In activation patching, you swap a component between a working and a broken run to see if the output moves. This lets you see what the model actually uses to come to its decisions.
Probing. You can freeze the model, grab its internal activation at some layer, and train a small classifier on top of that to predict a property. Essentially, see if with some internal representation, you’d be able to find some information you care about, or think the model ought to care about. If the classifier succeeds, that information is linearly present in the representation. This is cheap to run and popular, with of course the caveat that present doesn’t mean used, so the probe can read off something the model itself never acts on.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs). A single neuron usually fires for many unrelated things (called being “polysemantic”), because the model crams far more concepts than it has neurons by spreading them across combinations of neurons (called “superposition”). An SAE is a second, small network trained to take one of the model’s activation vectors and rewrite it as a short list of active features pulled from a much larger learned “dictionary” of directions, forced to use only a few at a time. When it works, each dictionary feature means one clean thing, so you can finally read an activation as “these specific features fired.” This is the current frontier, and where a lot of today’s excitement lives, so a lot of active work is being done here.
Tracing whole circuits. Less a separate tool than the goal the others serve. Once you can examine components one at a time, you can try to find the handful that together carry one specific behavior, work out each one’s job, and show how they wire into a complete mechanism - a “circuit.” It’s the closest you can get to reverse-engineering a piece of a model. (The famous work on this is via “induction heads,” the mechanism behind in-context copying, though it’s quite involved and difficult to describe in just a few sentences.)

And it goes much deeper. If you want a sense of the frontier, the work on sparse autoencoders and “monosemanticity” (Elhage et al., 2022; Bricken et al., 2023) is where a lot of the current excitement lives, and the effort to trace full circuits (Olah et al. , 2020; Olsson et al., 2022) shows how far the reverse-engineering can go. These are massive, active areas of research. On a model as small as ours, you can be fairly thorough without many tools at all, but on a frontier model, interpretability is very much a live problem. And it’s quite an important one, since much of the case for trusting these systems rests on being able to see inside them. There’s easily a whole other notebook’s worth of content here, so we’ll leave it at that!

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
If you’ve somehow made it all the way to the end of this tutorial, then you (hopefully!) have a strong grasp on all of the fundamentals of the transformer model - from the math that drives it, to how to build one in code, to how to prod at it once it’s trained. And though the transformer we built here is small, it is the same exact underlying fundamentals that even the largest, most capable models today use.
Of course, outside of the fundamentals, there is a lot that modern, large LLMs do a little bit differently. And the field is constantly evolving to continue to develop new methods. So while the underlying architecture still stands, many of the individual pieces we’ve discussed have been updated to a more efficient or better-behaved version of itself. And the exact ways in which these models are now used, and the cases to which they’ve been adapted, has also evolved as the problems the field tries to solve evolve.
So while we absolutely cannot exhaust a decade of research in this section, I’ll try to give a little bit of a map of the landscape of current, modern models you may see out “in the wild”.


One of the most obvious things that’s happened in the last decade is that many of the components of the original transformer have been swapped out for “better” versions of themselves. And almost every one of those swaps is driven by the pressure of massive scale, so in particular, every component has mostly been re-engineered to be faster, lighter on memory, more stable to train, and able to handle far longer inputs.
Now that we have a full understanding of the core components, it’s hopefully a little bit easier to understand why you’d swap these things. I’ll give a brief intro, but mostly here just enumerate what, for each of the things that we built, the more modern common alternatives are, and what they buy us.


Our implementation: We used fixed sinusoids, added to the embeddings at the input. This works, but some of the most useful structure of those position vectors gets muddied in the addition. The model has to learn to exploit how this encodes relative position, the absolute positions are too easy to learn on instead, and it can’t extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training.
Key alternatives to know about:

RoPE (rotary position embeddings). This takes the rotational property that should have been useful about sinusoidal encodings, and exploits it better by moving it to inside attention. Rather than adding a position vector, you rotate the query and key vectors themselves by a position-dependent angle. The query-key dot product then depends only on the relative offset between the two tokens. Absolute position cancels by construction, instead of being something the model must learn to ignore. This also makes base-frequency length-extension methods possible. (See Appendix 2 for some more details if you haven’t - we extensively work through some of the main properties of sinusoidal encodings, and touch on RoPE, there.)
ALiBi (attention with linear biases). This method is even simpler. It skips position embeddings entirely and just adds a penalty to each attention score that grows with the distance between the two tokens. Its appeal is that it carries no learned position parameters at all, and it was built specifically to extrapolate well. You can train on short sequences, and run on much longer ones, out of the box.

The state of the field: RoPE is the default in most modern LLMs, with ALiBi as a less-common alternative. The reason is roughly what you’d guess from the two descriptions - ALiBi’s linear penalty hard-codes a “closer is always better” bias that it never gets to unlearn, which is fragile, especially for the long-range cases (retrieval, a fact buried early in a long document) that models increasingly have to handle. RoPE assumes none of that, which is a big part of why it won out. The active frontier here is all about context length: how to take a model trained at one length and stretch it to far longer ones. A lot of the active research tries to rescale RoPE’s frequencies or the positions they act on (position interpolation, YaRN, and relatives).



Our implementation: We built “full” multi-head scaled dot-product attention. This version includes every token attending to every other one (every earlier one, under the causal mask), and each head with its own queries, keys, and values. It’s the heart of the model, but has two major costs that become the defining problem at scale. First, the attention matrix is sequence-length by sequence-length, so both compute and memory grow with the square of the input length - double the context, quadruple the cost. Second, when generating autoregressively, a naive implementation must re-run the entire past through attention at every single new token, costing tons of time, again, especially for longer sequences.
Key alternatives to know about: Since it’s the most central part of the transformer, a lot of work has been done here. Major upgrades come from two very distinct sides - 1) trying to compute the exact same result, just faster and/or with less memory, and 2) changing what attention actually computes, to trade a little quality for a lot of efficiency.
1) Same result, just faster or lighter:

KV caching. If you store the keys and values you already computed for past tokens in the sequence instead of recomputing them each time, then each new token can be produced much, much faster. The output is exactly identical, you just store a bit of the information instead of recalculating it every time. It results in massive time speed-ups, and is what makes autoregressive generation practical at all. So this is actually so standard that you’ll basically never see generation without it in the backend, unless it’s a very small model anyway or quick demo. (We dive deep into why this is possible and relatively easy to do in Appendix 4, which also sets up the notebook I have on KV Caching. Read both for more details!)
FlashAttention. This is a way of computing exactly the same attention we already know, but with the work reorganized so the full n×n matrix is never written to slow memory. Essentially, the computation is broken up into pieces that can be done in faster memory. You end up with the exact same numbers out, but just much less memory traffic. By avoiding storing the full matrix, memory grows linearly rather than quadratically, and skipping all that memory traffic makes it much faster.

2) Changes to attention itself (and therefore a real tradeoff):

Multi-query and grouped-query attention. The KV cache makes generation much faster, but the cache rapidly becomes huge and memory intensive, in part because every head keeps its own keys and values. MQA goes to the far extreme to reduce that size - it makes all query heads share a single key/value head, shrinking the necessary size of the cache by a factor of the head count. Huge memory saving, but it costs quality, so GQA splits the difference by keeping a handful of key/value groups instead of just one. That way, you get most of the memory savings and most of the quality. Note, this is a trained-in architectural choice, so not a totally free optimization you can do at inference-time (though, can require only minimal extra training to apply). GQA is where most large models have landed.
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA): Introduced with DeepSeek-V2, it’s a way to shrink the KV cache. Where GQA saves memory by having heads share K/V, MLA instead compresses each token’s keys and values into a single small latent vector. Only that latent is cached, and it gets projected back up into full per-head K and V when it’s time to attend. In effect, it’s a learned low-rank bottleneck on what the cache has to remember. Rebuilding K/V costs extra compute at every step, though, so you’re trading memory for compute. It also doesn’t play nicely with RoPE out of the box, so MLA carries a small separate key just for position information. Like GQA, it’s a trained-in architectural choice.
Sliding-window / sparse attention. Here, you simply drop the “every token sees every token” rule and let each token attend only to a local window, or a sparse pattern plus a few global tokens. It makes the computation an approximation rather than the full thing, but it does pull the quadratic cost down toward linear. Information still travels across the whole sequence because each layer’s window compounds with depth, so it’s not quite as bad as it first seems. Though the bet is still that most of what a token needs is nearby.

The state of the field: These are mostly complementary rather than competing / “choose one”, so a modern model typically runs all of the “exact” ones together (KV caching and FlashAttention), with GQA also being very popular (even though it does lose some quality). MLA is a newer alternative that some frontier open models (notably DeepSeek’s) have adopted. Sliding-window and sparse variants show up more selectively, often where very long context is much more of the point, since their efficient growth with sequence size is such an advantage. The active question is whether attention’s quadratic cost can be escaped without surrendering quality. Faster attention implementations that actually change the computation are rarely chosen to replace full attention outright. The most serious alternatives right now actually scrap attention entirely rather than make it faster. State-space models like Mamba, which process sequences in linear time and are strong on long inputs, are a strong contender, though whether they fully match attention-based implementations across the board is still being argued. So attention’s computation cost remains the central engineering problem of the modern transformer, with much active work still being done.



Our implementation: We used LayerNorm, in the pre-norm position. For each token’s vector it subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation (across the d_model features), then applies a learned scale and shift. The things to note there are 1) it runs at every block (twice per layer, before attention and before the feed-forward), and 2) it’s really doing two jobs at once, both re-centering (subtracting the mean) and re-scaling (dividing by the standard deviation). There’s really nothing wrong with it. But, it turns out the re-centering pulls much less weight than the re-scaling, while still costing a full mean-and-subtract every single time it runs.
Key alternatives to know about:

RMSNorm (root-mean-square normalization). It drops the mean-subtraction entirely: it normalizes only by the root-mean-square of the vector. It usually drops the learned shift too, so just keeps the re-scaling. The reasoning is exactly what we just mentioned about the LayerNorm - the stabilizing benefit is coming almost entirely from controlling the scale, not from re-centering, so you can just skip that part with no measurable loss in quality. It’s a small change, but it’s run at every block of a very deep network, so it adds up.

The state of the field: RMSNorm is the default in most modern large models now. But more than just the method, there are two more things worth knowing.
First, on placement. The original paper put the norm after each sublayer’s residual addition (“post-norm”), whereas we used “pre-norm” (normalizing before the sublayer). We did this because it changes nothing about the method itself, so we didn’t have to learn anything new. But it has been shown to make very deep stacks far more stable to train. So we went ahead and did the modern version there already rather than staying faithful to the paper. But just pointing out that post-to-pre norm is something that was investigated, and then settled on in the field.
Second thing, is that normalization is actually one of the fiddlier levers in training enormous models. Beyond just the RMSNorm swap, which is nearly universal, there is a lot of work being done on where to add normalization. Some teams have added normalization in new spots as a way to keep training stable at scale - like normalizing the queries and keys before attention (QK-norm). Exactly where norms can benefit is still something people tune.



Our implementation: We used a position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with a ReLU in between, applied independently to every position (with an inner dimension four times d_model). We talked extensively in Appendix 3 about why models need a non-linearity like ReLU, but ReLU itself is a rather blunt one. It hard-zeros every negative value, so has a hard corner at zero, it discards everything on the negative side, and a unit stuck in the negative region gets no gradient at all, so it can effectively “die.” It still works, but is also improvable.
Key alternatives to know about:

GeLU (Gaussian error linear unit). This is a smooth drop-in for ReLU - instead of a hard cutoff at zero, it multiplies each input by a smooth gate (the Gaussian CDF) that’s near 0 for very negative inputs and near 1 for clearly positive ones. This just means negatives are suppressed gently rather than clipped off. It gives cleaner gradients and a modest quality bump. It’s the activation in BERT and the GPT-2/3 line.
SwiGLU and other gated units. This involves more than simply switching the activation function. It also changes the block’s shape. Instead of one projection → activation → projection, you run two parallel input projections: one passes through an activation and then gates (elementwise-multiplies) the other, before the final projection. That gating gives the layer input-dependent, multiplicative control over what flows through, and it trains better per parameter. (Because it adds a third weight matrix, the inner dimension is usually shrunk to about two-thirds to keep the parameter count comparable.) It’s the default feed-forward in most modern LLMs, like LLaMA and PaLM.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). This is an even bigger departure. You replace the single feed-forward network with many parallel ones (“experts”), plus a small router that, for each token, picks just a few to actually run (say 2 of 8). Each token only flows through those few, so the compute per token stays roughly fixed while the total parameter count can grow enormously, since now how big the model is, is very different from how much it costs to run. It has downsides though, like how you still have to store every expert (so, large memory), and because the router has to be trained and kept load-balanced, it adds a real training instability. Mixtral is the best-known open example.

The state of the field: Gated feed-forwards of the SwiGLU family are the standard middle of a modern transformer block now, with plain ReLU mostly historical. MoE is increasingly common at the frontier. One of the main reasons why is, as we’ve discussed, the feed-forward network is actually where the majority of a transformer’s parameters are. So when you want to grow a model’s capacity, the feed-forward is where the capacity already is. When you want to sparsify your model, it’s also where it makes the most sense to. MoE helps to do that. However, its surrounding engineering - handling the routing, load-balancing, and the cost of holding every expert in memory - is complicated and hard. So it’s powerful, but far from free.



Our implementation: In our date formatting model, we tokenized at the character level deliberately, so every token stayed legible while we learned. The cost is that sequences get long (every character is its own token, which is expensive given attention’s quadratic scaling) and the model has to rebuild every recurring pattern from loose characters each time. But back in Section 1, we talked about the way that tokenization is more commonly done, using BPE, in depth.
Key alternatives to know about. Most of the modern alternatives and extensions: byte-level BPE, WordPiece, Unigram/SentencePiece, as well as their quirks, we covered in Appendix 1. So I will point you there to learn about the modern alternatives. But summarize just briefly here. Essentially every modern model will use subword tokenization of some sort. Recent frontier models have converged specifically on byte-level BPE with large (100k+) vocabularies.
Character-level, like we did above, is the kind of choice you’d really only make if, for some specific reason, you have a very narrow task or very specific set of tokens (like we did!)
The state of the field: As we said, byte-level BPE is the most commonly used tokenization scheme. But one more thing being looked into is whether to drop the tokenizer entirely, with byte or character-level models that learn straight from raw bytes with no merge step at all (ByT5, MEGABYTE). They erase tokenization’s quirks, but reintroduce exactly the long-sequence problem our character-level scheme had, which then causes the exact attention efficiency issues we got into in 11.1.2. So for now, the tokenizer stays standard.




Back in Section 4.1, we discussed briefly how the full transformer - an encoder-decoder - in its complete form is not actually the only transformer architecture you’ll see. There’s also encoder-only models for understanding, and decoder-only models for generation. And while the encoder-decoder is still used for turning one sequence into another, decoder models are actually the most common type, and what almost all modern frontier models are. But all still have use cases, and you’ll see each of the three show up as modern models.
So now that we’ve completed our understanding of the full encoder-decoder architecture, let’s revisit the three types to talk about when you’ll still see them, what modern examples are, and how the three differ in how they’re trained.


Decoder-only models, of course, contain only the decoder part of the architecture, with one additional edit. There’s no cross-attention, because there’s no encoder output to cross-attend to. They’re a single stack of masked (causal) self-attention that only ever looks backward, producing one token at a time.
At training time, you simply give full sequences from your data, shifted one like we did with teacher forcing. It’s just next token prediction over your enormous corpus. At generation time, they produce one token at a time, starting typically from a prompt that sets up what to generate next. The prompt often uses special tokens for tagging (similar to the <bos>, <eos> tokens) to help separate what was “input” vs “output” (though it’s all processed the same way).

This is what most models you’ll hear about are. The GPT line, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, and essentially every frontier chat and generation model.
Today, they’re the most common because that single objective (predict the next token) can actually cover an astonishing range if you just define your task right. Many tasks can be reframed as generation, even ones that sound like they should require understanding: \[ \text{"[REVIEW]. The sentiment here is \_\_\_"}\]
as we noted in 4.1.
Of course, this works because the decoder stack can also understand, just only based on things behind it. But the same understanding benefits that you get from attention and the feedforward network are of course still there.
It’s also the simplest of the three, the one that scales most cleanly, and in-context learning falls out of it for free.



Encoder-only models are then, the encoder stack alone. The blocks have the full bidirectional self-attention, and they aim to produce rich representations rather than generated tokens.
At training time, you add a prediction head whose job is to predict what word was masked out from your input data. Then, when you want to actually use the encoder, you just throw that out and the rest remains the same.

The original canonical example of an encoder-only is BERT. But although that’s an older model, the family is very much alive in modern times as well. The encoder-only architecture is the backbone of the embedding and retrieval models behind semantic search and RAG (Sentence-BERT and its descendants), and it’s still being actively modernized (ModernBERT, 2024).
The field is still alive, because you sometimes do genuinely just want to represent text rather than produce it. Classification, retrieval, reranking, entity tagging, are all tasks where a bidirectional encoder that can look over the whole sequence at once gives richer representations, and can be far cheaper to run.
Typically, what comes out of an encoder is an embedding you want to use for something. It’s very common to attach a small task-specific head to the output, and train that to do a specific task (like score sentiment). Because you can often do this trusting that the encoder’s embeddings are already good, this means you can freeze the encoder portion and just train the head. So for tasks like that, an established encoder + head is often much, much cheaper to train as well.



Encoder-decoder models are the full version that we looked into. They’re by far the most complicated since they have both an encoder and decoder. The encoder reads the entire input bidirectionally, and a decoder generates the output one token at a time while attending back to the encoder through cross-attention.
As we already saw, they’re trained with the encoder turned on and the decoder doing the task with teacher forcing. At generation time, the encoder path still runs, passing its representation into the cross-attention of the decoder, which generates one token at a time.

The canonical modern example is T5, which frames every task as text-to-text. But a model like Whisper, which is a speech-to-text model, is an enormously popular one too. It takes audio in through the encoder, text out through the decoder. We’ll discuss different modalities like this a bit more in depth in just a little bit.
Encoder-decoders persist even though decoder-only models now translate and summarize perfectly well by prompting, because sometimes having the entire input available up front just really is a major advantage. This is especially true of course when the output is a genuinely different sequence - those cases where we needed “Input” and “Input2” to be distinct segments. The clean separation of tasks means the encoder can process the source with no causal constraint while the decoder focuses on generating. That means it’s still the natural fit for tasks like translation, speech, and much multimodal work where “read this completely, then produce that” is still the best way to approach the problem.




In this tutorial, we saw actually a quite narrow view of training. We had a very specific task, input and output data that we could generate and match exactly, and so we were able to put that through a standard training pipeline and easily grade behavior.
But “training” can take a lot of different shapes. As we just saw in 11.2, the pretraining objective (the thing you train to produce) is tied to the architecture family. Decoder-only models learn on next-token prediction, encoder-only models learn to fill in masked tokens, and encoder-decoders learn sequence-to-sequence. And even within those families, the space of training techniques that are done is very vast.
So while the core loop of training never changes: find a way to measure how well the model is doing, then nudge its parameters toward improving that measure - the exact way you do that, what you measure and how you improve, actually has a lot of wiggle room. We’ll talk about what some of those different choices are, as well as some of the additional considerations of modern training here.


The first thing to be aware of is that modern models, for a variety of tasks, are very often trained in a multi-stage sort of way. This means training the model distinct phases, where each is able to use different data, a different objective, or even to train a different part of the model.
The logic and reasoning behind doing multi-stage training is always the same. It’s cheaper and more effective to teach something broad and general, or easy and concrete, first, then specialize, than to do everything at once from scratch. And this is a general idea, well beyond language models. The core versions of this that show up in many places are:
1) Starting with a “pre-training” phase. Especially when teaching a model from scratch - fully randomized weights - a lot of what the model needs to learn doesn’t require high-quality, or even task-specific data. For example, learning the basic rules of grammar and sentence construction doesn’t need well-written novels and textbooks - you could do it from (presumably readable) Reddit comments. But this idea applies to tons of cases - you can start your training on a large, general dataset to build broad capability, then fine-tune on a smaller, task-specific one.
This is the backbone of modern transfer learning across all of deep learning. And it’s not just about “saving the good stuff”, even though that is a huge advantage (high-quality, task-specific data is often very scarce compared to broad, large datasets). It’s also been shown to make the model a better generalizer when it finally trains on the specific task.
The deeper reason is about representations: a pretrained model has built a general-purpose internal model of its domain. For language, that’s grammar, structure, meaning, broad world knowledge - all things that transfer to almost any task. Fine-tuning, then, doesn’t need to and shouldn’t rebuild them. It just learns to use them for the job at hand, so the scarce task-specific data is spent entirely on the task rather than relearning the basics. This has become so central that the whole modern field is largely organized around it: train one enormous, general “foundation model” once, at great expense, then adapt it to countless downstream uses (Bommasani et al., 2021).
2) Freezing certain parts of the model and training others. There are also often cases where you want to train the model in parts - holding some portions frozen while updating others - rather than the whole thing at once. The advantage is that training this way is often cheaper, but also that it protects what the model already learned from being trampled. A few common cases and ways you’ll see this done:

Hold a pretrained backbone frozen, and train only a small new head on top for a specific task. This is exactly what we described for how most encoder-only models are used. Assuming the embedding out of the frozen part is good, you can take good advantage of those without tweaking them at all.
Unfreeze just the last layers, and continue to train those. It’s been shown that, in particular, the earlier layers of a model tend to be where most broad, general knowledge is learned, and later layers tend to be where more of the task-specific subtleties are learned (see Yosinski et al. (2014), and notice, this predates transformers - it’s a much more general property). So one common technique is to fine tune a model by freezing everything but the last few layers, and allowing those to adjust to the new data and task.
Training portions of a complex architecture on their own. The idea here is a bit like holding the backbone frozen, but instead of taking an established backbone, you inspect which parts of your model could be trained on their own. A classic example in modern architectures are latent diffusion models (like StableDiffusion), which first train a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn how to compress and then decompress an image. Since this task is highly well-constrained, and does a very specific thing (taking in an image, and giving out the same image), it can be trained on its own, as a separate task, before becoming part of the larger architecture.

3) Training using something, then throwing it out. We’ve already talked about a specific instance of this in encoder-only training, where a prediction head is used during training time and thrown out later. But this is a general pattern that can be used for training many models. You use a piece of the architecture just to create a useful training signal, and throw it away once training is done. What you keep is the representation it forced the rest of the model to learn. It often looks like:

A task head used only in training. The clearest case is the masked-language-model head on an encoder-only model. It’s used to define the fill-in-the-blank task, then discarded. The point of the head was just to define something to measure, but the goal was to keep the encoder’s representations, not the head that trained them.
An autoencoder where you keep only the encoder. This is a common pattern to train a feature extractor. An autoencoder is a network that compresses an input, then reconstructs it (input in, same input out). If you train this well, then throw away the part that reconstructs the image, then the first part is just a high quality feature extractor. The reconstruction task was only ever a way to force the encoder to learn a good compression. (This is a different use of an autoencoder than the latent-diffusion VAE we just discussed, which is trained separately and then kept - its encoder turns training images into latents during training, and its decoder renders the final image at generation. What we’re talking about here is throwing one half away entirely.)

The Modern Case
One of the fullest expressions of the idea of multi-stage training actually comes from the pipeline behind a modern chat assistant, which stacks several of these moves into one process. These models are built in three distinct stages, with a changing objective, and even changing training procedures in the different stages. And remember, the architecture to have in mind here is the “simple” decoder-only model.
The stages are:
Stage 1: Pretraining. The model is trained on next-token prediction over an enormous, diverse corpus, created from much of the web, books, and code. This is the task we’ve already discussed in detail, with the input and a teacher-forced shift of the input making up the data. The model’s goal is just to learn text at colossal scale. The crucial thing here is that this training is self-supervised - the “label” for each position is simply the next token, that literally comes from all of the text you scraped. So you’re just learning from massive data, no “truth” labeling needed, which is what lets it scale to trillions of tokens.

What comes out is a base model: an extraordinary text-completer, with an abundance of knowledge baked in.
If you input text, you’ll get out completion. Finishing of your sentence. It can’t yet, especially reliably, answer questions, because all it has learned to do is continue text, not answer.

Though it’s not a full-fledged chat assistant, a model coming out of this stage is still very capable. This is where the majority of the model’s world knowledge and language ability is learned. GPT-3 is the canonical demonstration that at enough scale, this stage alone produces startling few-shot ability.
Stage 2: Instruction Tuning. This is where the “following instruction” behavior is learned. The base model is fine-tuned on curated examples of (instruction, good response) pairs. This is ordinary supervised learning, so the same type of training task we did on our toy model, just on instruction-following data instead of dates. It mostly doesn’t add new knowledge, but it does teach new behavior: given a request, produce a helpful response rather than ramble onward the way a base model would.

What comes out is an SFT model (or sometimes called IFT): a model that can be chatted with and asked questions.
If you input text, you get a response, the assumption after this stage is that what you say is meant to be answered, not continued.

Though it’s not yet tuned for the quality of its answers, a model coming out of this stage is already a genuine assistant. This is where the ability to follow instructions - including ones it was never explicitly trained on - is learned. FLAN is the canonical demonstration of exactly that: instruction-tuning on a collection of tasks produces strong zero-shot performance on entirely new ones.
Stage 3: Preference Learning. The last step shapes the qualities that are hard to pin down as a supervised target. Things like helpfulness, tone, honesty, and harmlessness are all features you want the model to have, but they’re hard to put your finger on and rare to find cleanly labeled in data. You can’t easily write the one “correct” response that perfectly encapsulates helpfulness, but you can reliably say “this response is more helpful than that one.” So the classic recipe for this stage, RLHF, does just that. You collect human comparisons between responses, train a reward model to predict those preferences, then use reinforcement learning to push the model toward higher-reward outputs.

What comes out is an aligned model: This is the finished chat assistant, which is now not only capable and responsive, but shaped to be helpful, honest, and pleasant to interact with.
If you input text, you still get a response - but now one pushed toward what a person would actually prefer. The change from the last stage is in the response’s quality and character, not in what the model fundamentally does.

This is a genuinely different paradigm from everything above - the model stops being trained by “here’s the right answer” and starts being trained by “here’s which answer people preferred”. And the full machinery to train via reinforcement learning is pretty different from supervised and self-supervised training.
If you want all of the details, I have a notebook all about classic reinforcement learning here: RL for LLMs!
(Or, if you prefer other reading, a popular modern simplification, DPO, skips the separate reward model and optimizes for the preferences directly. InstructGPT is the canonical full RLHF pipeline.)
All modern models are trained in some mix of these stages. And with the typical pipeline of broad ability first, then instruction-following, then final alignment to preference. But treat that order as a common backbone, not a strict law. Both the sequence and the weight of each of these stages can actually vary quite a lot, and stages can get repeated, interleaved, run in multiple rounds, or occasionally skipped.
More importantly, how much a model actually learns in each stage has recently undergone pretty major shifts. In a standard chat model, the final RL stage is mostly used for polish - aligning tone and helpfulness on top of abilities that pretraining already established. But in, for example, reasoning models, that stage does far heavier lifting. RL algorithms like GRPO, with rewards that can verify an answer (did the math check out? did the code pass its tests?), have been able to teach the model a large portion of its actual reasoning capability, not just how it answers, but what it answers. DeepSeek-R1-Zero even showed strong reasoning emerging from large-scale RL run directly on a base model, with no supervised fine-tuning first.
So the three stages are the right mental model to start from, but where exactly most of the real learning happens is very much flexible, and the field is actively experimenting with how far each stage can be pushed.



There’s something beyond training methodology that’s often overlooked, and it’s about the data quality. When you train, you start from enormous amounts of messy, uneven, often outright junk data scraped from the internet, and a huge share of the real work is in cleaning it and deciding what goes in. In fact, now that the architecture has largely settled - nearly universally some version of the transformer we built here is the go-to architecture, data has become the single biggest lever separating a great model from a mediocre one.
I’ll keep this section brief, but a few things are worth knowing about how that plays out:
1) Quality beats raw quantity. More data is not automatically better, with low-quality text actually often degrading a model. So much of the work at the pretraining stage is really filtering. Removing junk, and especially deduplicating, as repeated data wastes compute and drives memorization (Lee et al., 2021), reliably improves the result. Pushed to the extreme, carefully curated high-quality data can let a much smaller model punch far above its weight - “Textbooks Are All You Need” showed surprisingly strong small models when trained on small, clean, textbook-like data.
2) Composition matters a lot. It’s not only how much data but what mix of it. How much web versus code versus math versus books versus other languages changes what the model is good at. Those proportions are often carefully tuned.
3) Synthetic data and distillation are rising fast. Increasingly, training data isn’t scraped at all, but is instead generated by prompting a capable model to produce examples, or by training a smaller model on a larger one’s outputs (distillation). This can be very powerful where good human data is scarce, like step-by-step reasoning traces. But it carries a real risk - lean too heavily on model-generated data and quality can degrade across successive generations, a failure mode called model collapse (Shumailov et al.).
Unfortunately, the good data might be running out. Frontier models are now large enough to be bumping against the limits of high-quality human text on the internet - the so-called “data wall” (Villalobos et al.). That pressure is much of why synthetic data, multimodal data, and squeezing more signal from less are such active frontiers.
So while data work is unglamorous, it’s where an enormous share of real frontier progress now comes from. It’s also increasingly the part labs want to keep secret - two models with near-identical architectures can differ wildly based purely on what they were fed, so the data is truly one of the most important components of training.



We’ve covered pretty extensively here what models to train, on what data, and even how, conceptually. But there’s a major reality that we haven’t touched on much which is about how, physically you pull it off. A frontier model is far, far too large to train on a single GPU. In fact, most “small” (few billion parameter) models are, too. But the bigger the model gets, the more challenging dealing with all of that size, and all of that compute, gets. Most large, or even medium, models need to run across many computers at once, for weeks or months on end. So training at scale is a difficult engineering problem in its own right. Knowing some of the most major considerations that need to happen for large scale training can be helpful context, so we’ll touch the main ideas here quickly.
The core idea for making training feasible is that you need to intelligently split the work by parallelizing the problem. There are three main ways to spread training across many devices, usually combined:

Data parallelism - put a full copy of the model on each device, split the batch between them, and average the gradients. It multiplies throughput, but every device still holds the whole model, so it doesn’t help when the model itself is too big.
Tensor (model) parallelism - split the individual layers across devices, so each holds and computes a slice of each weight matrix. This is necessary when a single layer won’t fit on one chip.
Pipeline parallelism - you can also split the stack of layers into stages, one group of layers per device, and feed micro-batches through like an assembly line. This helps when the whole depth of the model won’t fit.

But even split up, memory is often still very tight, so several additional tricks can help keep it in check. Some of the most common ones include:

Sharding - with plain data parallelism, every device redundantly stores a full copy of the parameters, gradients, and optimizer state (Adam’s running averages alone are about twice the size of the model). Sharding methods partition all of that across devices so no single one holds the whole thing.
Mixed-precision training (storing most things in 16-bit) and gradient accumulation (simulating a big batch in several small steps) are both very common techniques, which we already discussed briefly in Section 7.
Gradient checkpointing is a similar idea, where instead of storing every activation for the backward pass, you recompute some on the fly, trading extra compute for memory.

There’s also, of course, the whole hardware side of things. All this parallelism requires constantly shuffling enormous tensors between chips, so not only how big the chips are, but how they interconnect, becomes as much of a bottleneck as the chips themselves. Frontier training runs on clusters of thousands of specialized accelerators (GPUs or TPUs), wired together with very high-bandwidth links, for extended stretches of time.
That’s all I’ll say, and honestly, all I can. First, as I’m no expert here. But also, because engineering around large-scale training is a deep and specialized engineering discipline of its own, and much of the knowledge that is necessary to train frontier models lives in those labs, as they’re the only ones with the scale to do it! So I’ll point you in the direction of some canonical references for deeper reading, but otherwise leave it at that. (See Megatron-LM, GPipe, ZeRO)



Ok, one final thing to touch on when it comes to training. We talked already about some methods for avoiding retraining an entire, large model, like freezing sections, or fine-tuning on top of an existing, well-performing model. But there’s an additional trick that makes doing additional fine-tuning very time and memory efficient, and it’s called parameter efficient fine-tuning.
The idea is this: if you start with a model that has plenty of existing knowledge for a task, but you just want to tweak it, doing additional full fine tuning is kind of a waste. It costs enormous memory and compute, and you risk messing up good behaviors the model already did have, especially if you’re fitting an enormous model to a relatively small problem.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods get around this by freezing the pretrained model entirely, and training only a tiny set of new parameters bolted onto it. The best-known method is LoRA (and its cousin, DoRA). Instead of changing a big weight matrix W directly, LoRA leaves it frozen and learns a small low-rank update beside it - two skinny matrices whose product has the same shape as W but far fewer parameters. The intuition is that the change to the model that a given task requires actually just lives in a low-dimensional subspace, so you don’t need to touch the full matrix - a thin low-rank correction captures it. In practice, this can mean training well under 1% of the model’s parameters. Extensions like QLoRA push it further still, quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit so even very large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
The payoff is huge, and the technique allows you to fine-tune a huge model on modest hardware, since you only ever compute gradients and optimizer state for that tiny slice. And because the base is untouched, you can sidestep the catastrophic forgetting that full fine-tuning risks.
If you want to know more, see my LoRA Tutorial!




Throughout this whole notebook, we’ve mostly been talking about feeding our transformer text data. And indeed, most modern transformer-based models you interact with are largely text-based. But there’s nothing really special about text. Looking back to Section 1, we had to do a ton of work to even get text to look like something the model could process: numbers. And the architecture itself doesn’t care at all where the numbers come from. Really, the only thing that matters is that the numbers ultimately come to represent some sort of a sequence so that attention can exploit that structure. Where you get that sequence from… well that can be a ton of different places, actually.
So, if you haven’t fully appreciated it already, do now: a transformer is a general-purpose engine for processing sequences of vectors. As long as your data is, or can be interpreted as, a sequence. A transformer will work. That’s really why they are so ubiquitous. Yes, they’re amazing general purpose learners. But also, sequences are everywhere. And for so many other data types, it’s barely even a stretch to turn them into the kind of input data the transformer wants. A few key examples:

Images. The Vision Transformer (ViT) chops an image into a grid of small patches, linearly projects each patch into a vector, and feeds that sequence into a standard transformer, with patches as “tokens.”
Audio. We talked briefly about Whisper already, which turns speech into a sequence of audio-frame vectors and runs them through a transformer encoder-decoder.
Others. Beyond what’s easily perceptible to humans entirely, there are tons of other cases. Protein sequences, DNA, time series, even sequences of game states - anything you can lay out as a sequence of vectors is fair game.

And of course, many models can now effortlessly deal with combinations of modalities. Image-patch tokens and text tokens can go into the same model (the basis of modern multimodal and vision-language systems), or image and text encoders can be trained to share an embedding space, as in CLIP. The list goes on, because the space of different modalities that the model can accept isn’t really bounded by much - it’s as big as the space of problems you could think to solve, and as architectures you could think to put together.
So the key takeaway here isn’t that certain modalities need certain architectures. It’s that almost all modalities are compatible with the transformer. Yes, with their own nuances of how to process the input (like we needed with text), and always their own considerations for the specific task you’re solving, but not simply because the data comes from somewhere different.
And that’s true of this whole section. And a takeaway of the whole notebook! Even though we’ve spent a lot of time talking about different ways to train and use these models, how to pick them apart, and know what they do, the architecture we built here is the reusable idea, and remains, at the core. Everything else builds on, and works with, those central components. But the backbone - the basic transformer - is still all you need :).

title: The Transformer Architecture
text:
The appendices here are “optional reading” - meant to give more clarity or detail to something we already touched on in the main tutorial. I suggest referencing them alongside the main tutorial’s content when you read them!


One of the most important things for keeping straight in your mind everything that’s happening in a model is what dimensions things are as they are getting transformed. Here, I’ll lay it all out simply as a place to re-reference as you work through this notebook.
Key dimensions:

\(\bf{n_\text{seq}}\): the sequence length going into the model.
\(\bf{d_\text{model}}\): the dimensionality of the model
\(\bf{n_\text{embeds}}\): the size of the word embeddings (\(\bf = {d_\text{model}}\)), see note below

1. Word Embeddings
Word embeddings create, for each value in the starting sequence, \(n_\text{seq}\), a vector of size \(n_\text{embeds}\) that makes up our input into the model \(X\):
\[
X = n_\text{seq} \times n_\text{embeds}
\]
2. Positional Encodings
Positional encodings are added element-wise to the word embeddings, so they must be the same shape: \[
PE = n_\text{seq} \times n_\text{embeds}
\]
3. Attention
Attention starts by making \(Q, K, V\) matrices out of \(W^Q, W^K, W^V\) weight matrices.
\(W^Q, W^K, W^V\) must all have the same dimensionality:
\[
W^Q, W^K, W^V = n_\text{embeds} \times d_\text{model}
\]
so then, \(Q, K, V\) end up with size: \[
Q, K, V = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\]
Attention is calculated by doing \(Q K^T\), \[
A = n_\text{seq} \times n_\text{seq}
\] Scaled and softmax’ed in scalar operations which don’t change the shape, then multiplied by \(V\), resulting in: \[
O = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\]
This \(O\) becomes the input for the next layer.

📌 Note: Notice, that this means that, for attention specifically, \(d_\text{model}\) does not need to be a fixed value/property. Here, we see the \(n_{embeds}\) dimension drop out and get transformed to \(d_\text{model}\). The math for attention would work out all the same if the next layer had a different \(d_\text{model}\) size.
In practice though, we do fix \(d_\text{model}\) for every layer in the entire model because we use residual connections, which do need it to be the same for every layer. In fact, these need the input and output to an attention layer to be exactly the same size. So it must be enforced in a transformer that \(\bf{n_{embeds} = d_\text{model}}\) as well, and that \(d_\text{model}\) is a fixed property for all layers in the model. If the desired embedding model has \(n_{embeds} \neq d_\text{model}\), a simple linear projection layer takes care of this. 
I will continue to label them separately for clarity of their meaning, but know that this is true, general property.

4. Multi-Head Attention
This is also why multi0head attention works so smoothly. In multi-head attention, we additionally have:

\(\bf{\text{h}}\): the number of heads
\(\bf{d_k}\): the dimensionality of heads (\(d_\text{model} / \text{h}\)), by definition

Similar to self attention, we start by making \(Q, K, V\) matrices out of \(W^Q, W^K, W^V\) weight matrices. Except now, we have \(i = 1 ... \text{h}\) heads of size \(d_k\) instead.
\(W^{Q_i}, W^{K_i}, W^{V_i}\) must all have the same dimensionality:
\[
W^{Q_i}, W^{K_i}, W^{V_i} = n_\text{embeds} \times d_\text{k}
\]
so then, \(Q_i, K_i, V_i\) end up with size: \[
Q_i, K_i, V_i = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{k}
\]
Attention is calculated by doing \(Q_i K_i^T\), \[
A_i = n_\text{seq} \times n_\text{seq}
\]
This is scaled and softmax’ed in scalar operations which don’t change the shape, then multiplied by \(V_i\), for each of the heads, resulting in: \[
O_i = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{k}
\]
The \(\text{h}\) \(O_i\)’s are combined with a concatenation: \[
O' = \begin{bmatrix} O_1 & O_2 & ... & O_\text{h} \end{bmatrix} \\
O' = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\]
Then, \(W^O\) recontextualizes these relative to each other, \(W^O = d_\text{model} \times d_\text{model}\) \[
O = O' W^O \\
O = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\]
Same result in terms of dimensionality! Even though we broke into distinct heads.
5. The Feed-Forward Network
The FFN is applied to each position independently. It expands to a larger inner dimension and then contracts back. We add:

\(\bf{d_\text{ff}}\): the inner (hidden) dimension of the FFN, typically \(4 \times d_\text{model}\).

With \(W_1 = d_\text{model} \times d_\text{ff}\) and \(W_2 = d_\text{ff} \times d_\text{model}\), the input \(O = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\) is widened, passed through a nonlinearity (which doesn’t change shape), then narrowed back: \[
H = O\,W_1 = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{ff} \qquad\rightarrow\qquad O\,W_1 W_2 = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\] So the FFN takes \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\) right back to \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\) - same in, same out - just passing through a wider \(d_\text{ff}\) in the middle.

📌  Note:  LayerNorm and the residual additions don’t change shape either - everything stays \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\). That’s the whole point: because every sublayer returns \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\), a full encoder (or decoder) block takes \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\) in and hands \(n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}\) out - which is exactly what lets us stack \(N\) of them.

6. Cross-Attention
Cross-attention (in the decoder) is the same process as multi-head self attention, but the two sides’ lengths differ. The query comes from the decoder’s sequence (length \(n_\text{out}\)), while the keys and values come from the encoder output (length \(n_\text{seq}\)): \[
Q = n_\text{out} \times d_\text{model} \qquad K, V = n_\text{seq} \times d_\text{model}
\] So the attention matrix is rectangular, not square: \[
A = Q K^T = n_\text{out} \times n_\text{seq}
\] (each decoder position attending over every encoder position). After softmax and \(\times V\): \[
O = n_\text{out} \times d_\text{model}
\] So this attention’s score matrix isn’t square - it aligns a length-\(n_\text{out}\) sequence against a length-\(n_\text{seq}\) one.
(Masked self-attention, by contrast, keeps the square shape - the mask just zeros the upper triangle before the softmax, changing the values, not the dimensions, so we won’t re-cover it here, it’s the same.)
7. The Output (Prediction) Layer
Finally, the decoder’s output is projected from \(d_\text{model}\) out to the full vocabulary, with \(W_\text{out} = d_\text{model} \times n_\text{vocab}\): \[
\text{logits} = X_\text{out}\,W_\text{out} = n_\text{out} \times n_\text{vocab}
\] A softmax over the vocabulary dimension turns each row into a probability distribution over the \(n_\text{vocab}\) possible next tokens. (At generation time we usually only need the last row, \(1 \times n_\text{vocab}\))
So, dimensionally, the whole forward pass is \(n_\text{seq}\) (or \(n_\text{out}\)) \(\times\, d_\text{model}\) everywhere inside, widening to \(d_\text{ff}\) within each FFN, and finally fanning out to \(n_\text{vocab}\) at the very end.
Take me back to the main tutorial



In Section 1.2 we ran BPE by merging characters. And in that section, we saw that we needed a special <unk> token to accommodate anything that wasn’t a known letter from our vocabulary. You can imagine, real text scraped from the internet would have the opportunity to have tons of things represented by an <unk>, especially if we didn’t have an ideal, complete, representative corpus to begin with.
But as we’ve also discussed, there’s nothing really special about letters other than that they’re the symbols of which words are comprised. But are letters really the best symbols you can use to represent words? Well, just words, maybe, but real life text is full of all sorts of non-word things.
Real tokenizers choose a different symbol to represent words and other text - bytes. It’s the reason they can handle emojis, Chinese characters, code snippets, or any random string of pure garbage, all without ever needing to actually rely on that <unk>.


Everything on a computer is ultimately stored as numbers, and text is no exception. The system for deciding which numbers represent which characters is called Unicode - a giant, agreed-upon table that assigns a unique number to essentially every character in every writing system humans use: the English alphabet, every other alphabet, mathematical symbols, emojis. Unicode just assigns an ID per character - say, 界 is number 30028, 🙂 is number 128578, and so on - for ~150,000 characters and counting.
It’s sort of like starting with a 150,000-character alphabet. Which is useful, but very extensive and large numbers are difficult to store. That’s where UTF-8 comes in. It’s the standard way of writing Unicode characters as sequences of bytes. A single byte is a single value from 0 to 255 that takes up the smallest unit of memory on a computer. Since 0 to 255 isn’t enough to hold all of the different Unicode options, UTF-8 uses a variable number of bytes per character: the common ones (ordinary English letters) take a single byte, while rarer characters take two, three, or four. Let’s see how a few words actually get encoded:

for s in ["hi", "café", "世界", "🙂"]:
    b = s.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{s!r:8} -> {len(b)} bytes -> {list(b)}")

'hi'     -> 2 bytes -> [104, 105]
'café'   -> 5 bytes -> [99, 97, 102, 195, 169]
'世界'     -> 6 bytes -> [228, 184, 150, 231, 149, 140]
'🙂'      -> 4 bytes -> [240, 159, 153, 130]


So “hi” is 2 bytes, 2 letters, while an emoji takes 4 bytes for the single character.
But in this way, we’ve actually reduced our “alphabet” to 256. The unit of the “letter” or “character” is now no longer the smallest unit - some will take more than 1 byte to represent, but everything can be represented by the set of numbers between 0 and 255. Everything.
And every possible new thing, not even in our dictionary, can be represented by a series of bytes. With how we did things in Section 1.2, having the vocabulary contain all of the individual letters means some non-real word like “blacapeptopotamus” could still be represented, at worst by all of its letters. With bytes, everything that can be typed into a computer can be represented by bytes - the <unk> is all but completely unnecessary.



The nice thing is that it doesn’t! Everything about how we worked through BPE works exactly the same. You count adjacent pairs, glue the most frequent, repeat. It’s just that the starting alphabet is 256 byte-values instead of all of the letters. Frequent byte-sequences get merged into single tokens exactly as frequent character-sequences did - so naturally multiple bytes in a row that make up a single letter probably get merged early on. Common English words still likely build up as whole tokens (their byte sequences are everywhere in the corpus). And other common byte sequences, like a very common emoji, might get merged into a single token too. The algorithm is completely indifferent to what a byte represents, it works just the same.
For that reason - I’ll skip reworking the example here over bytes. It’s not really intuitive to watch bytes connect, or build up a vocabulary and really it all does come together the same way. The intuition is still best developed using an example like we did in Section 1.2.



Two final little things worth noting on the BPE discussion (one specific to bytes and one not), because some real model behaviors can be explained by tokenizing this way.
Consequence 1 is general to tokenization. Tokens are usually bigger than letters. So a word like “strawberry” won’t be treated as ten letters - BPE will merge it into a couple of chunky tokens, maybe straw + berry. Each of those is a single ID pointing to a single learned vector. The token for berry relates inherently not at all to the tokens for b, e, r, or y. So the famous case, asking “how many r’s in strawberry?”, is something models will be bad at, for a reason coming all the way from how they understand words at all. Being able to do this task must come from specifically memorizing that berry contains two r’s, and straw contains one. This can be held in the embedding of the tokens “straw” and “berry” themselves, but it’s NOT going to come from knowing to divide either component back down into its letters. Models are famously so bad at spelling and letter-counting because all access to that level of word construction is really gone unless it gets baked back into the embedding during training.
Consequence 2 does come from specifically using bytes, and it’s that doing BPE on bytes can mean you end up with tokens that contain sub-characters. Take ‘🙂’ -> [240, 159, 153, 130]. BPE could merge just the first two of those bytes into a unit, and leave the other two. A token can end up as a fragment of a single character - a couple of bytes that don’t complete any single letter on their own. Literally, half an emoji. And this can complicate things at decode time, because the model can now also theoretically output half of an emoji… which is invalid UTF-8 that can’t be turned back into anything at all (UTF-8 is constructed smartly enough that two bytes of what was a 4-byte string simply map to nothing at all). In practice, this really won’t happen, the model won’t learn to print out the first half of 🙂 without the second half. But if it gets cut off for some reason, reaches an output limit before it could finish, we can end up with a � after decoding - the universal symbol for “I don’t know what those bytes are”.
So, the mismatch between tokens and characters can run in both directions. Sometimes a token can encompass many letters and lose sight of what those letters were, and sometimes a single character gets split in half. Either way, the clean “characters” we take for granted are not the units the model actually operates on. Fortunately, both lead to just small quirks, not critical failures.



In your study of modern architectures, you may find that tokenizers use some common alternates to BPE. They all share the same goal of building a vocabulary of common subword pieces, but they differ in the exact rules for how to choose which pieces to form. We won’t cover these in depth, but here are some of the common ones you might see, and what’s different.
WordPiece (used by BERT). This is a common alternate that’s very close to BPE. It also merges pairs, but instead of merging the most frequent pair, it merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training text. In practice that means scoring each candidate pair by roughly: \[
\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\,\text{count}(b)}
\] and favoring pairs that co-occur more than their individual frequencies would predict rather than pairs that are merely frequent. It also tokenizes new words a bit differently. Instead of replaying merges in order (as we did), it greedily takes the longest vocabulary piece that matches at each step (which we actually discussed as a potential way to tokenize in the main tutorial). WordPiece also marks pieces that continue a word with a ## prefix, so “playing” becomes play + ##ing.
Unigram / SentencePiece (used by T5, mBART, and many multilingual models). This employs a truly different algorithm, in that rather than building up by merging small pieces, it starts with a large candidate vocabulary and prunes down by repeatedly removing the tokens that “don’t matter” in a probabilistic model of the text - basically asking, “if I removed this piece, could I still come up with essentially the entire corpus anyway?”. It’s also probabilistic at tokenization time - a word can have several valid segmentations, each with a probability. In normal use, it just takes the single most likely one (so it’s used deterministically), but it can sample among the alternatives, for instance, to add variety during training. (One note: “SentencePiece” is technically the library that usually runs this, but it can also run BPE.)
So how does a team building a real model pick one? Why would someone use BPE vs WordPiece? It really is less about quality, as most of these schemes have been shown to perform pretty similarly, and more about some practical implications.

The biggest factor is language coverage. Approaches like SentencePiece run on raw text with no assumptions about spaces, which matters enormously for languages like Chinese, Japanese, and Thai that don’t separate words with spaces, so multilingual models tend to favor it.
Another factor is robustness. Byte-level fallback (like we have with byte-level BPE) guarantees anything can always be encoded and represented, with truly no unknowns.
Finally, there’s of course the very practical consideration of ecosystem. The tokenizer is a fundamental choice to the model that can’t be changed, so teams often just inherit whatever tooling they already have and whatever the models they build on have already used.

But really, the above considerations are fairly small, and tweaks can help accommodate them, so truly all of the above choices for algorithm here will work well. In modern times, the choice is converging, and most recent frontier models have landed on using byte-level BPE with large (100k+) vocabularies.




As we saw in the positional encoding section, the cosine similarity between all consecutive positional encoding vectors is exactly the same value: approximately 0.9691 (for \(d_\text{model}=100\)). The similarity between positions 1↔︎2 is identical to 200↔︎201.
This isn’t a coincidence, and it hints at a deep structural property of sinusoidal encodings. Let’s work through why this happens mathematically, and then uncover the more fundamental property underneath - the one the transformer actually exploits.


Recall that a positional encoding vector for position \(pos\) has \(d_\text{model}\) entries, arranged in sin/cos pairs. For frequency index \(j\) (where \(j = 0, 1, ..., \frac{d_\text{model}}{2} - 1\)):
\[\text{Column } 2j: \quad \sin\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right), \qquad \text{Column } 2j+1: \quad \cos\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\]
where \(\omega_j = 10000^{2j/d_\text{model}}\) sets the scale of that frequency-specific band (whose wavelength is \(2\pi\omega_j\)).
So we can think of each PE vector as \(d_\text{model}/2\) pairs of (sin, cos) at different frequencies:
\[PE(pos) = \left[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_0}\right),\ \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_0}\right),\ \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_1}\right),\ \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_1}\right),\ \ldots\right]\]
Step 1: The Norm is Constant
The squared norm of any PE vector is:
\[\|PE(pos)\|^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \left[\sin^2\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos^2\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\right]\]
By the Pythagorean identity (\(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\)), every term in the sum equals 1:
\[\|PE(pos)\|^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} 1 = \frac{d_\text{model}}{2}\]
Therefore:
\[\|PE(pos)\| = \sqrt{\frac{d_\text{model}}{2}} \quad \text{for all } pos\]
Every positional encoding vector has exactly the same length, regardless of position. This already tells us something: positions are distinguished purely by direction, not magnitude. They all live on the surface of a hypersphere of radius \(\sqrt{d_\text{model}/2}\).
Step 2: The Dot Product Depends Only on the Offset
Now, consider the dot product between two PE vectors at positions \(pos\) and \(pos + k\) (for any offset \(k\)):
\[PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k) = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \left[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\right]\]
The cosine difference identity states:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
So if \(\alpha = \frac{pos}{\omega_j}\) and \(\beta = \frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\), each pair collapses:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j} - \frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{-k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
Since \(\cos\) is an even function (\(\cos(-x) = \cos(x)\)):
\[PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k) = \sum_{j=0}^{d/2-1} \cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
The absolute position \(pos\) has completely cancelled out. The dot product depends only on the offset \(k\).
Step 3: Therefore, Cosine Similarity is Constant at Fixed Offset
Cosine similarity is defined as:
\[\text{CosSim}(PE(pos),\ PE(pos+k)) = \frac{PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos+k)}{\|PE(pos)\| \cdot \|PE(pos+k)\|}\]
We’ve shown:

The numerator = \(\sum_{j} \cos(k/\omega_j)\), which depends only on \(k\)
The denominator = \(\sqrt{d/2} \cdot \sqrt{d/2} = d/2\), which is the same for all positions

So:
\[\boxed{\text{CosSim}(PE(pos),\ PE(pos+k)) = \frac{1}{d_\text{model}/2}\sum_{j=0}^{d_\text{model}/2-1} \cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) \quad \text{for all } pos}\]
This is a constant that depends only on the offset \(k\) and the model hyperparameters (\(d_\text{model}\) and the base 10000).



For our case (\(d_\text{model} = 100\), \(k = 1\)):
\[\text{CosSim} = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{j=0}^{49} \cos\!\left(\frac{1}{10000^{2j/100}}\right) = 0.969108...\]
We can verify this in code:

d_model = 100
k = 1
def cosine_sim(d_model, k):
    return sum(np.cos(k / (10000 ** (2*j / d_model))) for j in range(d_model // 2)) / (d_model / 2)

print(f"Predicted: {cosine_sim(d_model, k)}")

Predicted: 0.9691077369162043


This matches the flat line in our cosine similarity plot exactly. Of course, the usefulness of this is much more than just the fact that two neighboring positions have the exact same offset. The usefulness is that any two positions separated by an offset k have the same value as any other two positions separated by that same k.



Let’s talk about why this really happens. We’ve proven that cosine similarity is constant at fixed offset. But cosine similarity is a scalar summary - it collapses the relationship between two 100-dimensional vectors down to a single number. And the model doesn’t actually compute cosine similarities between PE vectors - it operates on the full vectors through learned linear projections. So cosine similarities being the same is not a useful property in and of itself. Rather, it’s a visible symptom of something deeper: shifting position by a fixed offset \(k\) is a rotation in embedding space.
In their paper, Vaswani et al. state a much more generalized property of sinusoidal positional encodings:

“We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset \(k\), \(PE_{pos+k}\) can be represented as a linear function of \(PE_{pos}\).”

If that doesn’t make immediate intuitive sense to you - it didn’t to me, either. So let’s dig into what exactly they meant, and why that leads to the downstream property we saw.
What This Means
Consider a single frequency band \(j\), which contributes a (sin, cos) pair to the PE vector. When we move from position \(pos\) to position \(pos + k\), these two entries transform as:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \longrightarrow \sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\] \[\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \longrightarrow \cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
Applying the trigonometric addition formulas:
\[\sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) + \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
\[\cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right) - \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{k}{\omega_j}\right)\]
This is a matrix equation:
\[\begin{bmatrix} \sin\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) \\[4pt] \cos\!\left(\frac{pos+k}{\omega_j}\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(k/\omega_j) & \sin(k/\omega_j) \\ -\sin(k/\omega_j) & \cos(k/\omega_j) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \\[4pt] \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{\omega_j}\right) \end{bmatrix}\]
That transformation matrix is a 2D rotation matrix \(R_j(k)\), rotating by an angle of \(k/\omega_j\) radians. A rotation matrix is a transformation that changes the direction a vector points without changing its length. This is consistent with what we showed earlier, that all positional encoding vectors have the same norm. They’re distinguished purely by direction, and moving between positions is just a rotation. Since each frequency band transforms independently, the full PE vector transforms as:
\[PE(pos + k) = M_k \cdot PE(pos)\]
where \(M_k\) is a block-diagonal matrix:
\[M_k = \begin{bmatrix} R_0(k) & & & \\ & R_1(k) & & \\ & & \ddots & \\ & & & R_{d/2-1}(k) \end{bmatrix}\]
Each 2×2 block rotates its frequency band by an angle that depends on \(k\) and that band’s wavelength (\(2\pi\omega_j\)), but is completely independent of \(pos\). Shifting by \(k\) positions is a fixed linear transformation, regardless of where you start.

So cosine similarity is constant because rotations preserve geometry. A rotation doesn’t stretch, shrink, or distort vectors. It preserves all norms and all angles. So the angle between \(PE(pos)\) and \(PE(pos+k)\) is determined entirely by the rotation \(M_k\) that connects them, which depends only on \(k\). Cosine similarity measures the cosine of that angle, hence it’s constant. That is an outcome of how rotational transformations operate.




This rotational property is really what Vaswani et al. were referring to. Here’s why it’s so important. The attention mechanism computes:
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]
where \(Q = XW_Q\) and \(K = XW_K\) are linear projections of the input. If the input \(X\) includes positional encodings, then the attention score between positions \(pos_a\) and \(pos_b\) involves, among other things, the interaction between \(PE(pos_a)\) and \(PE(pos_b)\) through these learned weight matrices.
Suppose the model needs to learn “attend to the word 3 positions back.” That means it needs the attention score to be high when \(pos_a - pos_b = 3\). Since:
\[PE(pos_a) = M_3 \cdot PE(pos_b)\]
The relationship between the two PE vectors is captured entirely by the fixed matrix \(M_3\). The model’s learned projections \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) can compose with \(M_3\) through ordinary matrix multiplication, so the same \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) that detect “3 positions back” at position 10 will automatically detect “3 positions back” at position 200. The model learns this pattern once and then, (in theory), it could generalize everywhere.
If the positional encoding didn’t have this rotation structure and moving by \(k\) positions involved a different transformation depending on where you started, then the model’s fixed \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) couldn’t capture relative position as a general concept. It would need to learn separate attention patterns for every absolute position, which scales terribly with sequence length.
Ok, one more thing though. Because the keen eye might have noticed - we DO have fixed cosine similarities between fixed positions k, great. And typically distinct cosine similarities for any k. And we have rotational transformations as a general property.
But we do not have monotonically decreasing cosine similarities for increasing k, and we made a statement earlier that we want close positions to have similar embeddings as one another. So, does that matter?

ks = np.arange(1,101,1)
def cosine_sim(d_model, k):
    return sum(np.cos(k / (10000 ** (2*j / d_model))) for j in range(d_model // 2)) / (d_model / 2)

cossims = [cosine_sim(d_model, k) for k in ks]

plt.scatter(ks, cossims); plt.show()








Short answer, not totally, but a little. We know that cosine similarity is a lossy scalar summary of a rich high-dimensional relationship - so the number itself isn’t important.
BUT… it is a useful property that nearby positional encodings are similar, because it can help the model learn relationships more easily. This is actually up to that choice of frequency - the “10000” that we sort of shrugged off before.
In truth, sinusoidal positional encodings have been largely replaced in modern transformers by methods like Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), which apply the same frequency-based rotation idea inside the attention mechanism rather than as an additive encoding. Because, as it turns out, while the rotational properties of sinusoidal encodings are present, the model can have issues fully exploiting them.
